text: For two pairs, repeatedly differentiate combinations required to remain constant when ε is constant, solve the resulting algebraic constraints, and expand the velocity equations to linear order around the listed solutions.

Reduce the homogeneous equations to dimensionless saxion and axion velocities, derive the evolution of ε, and impose consistency with both velocity equations rather than using dε/dt=0 alone. Study nearby trajectories through linearized component equations and phase-plane sign regions.

Reduce each higher-order problem to coupled elliptic equations for the traceless spatial metric deformation and Z^(n−1). Vector and tensor spherical harmonics diagonalize the relevant operators, converting possible nontrivial solutions into algebraic resonance conditions.

Fix the residual horizon cross-section gauge by setting the first metric deformation's trace to the constant 2C, using Poisson's equation on S². Einstein–Maxwell constraints algebraically determine remaining components from the metric deformation and Maxwell one-form.

Use Gaussian null coordinates and the scaling (v,ρ,x)→(v/ε,ερ,x) to separate near-horizon data from transverse derivatives. Analytic Taylor expansion and induction then connect uniqueness at every transverse order to the local spacetime.

Linearize the beta functions at the fixed point and use stability eigenvectors to construct tangent and normal directions. Their normal linear constraints supply local boundary data for the generating functions defining the UV-critical surface.

Approximate implicit generating functions by a finite basis and impose the transport equation at collocation points. Fix F at the fixed point to zero and match its first derivatives to the linear constraints, excluding the trivial solution. Suggested bases include Chebyshev polynomials and radial basis functions.

The two-coupling example compares shooting, explicit power series of orders 10–15, and an implicit spectral solution using 500 multivariate Cauchy distributions on a regular lattice centered on the fixed point. These are author-reported comparisons.

Study fixed points using the Jacobian and center-manifold theory because a zero eigenvalue prevents a linear stability conclusion. Numerical phase-space trajectories estimate inflationary duration and the evolution of H, b and ḃ.

Rewrite the scalar Friedmann–Klein–Gordon equations using expansion-normalized variables x=κḃ/(√6H), y=κ√V/(√3H). For positive V and a single scalar, x²+y²=1 and y≥0, allowing x=cosφ, y=sinφ and a two-dimensional autonomous system.

Second-quantize weak GW helicities through a complex-scalar mode description, compute the quadratic anomaly expectation value with a physical momentum cutoff, and use late-stiff Bessel-mode asymptotics or inflationary subhorizon plane waves.

Estimate gonion masses through D6 Fayet–Iliopoulos terms and elementary D4-string tensions, obtaining proposed lower and upper bounds. Separately sum tower contributions to one-loop kinetic terms up to the species cutoff.

Combine worldsheet-disc Yukawas, toroidal Γ-function matter metrics, and N=1 supergravity normalization Y_ijk = e^(K/2) W_ijk/(K_ii K_jj K_kk)^(1/2). General-Calabi–Yau expressions are motivated through locality of intersection data.

For the restricted sourced-flux Ansatz, inspect an off-diagonal Einstein equation. Metric and dilaton terms have Cartesian parity xp−1xp+1, while the cross-source flux term has parity xpxp+2; equality for all coordinates forces both sides to vanish separately.

For generic invariant fluxes, impose vanishing gravitino and dilatino variations on eight independent projected spinors. Combine the resulting first-order equations with flux closure and equality of mixed warp-factor derivatives. The detailed example is p=6; the authors report repeating the analysis for p=1,…,5.

Solve the displayed sourced Bianchi identity by adding each source's flat-transverse-space field strength and an arbitrary closed contribution. The absence of warp factors in this equation permits the source-field superposition, without implying superposition of solutions to Einstein's equations.

Expand the metric and electric potentials around the two-charge Reissner–Nordström solution to first order in higher-derivative coefficients. Determine the extremal mass and horizon shift by perturbatively imposing f(rH)=f′(rH)=0.
Use the charged worldline action, proper-time normalization, and conserved Killing energy to obtain V±=qΦ+pΨ±m√f. Allowed motion requires E≥V+, giving the necessary horizon condition E≥qΦ(rH)+pΨ(rH).

Expand Mext(Q+q,P+p) to first order in particle charges and compare the resulting overcharging threshold with the corrected horizon potentials. Appendix B tracks metric field redefinitions, coupling transformations, and corresponding worldline corrections.

Apply perturbative metric field redefinitions, supplemented by gauge-field redefinitions in supergravity, to obtain a Weyl-based action with renormalized two-derivative parameters; evaluate it on the uncorrected black-hole solution.

Use Iren = βG in the grand canonical ensemble. Obtain entropy, electric charge and angular momenta by differentiating G with respect to their conjugate potentials, and reconstruct mass through the thermodynamic relation.

Numerical tests integrate the equal-rotation perturbation equations from the extremal horizon, tune away an asymptotic logarithmic mode, extract charges using generalized AMD expressions, and compare mass corrections at fixed angular momentum.

The note compares known string/M-theory descriptions and uses the heterotic interval construction to propose an alternative implementation of the dark-dimension scenario. It does not supply an explicit compactification reproducing the Standard Model.

For possible gravitational discrimination, the author sums Yukawa contributions from graviton KK excitations and compares their distance asymptotics. A separate qualitative cosmological argument uses G_N ∼ G₅/ρ and L ∼ ρ⁻⁴ to discuss time variation; the extracted derivative display is disrupted.

Numerically integrate the Bogoliubov equations to evaluate ⟨N_n,k⟩=|β_n,k|². For the constant-field example, compare with the usual Schwinger estimate; use numerical oscillatory examples to illustrate repeated production and resonance.

KK-decompose the charged scalar, canonically quantize each mode, and solve f̈_n,k+[k²+M_n²(t)]f_n,k=0 using time-dependent Bogoliubov coefficients with |α|²−|β|²=1. The chosen initial adiabatic vacuum has α=1 and β=0.

For backreaction, couple ζ_c to a renormalized scalar two-point function/current. Subtract the vacuum contribution, average away a rapidly oscillating term, and approximate the momentum integral on a small lattice while retaining a finite set of KK modes.

Decouple a restricted component sector and use Lommel's differential-equation form to obtain Bessel functions. Formal imaginary-mass continuation yields modified Bessel functions; imposing the stated Majorana conditions produces Whittaker-type equations.
Choose a Newman-Penrose null tetrad, compute spin coefficients and directional derivatives, and separate the spinor components into z-dependent functions times exp(iωt+ip1x+ip2y).
Use cyclic t,x,y coordinates in the geodesic Lagrangian to derive conserved quantities and a radial equation ż² = ξ²z⁴−z². The appendix obtains a minimum z0 = 1/ξ for the trajectory considered.

Reviewed perturbative methods include Feynman diagrams, dimensional regularization and higher-curvature counterterms. Long-distance information is isolated through nonanalytic contributions, including logarithmic quantum terms and square-root terms associated with classical corrections.

The account uses Wilsonian floating cutoffs and renormalization-group trajectories: couplings depend on the cutoff while physical quantities remain cutoff independent. Gravitational effective actions are organized as the Einstein–Hilbert term followed by an infinite higher-derivative expansion.

Reviewed string methods include the superstring S-matrix, genus expansions and hyperelliptic analysis of a two-loop four-graviton amplitude for s → ∞ and t → 0. Earlier authors also calculated QFT diagrams to compare string and field-theory corrections qualitatively.

The bilayer-inspired covariant prescription divides a Cauchy slice into L, E and R regions. In each region, candidate codimension-two surfaces must satisfy regional homology and belong to compatible Cauchy slices. The generalized entropy uses the sum of their areas divided by 4Gℏ plus the semiclassical entropy of the UNION of the associated bulk regions, followed by joint extremization and minimization. It does not sum three independent bulk entropies.

The entanglement wedge is the union of the three regional domains of dependence. Where ordinary stationary-area surfaces are absent, the paper enlarges the extremization problem with Lagrange multipliers enforcing regional inequalities; constrained solutions on causal-diamond boundaries are admitted, and the least-area candidate is selected.

Tensor reductions use SO(D−2) little-group Young diagrams, removal of at most one box per column per circle, columnwise Hodge duality, and self-duality identifications. Appendix A gives the authors' combinatorial count Ngrav(k,l) = (k−1)!/[(l−1)!(k−l)!] for the initially self-dual [k,l] representations considered there, starting in D_initial=2k+2 and reduced on T^(k−1) to D_final=k+3. The count relies on the initial self-duality projection to prevent intervening dual-graviton contributions.

The central argument uses Poincaré representations and a translation quotient: retain flat-space states invariant under x5 → x5 + 2πR, obtaining p5 = n/R. It requires only some circle states to arise this way, not a complete construction of the compactified Hilbert space.

Compare entropies at fixed mass and free energies at fixed temperature; estimate a transition shift by matching R4-corrected entropies. Appendix A analyzes gravitational loop thresholds with μ set by inverse black-hole radius.

Define the species scale by comparing generic higher-curvature terms with the Einstein term at μ=Λs, up to constants. Supersymmetrically protected couplings provide examples; the reviewed type IIA R4 coefficient receives tree-level and one-loop contributions only.

A minisuperspace path integral uses ds²=(N²/q)dt²+q dΩ₃², constant lapse N, Dirichlet endpoint sizes, and integration over the initial brane size q₀. Saddle-point evaluation selects the smaller-N² branches, with N>0 for Hartle-Hawking and N<0 for Linde/Vilenkin. WKB matching to q₁>ℓ_dS² imposes reality for HH or an outgoing wave for LV.

The geometric calculation evaluates the bulk and boundary instanton actions. A half-instanton is joined at its equator to the expanding Lorentzian de Sitter solution using continuation at the turning point; the authors explicitly distinguish this local continuation from a global continuation of the entire bounded geometry.

Photon bounds are translated from 4D to 5D by assuming comparable limits on PBH mass density at fixed Hawking temperature. The mappings are T_H,4D≈(M/10^16 g)^−1 MeV and T_H,5D≈(M/10^12 g)^−1/2 MeV. Thus the quoted f_PBH≲5×10^−5 bound at 10^16 g in 4D is mapped to approximately 10^12 g in 5D.

The phenomenology combines survival to the age of the universe with direct photon and positron-annihilation emission constraints, including Galactic line-of-sight intensity for an NFW profile. The paper identifies Galactic-center diffuse gamma emission as the strongest and most solid of its adopted photon constraints.

The evaporation review uses d-dimensional relations T_H=(d−3)/(4πr_s) and S_BH=4πM_BH r_s/(d−2). Approximate emission rates use greybody factors normalized to the effective area seen by brane fields: Γ₀=1, Γ₁/₂≈2/3 and Γ₁≈1/4. Species counts include particles with masses much below T_H.

A tree-level three-point string-amplitude calculation obtains Dμχ = ∂μχ + iβ Bτμχ/(2πα′) + iπ Aμχ/β. The paper emphasizes that these imaginary couplings determine the Euclidean reality properties of rotation.

Scaling reduces the leading condensate/radion equations to ∇̂²χ̂ ≈ (ζ+δâ)χ̂ and ∇̂²δâ ≈ 4π|χ̂|². Spectral Galerkin expansions use Legendre functions and Wigner 3-j symbols, followed by radial collocation and Newton-Raphson relaxation.

Large-|mϕ| analysis approximates the far potential by −1/r̂ and solves a Coulomb-type equation with regularity and decay conditions. Thermodynamic quantities are extracted from ADM falloffs and action derivatives at fixed angular velocity and winding chemical potential.
Uses explicit toroidal tadpole equations and a quoted Cauchy–Schwarz bound on Calabi–Yau D7 flux quanta to constrain flux-enhanced axion–photon couplings.

Expands the DBI determinant, canonically normalizes the gauge field, and dimensionally reduces RR kinetic terms and D-brane Chern–Simons couplings to relate gauge coupling, axion decay constant and internal flux.
Reviews helicity-mode quantization in an approximately de Sitter background, Whittaker-function solutions and estimates of electric/magnetic correlators as functions of the instability parameter ξ.

Gluing is specified by Israel junction conditions: matching induced metrics and an extrinsic-curvature jump related to the sum of brane tensions. Repeated gluing supplies the proposed connected geometries.
Uses warped dimensional reduction and imported gravity-localization results, with 1/G(d−1)=(1/Gd)∫dω exp[(d−3)A(ω)], to motivate equality of bulk-wedge and lower-dimensional gravitational actions.
Computes bulk Ricci tensors/scalars in dimensions d=3,4,5,6 and applies Einstein equations. Evaluates extrinsic curvature and solves the brane Neumann condition for tension.

Extend the Green–Gutperle–Vanhove one-loop four-graviton Schwinger integral from Kaluza–Klein states to wrapped transverse brane bound states, inserting their 1/2-BPS constraints and excluding the all-zero charge contribution.

Introduce a real UV cutoff ε>0, integrate, minimally subtract divergent terms, and use ζ-function regularization for infinite sums. Poisson resummation and modified-Bessel integral representations reorganize perturbative and instanton contributions.

Solve integer BPS constraints through linear Diophantine equations, gcd factorizations and coprime charge sectors. Regularized coprime sums and binomial cancellations are essential to obtaining the constant contributions.

Construct frozen duals by contracting base curves to match tensor counts, replacing selected I* fibers by frozen assignments, and assigning gauge divisors using embedding indices. Apply the imported frozen Green–Schwarz rule K→K+F.

Fuse LST sectors by gauging a common flavor algebra and adding a tensor multiplet. Use gravitational anomalies, toric hypersurface constructions and Hodge numbers to test the resulting compact models.

Use the weakly coupled type I D5/D9 orientifold frame, imposing Chan–Paton invariance under orientifold and orbifold generators. Projective group relations and discrete phase choices distinguish vector structure from its absence.

Extract the small-r expansion of the thermal free energy. Free-field calculations use modified Bessel functions, polylogarithms and zeta regularization; spatial-channel calculations subtract a continuum momentum integral from a discrete sum.

For integrable 2D theories, use the TBA bulk term and factorized S-matrices. For QCD, fit converted lattice pressure data with constant, r² and r⁴ terms; compare affine Toda weak coupling with a semiclassical potential minimum.

Use binned Poisson statistics with profiled signal/background normalization pulls and sum uncorrelated channel contributions. Constraints compare standard-oscillation truth with nonzero-potential tests; discovery reverses that construction. Pairwise symmetry tests use competing potential textures. Quoted significances assume one degree of freedom.

Numerically diagonalize the modified three-flavor Hamiltonian using GLoBES and a modified snu library. Simulate electron appearance and muon disappearance in both beam modes, including reconstructed-energy binning, backgrounds and wrong-sign signal contamination.

Sum Yukawa potentials from local and distant matter reservoirs, weighted by fermion charges. Compute electron contributions explicitly and rescale by proton/neutron abundances; subsequently translate potential sensitivity into effective coupling versus mediator mass.

Self-shadow refinement compares independently advanced adjacent resolutions through Δϕcf = |ϕcoarse−ϕfine| before synchronization. A temporary coarser shadow level supplies estimates for the base mesh. Threshold-based tagging, buffers and optional problem-specific tagging determine refinement.

Recursive time subcycling advances coarse levels first, then fine levels. Fine ghost cells use spatial and temporal interpolation from coarse states; synchronized fine data overwrite covered coarse cells by averaging. Finite-difference operators and several RK/RKN integrators are supplied.

Gravitational waves use auxiliary tensor fields with project-specific sourced evolution equations, followed by a lattice transverse-traceless projection. The interface supplies six symmetric tensor components and their momenta, together with automatic unbinned spectral output.

Model analysis uses Taylor expansion in a fundamental flux step, Euler identities for homogeneous potentials, naive dimensional analysis for operator towers, and cross-polytope shell counting for the asymptotically linear DBI landscape.

Semiclassical decay is treated using O(4)-symmetric Euclidean instantons, with Γ/Vol∼exp(−B/ℏ) and B=SE(instanton)−SE(parent). Only configurations with nonnegative membrane tension and finite tunnelling exponent are retained.

Legendre dualization replaces the four-form function by Lf(ϕ). Neumann conditions are imposed on three-forms and Dirichlet conditions on the metric and dual scalars; boundary terms and Israel junction conditions determine the bubble matching.

Separate the scalar into e^(−iωt)R(r)Yℓm and transform the radial equation into Schrödinger form. The asymptotic coefficient αinf=Mext(m²−2ω²)+2Qqω is used to diagnose candidate trapping wells; a well alone is explicitly insufficient to establish a bound state.

Chebyshev spectral calculations compactify the radius with x=(r−r+)/r, factor out singular boundary behaviour, and discretize the remaining equation. Grid convergence and comparison with shooting are used by the authors to assess the exceptionally small imaginary frequencies.

Shooting integrates high-order local series outward from the horizon and inward from large radius. Discrete complex frequencies are selected by matching logarithmic derivatives, equivalently imposing a vanishing Wronskian.

Two-point clustering is measured using fiducial comoving coordinates and Alcock–Paczynski scaling. Cosmological inference uses approximately Gaussian BAO-distance likelihoods; statistical and systematic uncertainties are combined in quadrature.

Galaxy/quasar catalogs were blinded through redshift and weight changes; Lyα correlations received an additive BAO-peak shift. Unblinding followed pipeline finalization, systematic budgeting and prescribed validation tests.
Bayesian inference uses CAMB and Cobaya Metropolis–Hastings sampling. Four chains are stopped at R−1 < 0.01, with an additional effective-sample-size requirement of approximately 1,000 or more.

Perturb the Einstein–Cartan equations using tensor harmonics. Numerically evolve the simplified tensor equation through prescribed radiation- and matter-dominated eras, illustrating wave numbers k = 5 and 15.
Describe perturbations through ladder operators and Bogoliubov transformations. Replace the asymptotic Bunch–Davies initialization by a finite-time vacuum prescription at physical momentum p = Λ.

Expand the inflaton action to quadratic order in δϕ = f/a, introduce the Einstein–Cartan background relation into its effective mass term, and Fourier-expand to obtain a modified scalar mode equation. Analyze limiting Bessel solutions and solve the full equation numerically.

Read mirror complete-intersection degrees and ambient weights from factorial coefficients of fundamental periods. Analyze boundary phases through semisimple/unipotent monodromy decomposition, asymptotic periods and limiting mixed Hodge structures.

Construct Frobenius series order by order and numerically match periods and derivatives in overlapping patches. Matching the resulting monodromies to the prescribed integral matrices fixes the period frame; the paper also relates this construction to a K-theory basis.

Parametrize integral LCS and conifold monodromies, determine M∞=(M0MC)^−1, and enumerate integer parameters by requiring quasi-unipotence. Allowed finite orders and nilpotency degrees are scanned; eigenvalues then determine local exponents and the fifth-order hypergeometric Picard–Fuchs operator.

GT matrix-model planar resolvent: A-cycle integrals determine cut endpoints and B-cycle integrals determine free-energy derivatives. Numerical saddle solutions and N→∞ extrapolation test subleading coefficients.
Construct c-function ansätze whose derivatives follow from the null energy condition; independently minimize the Jacobson–Myers entropy functional for wrapped entangling surfaces.

Perturbative field redefinitions, leading equations of motion and integration by parts simplify higher-derivative actions. Truncation consistency is tested through reduced bosonic equations and discarded gaugino variations.

For singular line and surface currents, the argument uses magnetic scalar potentials, Ampère circulation and Boltzmann distributions. Potential discontinuities imply arbitrary density discontinuities or pressure jumps incompatible with the proposed mechanical equilibrium.

The authors combine Euler and continuity equations, generalized Maxwell equations, Ohm's law and Onnes-type equations of state. Under stationary zero-flow equilibrium, pressure forces become gradients; taking their curl conflicts with Ampère's law wherever the test electric current is nonzero.

A second-quantized toy calculation evaluates a Grassmann determinant and sums antiperiodic Matsubara modes. It places an independent two-dimensional canonical massive fermion at each four-dimensional point, with A_tau=mu(x) and no kinetic terms along those four directions.

Mellin-Barnes representations connect classical grand potentials to periods. For the displayed non-compact example, the geometric contour includes the zero and negative poles: the zero pole produces polynomial terms and negative poles produce exponentials; the orbifold contour instead encloses strictly positive poles.

Classical state counting uses n(E)=area{H<=E}/(2*pi*hbar). In the high-energy tropical limit, the boundary becomes linear and the normalized phase-space area becomes the area AB of the dual toric polygon.

Slow-roll expressions relate CMB observables to model parameters. Allowed regions impose field ordering, positive Kähler and fermion kinetic terms, and nontachyonic soft scalar masses. Fermion masses are obtained in superunitary gauge by eliminating the goldstino combination.

Vacuum analysis expands jointly in small inflaton radius ρ and deformation δ, first locating waterfall extrema at ρ = 0 and then tracking them at nonzero ρ. The effective valley potential is retained through ρ⁴ at leading order δ⁴; its coefficients determine the minimum and vacuum-energy tuning.

Compare an imported analytic thawing approximation, obtained from a second-order potential expansion, with numerical background evolution. A numerical parameter search tunes the axion-like example to the desired present equation of state, slope, and density abundance.

Solve dark-energy continuity and Friedmann evolution; translate the resulting density and equation of state into scalar kinetic energy and potential. Integrate the field velocity and invert the typically monotonic φ(t) to reconstruct V(φ), also mapping observational parameter contours into potential-value and slope contours.

Evaluate UV-divergent real one-loop Schwinger integrals by introducing a regulator, minimally subtracting divergent terms, and zeta-regularizing infinite charge sums. The review compares this prescription with modular regularization in string theory.
Use Poisson resummation and modified Bessel functions to extract instanton actions. For Calabi–Yau topological amplitudes, sum D0/transverse-M2 contributions weighted by Gopakumar–Vafa indices.

The background-field one-loop effective action is expanded using heat-kernel coefficients through b8: b4 supplies curvature-squared terms, b6 supplies RF² terms, and b8 supplies F⁴ terms. Dimensional regularization identifies logarithmic divergences and beta functions.

Loop corrections are organized as polynomials az⁴+bz²+c on z≥0. Positivity is classified using coefficient signs, extrema, roots, and UV offsets; both photon operators must satisfy their bounds when d>3.

Field redefinitions, leading Einstein-Maxwell equations, integration by parts, and Bianchi/Ricci identities reduce the amplitude operator basis. The Gauss-Bonnet combination vanishes at quadratic order in graviton fluctuations in any d, allowing a further reduction for four-photon scattering.

The orbit radius is eliminated perturbatively at large angular momentum to obtain coordinate-independent binding energy. The AdS/CFT map E_CFT=ΔqÊ and J=Δq l̂/L_eff converts the binding correction into the anomalous dimension in ΔQ,q(J)=ΔQ+Δq+J+γ.
Circular orbits satisfy V(rc)=V′(rc)=0 for V=(1+l̂²/r²)f−(Ê+q̂At)². ISCOs additionally satisfy V″=0. Numerical roots are filtered using the paper's positive-angular-momentum criterion.

Uses the reviewed Green–Schwarz–Sagnotti anomaly-factorization conditions, irreducible gravitational and quartic gauge-anomaly constraints, and integral unimodular lattice embeddings. Additional filtering applies a string current-algebra central-charge bound and two previously proposed representation bounds.

A recursive branch-and-prune search uses lower bounds on the achievable charged gravitational-anomaly contribution Δ. Type-S vertices are inserted first, if present. Computational pre-pruning removes type-T vertices before constructing the much larger collection of type-T–type-T edges.

Multi-hypergraph vertices encode single-factor spectra and possible anomaly vectors; r-edges encode hypermultiplets charged under r factors. Face/incidence compatibility and nonnegative remaining multiplicities encode admissible models as labelled simplicial-complex embeddings.

Appendix B dimensionally reduces Einstein–Hilbert gravity and a periodic complex scalar using a radion/graviphoton metric parametrization and Fourier modes. The brane cutoff is extracted from the radion-rescaled momentum bound.

One-loop logarithmic determinants integrate noncompact momentum and sum KK integers. The authors impose a cutoff on the full five-dimensional loop momentum, correlating the momentum integral with a bounded KK sum; spherical and cylindrical cutoff choices are discussed.
Estimate Ninfl≈(8π/mPl²)∫V/V′ dϕ, ending at εV=1. Benchmark against direct background-equation evolution, while distinguishing slow-roll estimates from durations bounded by εH=1 crossings.

Apply the earlier work's semianalytic phase-matching prescription: determine a contracting-phase starting field, connect it to the kinetic-dominated arcsinh bounce solution, then solve numerically for kinetic/potential equality.

Normalize V0 using the scalar power amplitude at Hubble crossing. Evaluate r=16εV and ns=1−6εV+2ηV using model-specific field values, including finite-α expressions rather than only universal small-α limits.

Euclidean path integrals with displacement insertions; discretized Fourier momenta, binomial expansions, nodal diagrams and nested integrals organize one-point functions. Bounds on factorial growth motivate Gevrey-series Borel–Écalle resummation with principal-value prescriptions.

A change of integration variable yields the state-dependent Schwinger–Dyson relation ⟨δStot/δφ1⟩σ = ⟨δ log(D†D)/δφ1⟩σ. The Euclidean sign convention matters. Higher moments generally do not factor into powers of one-point functions.

Compute period series from complete-intersection data; decompose periods and fluxes into finite-monodromy eigenspaces; identify derivative periods with elliptic-curve or K3 periods by series matching and explicit submanifolds. Mirror maps then remove exponential corrections in the selected period directions, after an overall period rescaling.

Use Hodge classes and tensors, Mumford–Tate groups, and their Lie-algebra level to organize special loci. For the diagonal fourfold example, use K3 Picard–Fuchs equations, monodromy, a modular fundamental domain and a Hauptmodul to locate and identify vacua.

Track superspace measures, super-Weyl weights and component charges to construct FI-gauge-covariant operators. Test symmetry breaking through terms quadratic in chiral fermions. For the higher-derivative example, substitute bosonic auxiliary-field values, then perform the stated Weyl rescaling and fermion redefinition.

Revisit the Komargodski–Seiberg argument by expanding both the Lagrangian and gauge transformation in ξ. Examine how logarithms generated by expanding field-dependent fractional powers transform under the putative global generator.

Hilltop evolution is modeled by classical motion plus Gaussian field fluctuations of width H/(2π), sampled each Hubble time across expanding daughter patches. A branching probability estimate addresses survival near the maximum.

False-vacuum wall dynamics use a de Sitter interior, de Sitter–Schwarzschild exterior, and Israel junction conditions. An effective-potential analysis defines a critical bubble mass; Hawking–Moss nucleation supplies candidate upward transitions.

Finite-inflation estimates combine semiclassical vacuum-decay rates, Poisson bubble counts in exponentially expanding volume, a statistical vacuum-energy distribution, and gravitational thin-wall bounce actions.

Analytic bounds use Uhlmann purification and parameter-dependent environment 'hiding' unitaries. Gaussian weak-signal criteria use Williamson decomposition; the general support/null-space criterion uses a channel Taylor expansion.

Non-Gaussian probes are evaluated in truncated Fock spaces. Searches over sparse Fock superpositions use gradient descent and particle swarm optimization; an alternating convex search was also attempted without establishing global optimality.

CFI, QFI, symmetric logarithmic derivatives and weak commutativity organize estimation bounds. Spectral-parameter QFIMs follow by chain rule and summing independent frequency contributions; arbitrary orthogonal temporal bases are also considered.

An ADM decomposition provides another calculation of the exterior action. Thermodynamic analysis uses ADM energy and entropy from a microcanonical Legendre transformation, then reconstructs the exponent through B=(E−TS)/T.

Split the geometry into a cap B containing the tip and the exterior V−B. Evaluate both bulk and boundary actions, retaining the opposite outward-normal signs at the artificial cut and the asymptotic boundary contribution.

Conical-deficit regularization replaces the tip by a smooth cap with angular profile F̃(ρ). In the shrinking-cap limit, the F̃″/F̃ curvature term supplies the surviving Einstein–Hilbert contribution; the cap boundary term is evaluated separately.

Reviewed mathematical inputs are nilpotent-orbit and SL(2)-orbit approximations, monodromy weight filtrations, polarized Deligne splittings, and the Hodge-norm growth theorem. These determine leading kinetic metrics and flux-potential powers; allowed enhancements are organized by polarization-compatible Hodge–Deligne diamonds.

Solve Einstein gravity coupled to two canonically normalized scalars using logarithmic warp factors and profiles ψ1=b11 log y1+b12 log y2, ψ2=b2 log y2. A non-conformally-flat metric and linear scalar redefinitions produce an interpretation in terms of intersecting ETW branes.

Degree-n homogeneity reduces radial configurations ℓ(τ) ∝ q to an effective single axio-dilaton problem. The authors study linearized deformations and string-model tests; a CYtools sample of 71,908 Calabi–Yau manifolds supplies numerical evidence for the Gauss–Bonnet bound.

Axion/two-form duality and a Legendre transform give dual saxions ℓ_i = −(1/2)∂K/∂s^i and kinetic potential F = K + 2ℓ_i s^i. The SO(4) Euclidean ansatz reduces the saddle equations to one-dimensional motion with potential V_q = −G^{ij}q_iq_j/2 and conserved energy E.

The authors integrate the scale-factor equation, analyze local perturbations using the Hamiltonian constraint, and conformally transform to Einstein frame. Auxiliary functions F,G yield a differential condition on f. For Bianchi I they expand normalized elementary symmetric polynomials in directions transverse to the isotropic line.

The imported Hohm–Zwiebach construction uses field redefinitions, equations of motion and integration by parts to eliminate higher time derivatives. Single-trace and multitrace O(d,d) invariants reduce to an isotropic action proportional to ∫dt n e^−Φ[−Φ_n² + f(H)] in α′ = 1 units.

Dimensional reduction of higher-form gauge fields on internal cycles relates axion kinetic terms to geometry. The localized bound is motivated through a heuristic WGC argument varying the extra-dimensional size, and alternatively by integrating a five-dimensional kinetic term over a narrow localization region.

Phenomenology combines quoted cooling and helioscope limits with misalignment relic-density estimates. For bulk axions, accessible KK modes are summed through g_eff² = Σ g_n², using the approximate multiplicity N ≈ R m_exp below an experimental mass threshold.
Use a bulk-boundary dictionary including E = M/ω, T̃ = T/ω and S̃ = S to write dE = T̃dS̃ + μdC − pdV + Φ̃dQ̃ + Π̃dγ̃, and calculate boundary thermodynamic potentials.

Locate thermodynamic critical points by setting the first and second entropy derivatives of temperature to zero. RPST derivatives hold Q̂, C and γ̂ fixed; CFT derivatives hold Q̃, V, C and β fixed. Insert critical quantities into H and examine its sign computationally.
Obtain the mass from the horizon equation f(r+) = 0, calculate thermodynamic conjugates through partial derivatives of M, and construct the RPST Helmholtz free energy F = M − TS.

Use the quadratic minimum of ΥL, located at x = M/Q² with value (Q² − M²)/Q², to organize the graphical horizon analysis. Summarize conjecture compatibility by the sign of γ and its position relative to γext.

Identify an extremal configuration by tangency of ΥL and ΥR: impose equality of their values and slopes at x0, thereby introducing γext. The paper then expands the logarithm through two terms to approximate γext and the extremal charge-to-mass ratio.

Rewrite the horizon equation using x = 1/r as ΥL = ΥR, where ΥL = 1 − 2Mx + Q²x² and ΥR = −γx ln[1/(xγ)]. Graph intersections represent horizon candidates r = 1/x; the analysis separates Q²/M² ≤ 1 from Q²/M² > 1.

Fit Planck 2018 temperature, polarization and lensing data; transversal angular 2D BAO; Pantheon+ supernovae with SH0ES Cepheid-host distance anchors; and KiDS-1000 cosmic shear. The shear likelihood uses COSEBIs and nonlinear corrections use HALOFIT.
Estimate additional radiation through entropy conservation for fully thermalized relics, counting surviving orbifold zero modes and using the entropy degrees of freedom at dark-sector decoupling.
Use CLASS with MontePython and Metropolis-Hastings MCMC to constrain seven parameters: ωb, ωcdm, θs, τreio, ns, As and zc. The reported chain convergence criterion is Gelman-Rubin R − 1 < 10⁻².

Post-inflationary methods include QCD instantons, integrating out heavy Majorana neutrinos through dimension-six operators, and Euclidean bounce estimates of vacuum longevity. Late cosmology uses one-loop gravitons around approximately de Sitter spacetime and fits of logarithmically corrected gravity.

Weak chiral gravitational-wave perturbations are integrated up to a momentum cutoff to estimate the CS condensate. Dynamical-system analysis of its approximately linear axion potential describes the stiff-axion-to-inflation transition; an imaginary-Hamiltonian estimate supplies a separate, explicitly naive lifetime argument.

For Z_2×Z_2, reduce stabilization to intersections of conics in Re(S) and |S|², retaining physical roots and excluding flat directions. Enumerate bounded flux integers at fixed charge, map solutions into duality domains, and increase the integer range.

Construct invariant complex three-forms, expand them in a normalized real torus basis, and match flux expansions to obtain integer constraints and the flux superpotential. Solve Kähler-covariant equations D_aW=0 for the axio-dilaton and complex structures.

Fields are described intrinsically as a map γ:Σ→X=∂M and sections of target tensor/spin bundles. Metrics on Σ and X define norms and the formal path-integral measure; the ghost sector cancels its worldsheet Weyl anomaly.

A shift β′=β+ω(paθa) removes inhomogeneous orbifold transformations. Choosing a boundary conformal metric identifies ω∂γ with the pulled-back boundary spin connection, giving a covariant first-order action and homogeneous transition functions.

Integrating β imposes holomorphicity. Fermion zero-mode counting via Riemann–Roch supplies the printed degree selection rule; Riemann–Hurwitz and a moduli dimension count are then used to argue for discrete unbranched coverings in the free energy.

With gravity the functional is S[Vt]=(6π²/κ²)∫(D+Vt′)²/(D Vt²)dφ, with D²=Vt′²+6κ(V−Vt)Vt. Its Euler–Lagrange equation is solved by shooting from or near the false vacuum, producing families with different endpoint behavior.

AdS-maxima analysis compares critical D=0 solutions and CdL solutions with scalar asymptotic data. A small-field example contrasts the field-space action with a cutoff-regulated Euclidean action including gravitational and scalar boundary terms.

Without gravity the field-space variational functional is S[Vt]=54π²∫(V−Vt)²/(−Vt′)³ dφ, integrated from φ+ to φ0. Derivations reviewed include eliminating Euclidean variables, canonical transformation, and summing infinitesimal thin-wall shells.

Use the reviewed intermediate defect group D=Λ*/Λ and its Dirac pairing. Polarizations correspond to Lagrangian subgroups and simultaneous condensation of trivially linking operators, with necessary order condition |L|²=|D|. Polarization pairs refine choices distinguished by SPT phases or local counterterms.

Dimensionally reduce a generalized D3-brane topological action, including effects of the worldvolume gauge-field kinetic term, through an auxiliary five-manifold. The resulting line contains a one-dimensional twisted Dijkgraaf–Witten path integral; Wess–Zumino terms alone are explicitly insufficient.

Uplift IIB fluxes to differential cohomology on an auxiliary eleven-manifold N4×∂Y, then integrate over ∂Y. Torsion linking pairings Λ, Δ and Ω, valued modulo 1, supply quadratic and cubic SymTFT couplings; additional terms are obtained from wrapped-brane linking.

Fourier transform impact-parameter amplitudes and analytically continue to positive t; use Regge behavior and threshold matching to infer higher-derivative scales. Effective-string Gross–Mende saddles with graviton insertions constrain string tension; torus wrapping extends the argument to p-branes.

Propose the high-energy estimate −log(Λρ(E)) ∼ log|A2→2(E,b)|² + O(log(Λ/E)), at fixed b ≲ Λ⁻¹. Thermal branching probabilities motivate it; amplitudes incorporate sufficiently long-lived unstable states, bound states and mass averaging.

Use canonical partition-function convergence and microcanonical entropy in finite boxes. The authors derive αΩ ≥ 1 ⇒ α ≥ 1 and αΩ = 1 ⇔ α = 1, relating multiparticle thermodynamics to one-particle growth; spherical Einstein equations implement the weak energy condition.

The upper-bound argument uses crossing of light-operator four-point functions, global conformal blocks, positivity, OPE convergence, and contour projection functionals. The emergent-sector argument uses light-operator OPEs and current algebra; the lower bound uses an eigenvalue estimate.
Conformal perturbation theory gives d∆/dt = −C_OOM for unit-normalized operators. Normalized descendants ∂O = i√∆ J relate this coefficient to ∆ C_JJ̄M near the limit.

Canonicalize the scalar kinetic term by a field redefinition. For the potential-specific calculations, substitute φ(a)=φ_0a^m into the scalar conservation equation, obtain scale-factor ODEs, and present formal inverse-function expressions involving hypergeometric functions.

Use Friedmann and separate continuity equations to express the background through X(z)=(ρ_m+ρ_D)/(3H_0²) and Y(z)=[ρ_m(1+3ω_m)+ρ_D(1+3ω_c)]/(3H_0²), then rewrite the wave equation using redshift derivatives.

Dimensionally reduces the string-frame Einstein–Hilbert and dilaton action, integrates by parts and Weyl-rescales to the lower-dimensional Einstein frame. Internal-volume/dilaton mixing becomes diagonal in variables D and τ, with coefficients K_DD=d−2 and K̃_ττ=k.

Varies magnetic F4 through its electric dual F6=dC5 and then Hodge dualizes. The resulting derivatives select the AdS radial coordinate z. An additional radial metric factor σ1 is introduced; choosing σ1=3α/2 cancels the terms linear in derivatives before extracting the constrained quadratic metric.

Uses the prescription credited to earlier work: promote constant solution parameters to infinitesimally varying fields, extract two-derivative terms from the off-shell action, then impose relations inherited from the on-shell family to obtain its metric.

Variation of the linearized gravity plus one-loop electromagnetic action yields coupled wave equations. A slowly varying envelope approximation recasts them as a two-state Hamiltonian, whose matrix exponential supplies the conversion probability.

Weak- and strong-field estimates differentiate truncated asymptotic expansions of the proper-time QED effective action. The strong-field calculation regulates separately divergent integrals and uses gamma, digamma, and generalized zeta functions.

Use Hamiltonian constraints from nondynamical metric fields and gauge-invariant variables R=f−QΔE and Φ=δφ+ψφ̇/H. Compare dual formulations through the symplectic transformation X→ΠR, ΠX→−R, retaining its boundary contribution.

Expand the action directly in Euclidean signature to quadratic order using xPand/xAct, modified for Euclidean perturbations. Decompose metric fluctuations into scalar, vector and tensor sectors; the authors focus on scalars because vector and tensor sectors are unsourced by the scalar matter.

Rescale R=√cosh(2r) P and formulate a self-adjoint two-field Sturm–Liouville problem. Numerically shoot odd solutions from P≈P₀r, Φ≈Φ₀r, adjusting λ and P₀/Φ₀ to eliminate both asymptotically growing branches; Appendix B also describes shooting from infinity.

Use canonical momentum shifts to eliminate explicit X− dependence, then impose flux quantization and rewrite the Hamiltonian using symplectic covariant derivatives and curvature. Local and global area-preserving-diffeomorphism constraints remain.

Analyze fiber coinvariants CF={Q+gQ̂−Q̂}, with g in the monodromy subgroup and arbitrary integer Q̂. Construct charge-dependent Λ∈SL(2,R), transform moduli and winding data together, and compare these transformations with trace-classified one-parameter subgroups and inter-coinvariant maps.

Extract the analytic R⁴ term from the four-graviton amplitude and express its one-loop coefficient as a regularized modular integral I=∫F dμ Zreg. Rankin–Selberg–Zagier regularization subtracts the vacuum-growth Eisenstein contribution; c=2 requires a special anomalous regularization.

Use modular-invariance bounds to rule out a divergent integral with a finite gap or only finitely many light states. For scaling, derive the asymptotic operator Dc=−t²∂t²−(2−c)t∂t, control spectral sums by dominated convergence, and use Rankin–Selberg residues and harmonic expansions.

In geometric settings, employ heat-kernel/Seeley–DeWitt asymptotics for species counting and one-loop actions. Appendix C evaluates the worldsheet information metric using conformal perturbation theory and Riemann normal coordinates.

Engineer both singularities through Tate vanishing orders. Resolve the base using affine Kac multiplicities, which multiply the fiber vanishing orders, then resolve remaining singularities and exchange the elliptic fibrations to construct dual descriptions.

Compute defect groups using the Smith normal form of the Dirac pairing, removing the null little-string contribution. Test candidate center symmetries against matter screening and the BPS-string condition ΣJ ηIJ kJ²αGJ=0 mod 1 for every I; flavor twists are trivial.

Use bulk anomaly inflow to determine string-worldsheet anomalies, subtract the universal center-of-mass hypermultiplet, and compare the flavor Kac–Moody central charge with the available left-moving central charge.

Numerically solve the full scalar/background equations using N=−ln(1+z), obtaining HQ rather than relying on approximate analytic wQ expressions restricted to 1+wQ≪1. Match expansion histories rather than directly fitting the scalar equation of state.

Scan {w0,wa,Ωfit(0),Hfit(0)} to minimize the maximum fractional Hubble mismatch defined in Eq. (5), over z<4. Project out the fitted present-day density and Hubble parameters to assign a point, curve or region on the w0–wa plane.

Express averaged expansion as [F(λf)−F(λ0)]/(λf−λ0), using positive F. A uniform lower bound Δ>0 then bounds the available past affine interval by F(λf)/Δ. In generalized FLRW, null affine increments satisfy dλ=a(t)dt up to positive normalization.

Use contradiction, monotonicity and asymptotic scale-factor limits for the completeness lemma. Apply the mean value theorem and smoothness to obtain an open interval with increasing H; the remaining case is excluded by the amended averaged-expansion bound.

PBH abundance estimates use greybody-weighted Hawking evaporation and approximate rescaling of four-dimensional observational bounds at equal Hawking temperature, rather than a complete five-dimensional observational reanalysis.

Dimensional reduction and transformation to the four-dimensional Einstein frame relate compactification radii, field-space distance and KK towers. Radion stabilization is modeled with threshold-dependent Casimir contributions proportional to the light fermion–boson degree-of-freedom difference. The displayed construction uses positive Λ5, negative total brane tension T4 and suitable fermion-dominated thresholds Ri<Rmax.

The imported Reall–Santos method evaluates the higher-derivative Euclidean bulk action on the uncorrected geometry, using I=G/T to obtain leading thermodynamic corrections without constructing the corrected rotating metric.

Perturbed first laws and homogeneous Smarr relations generate response corrections. Legendre transformation and linear shifts of (r0,ai) implement changes of ensemble; Poisson brackets or Jacobian determinants locate candidate singular responses.

Thermodynamic stability is assessed through Hessian metrics, traces and principal minors. The analysis is analytic for even dimensions and D=5; higher odd-dimensional evidence comes from randomized scans in D=7 and D=9.

Compute winding through accumulated complex phase, locating zeros of the imaginary part along the oriented contour and evaluating the real-part sign there. This avoids explicit contour integration while tracking logarithm branches.

Construct periods with Frobenius expansions of the Picard–Fuchs equation around large complex structure, conifold and Landau–Ginzburg points. Mirror symmetry and analytic continuation match an integral basis; numerical period evaluations handle branch-cut contributions when necessary.

The authors solve field-space geodesic equations and integrate their proper length between endpoints. For endpoints connected by attractor evolution and L≪ϕf/Mpl, they approximate the geodesic separation by d≈ϕf.

Analytical treatment of homogeneous equations uses conserved field-space angular momentum and approximate force balance to obtain the hyperbolic attractor. Numerical background examples illustrate evolution and the approximation of attraction beginning today.

BS calculations additionally use matched asymptotic expansions for near-extremal modes and a WKB Bohr–Sommerfeld estimate for prompt ringdown. Numerical scattering integrates from the inner boundary and extracts incident/reflected amplitudes from asymptotic solutions and derivatives.

The radial confluent Heun equation is matched to quantum Seiberg–Witten curves of N=2 SU(2) theory with three massive hypermultiplets. Quantum periods follow from continued fractions and the NS prepotential; the imported QNM quantization condition is aD=n.

Leaver's Frobenius expansion imposes regularity at a TS cap or ingoing waves at a BS horizon, and outgoing waves at infinity. A three-term recurrence gives a continued-fraction eigenvalue equation. Direct integration locates QNMs through a vanishing matching Wronskian.
The reviewed geodesic approach imposes Veff=0 and ∂rVeff=0, giving (f/h)′=0. The topological construction instead uses H=(1/sinθ)√(f/h), with φr=√g ∂rH and φθ=(1/√h)∂θH.

Following Duan's mapping method, normalize n=φ/||φ|| and construct a conserved current supported at zeros of φ. Integrate it over a domain or sum winding numbers around isolated zeros; model applications examine field plots, photon-root locations and horizon roots.

Numerically determine corrected extrema and slow-roll quantities, construct benchmark models, and vary winding/F4 coefficients. The correction study fixes x=10^-4 and readjusts W0 rather than holding all underlying string parameters fixed.

Construct the N=1 F-term and magnetized-D7 D-term potentials, expand in inverse CY volume, transform to canonical volume/shape fields, and use extremization and Hessian eigenvalues to assess stabilization and mass hierarchy. Lambert-W branches describe extrema of the leading potential.

Diagonalize kinetic mixing for nonzero vector mass through Aμ → Aμ − εA′μ, up to O(ε²) corrections, obtaining coupling εqe to Standard Model charge qe. The exactly massless case permits a different field redefinition.

Use heavy-particle loop matching to estimate ε ∼ eg′/(16π²). Nonabelian symmetry breaking permits dimension-five mixing; confinement can instead produce a composite vector whose mass and mixing depend on the confinement scale.
Estimate PBH formation through the Gaussian Press–Schechter prescription, obtaining the smoothed density variance from the curvature spectrum and converting horizon scale to PBH mass.
Compute scalar-induced gravitational-wave spectra using the radiation-era convolution of two curvature spectra with a time-averaged transfer kernel, followed by redshifting to the present.
Numerically solve the background field and Friedmann equations, then the scalar and tensor Mukhanov–Sasaki equations. CMB spectral indices and tensor-to-scalar ratios also use slow-roll expressions.

Use the functional RG with scale-dependent field redefinitions to eliminate inessential operators, a background-field derivative expansion, harmonic gauge and a Litim regulator. Beta functions are computed using xAct; their complete expressions are assigned to an accompanying notebook outside the supplied spans.

Locate fixed points by randomized Newton–Raphson searches, linearize the flow for critical exponents, and integrate relevant perturbations to the IR. FP2 sampling requires 32-digit working precision; fits to 96 trajectory endpoints characterize its landscape geometry.

Numerical trajectories are selected by present density parameters and a past radiation or matter epoch. For observational parametrization, the authors compute both a local CPL tangent and least-squares fits of wϕ(a) over 0.2 ≤ a/a0 ≤ 1, corresponding to redshifts 0–4.

Autonomous dynamical system in x = ϕ′/√6, y = √V/(√3H), z = √(−k)/(aH), u = √ρr/(√3H), with Ωm = 1 − x² − y² − z² − u². Fixed points and Jacobian eigenvalues determine local stability; invariant subspaces, exact solutions and perturbative expansions describe selected trajectories.

Represent truncated series by exponent vectors e, normalized exponents e′, consecutive-exponent ratios r, and normalized ratios r′. Apply PCA by diagonalizing the displayed matrix S=N⁻¹Σₐxₐxₐᵀ and retaining eigenvectors with the largest eigenvalues.

For orthonormal PCA eigenvectors, define feature contribution p(bᵢₗ)=100(bᵢₗ)² percent and proportional variance p(λᵢ)=100λᵢ/Σⱼλⱼ percent. These are the paper's operational saliency and retained-information measures.
Use the imported GPPV contour-integral expression, including a lattice theta series over 2MZ^{|V|}+b. The prescribed principal value averages contours with radii 1+ε and 1−ε.

Starting from a chosen Kähler potential, solve the no-scale condition V = 0 along the assumed stable real direction for two superpotentials W0±. Their linear combination WΛ = W0+ − CΛW0− generates positive vacuum energy; quartic Kähler stabilization lifts the flat direction. Vacuum masses test stability.

Locate inflection points numerically using VI′ = VI″ = 0. Expand VI cubically around z0 and approximate the canonical-normalization factor J by J0; use slow-roll formulas for e-folds and observables, normalize the scalar amplitude, and compare semianalytic outputs with numerical results. Decay widths determine the reheating temperature.

Expand amplitudes at large s and fixed t, then require every coefficient A_n(t), n≥3, to vanish for all t. The authors examine all 5^4=625 external polarization assignments, with some related by crossing.

Construct tree-level four-spin-2 amplitudes from cubic exchange diagrams and quartic contact interactions. Internal harmonic overlap integrals encode the couplings; completeness expresses quartic overlaps through cubic overlaps and the constant harmonic.

Expand the metric around the product background, apply Hodge decomposition and obtain masses and interactions from the Einstein–Hilbert action. The compactification framework and couplings are imported from earlier work.

Relate the field distribution to the momentum marginal of a Wigner function; compare Gaussian entropies through a symplectic eigenvalue ν. For volume weighting, use an approximate WKB solution at small noise strength α. An appendix derives a Lindblad equation first for a quadratic potential.

Weight stochastic histories by exp[3∫Hdt] and normalize the result. The volume-weighted equation adds 3(H−⟨H⟩_V)P_V to the local Fokker–Planck evolution. The authors identify this history-dependent expansion effect as non-Markovian.
Use the stochastic Langevin equation dφ/dt=−V′/(3H)+H^{3/2}η/(2π), with normalized delta-correlated white noise, and its Fokker–Planck description for the local distribution P(φ,t).

Exponential maps and Cartan–Hadamard connect completeness, simple connectedness and nonpositive sectional curvature to contractibility and unique geodesics. For CY3 topology, the paper instead reviews period-map and auxiliary Hodge-metric arguments.

Asymptotic calculations separate overall scaling C(t) = C₀e^{αt} from fixed-volume geodesics, solve an explicit cubic example, and analyze leading singular terms in geodesic deviation, including a WKB-type argument for weaker divergences.

Near-core radial reduction of the scalar equations: combine divergent proper field distance with integrable gradient energy, introduce h(r) = √g(f(r)) f′(r), and impose the equations of motion. The Einstein equation then determines the transverse warp factor.

For a canonically normalized saxion ρ, use the target metric diag(1, f(ρ)²), scalar curvature R = −2f″(ρ)/f(ρ), and volume integral ∫dρ dθ f(ρ) to connect shrinking axion circles with curvature and asymptotic volume.

For black holes, combine universality arguments, soliton analogies and quantum N-portrait input. Count graviton spherical harmonics up to the assumed QFT cutoff to motivate the number and intrinsic gaps of memory modes.

Numerically evolve underburdened SU(4) bubbles in 2+1 dimensions, comparing winding n=0,1, thin and thick walls, several initial charges, and an optional derivatively coupled singlet. Finite differences implement the coupled-field evolution.

Minimize the prototype energy at fixed memory pattern using a Bogoliubov c-number approximation. For the prototype, E*=m_φN_φ/q separates patterns favoring nonzero master occupation from those favoring n_φ=0. Additional couplings to external modes are necessary to study decay dynamically.

The bulk equations are treated using large-ku Fefferman–Graham expansions and a perturbation in k2²/k². Matching the two sides requires coordinate rescalings and choices of integration constants; the first-order constants a1 and c1 are initially undetermined by the asymptotic equations.

Variation of the D3-brane DBI action relates its electric field to the jump in bulk H charge. Fundamental-string charge quantization and an S²-integrated junction condition then identify the effective thick-string tension; a difference of bulk masses supplies a second expression for that tension.

Israel junction conditions impose continuity of the induced metric and match the jump in extrinsic curvature to brane stress. The reviewed Gauss–Codazzi construction identifies the effective four-dimensional Einstein equations, including contributions from bulk curvature.

Use the trace anomaly and stress-tensor conservation, the Polyakov action with an auxiliary field, and Liouville variables for solvable backreaction. Entropies follow horizon derivatives of the gravitational and matter effective Lagrangians.

Sum one-loop contributions around static vacua and homogeneous instanton/anti-instanton pairs. With I_inst=2ma/3, the dilute-gas sum yields Z≈2exp[−2W_stat(a,β/2)]cosh N̄ and, at low temperature with N̄≫1, F_true≈2TW_stat−TN̄.

Evaluate static Casimir contributions using Abel–Plana summation; organize thermal determinants with zeta-function regularization and Poisson summation. Higher-dimensional torus estimates use a recursive Casimir construction and a leading-mode approximation.

Model comparison uses χ²=-2 ln Lmax and AIC=2n-2 ln Lmax. Relative to curved ΛCDM, qCDM adds one parameter and CPL adds two. The authors call AIC simplistic and leave computationally expensive Bayesian-evidence comparisons unperformed.

A modified CAMB implementation supplies cosmological evolution and observables. MCMC varies λ with seven cosmological parameters, using wide uniform priors, Cobaya and a Gelman–Rubin stopping value R-1=0.03. GetDist analyzes chains; Py-BOBYQA finds best-fit likelihoods.

Autonomous first-order dynamical systems and fixed-point stability analysis characterize background trajectories. For the closed case, variables normalized using H̄=H√(1-Ωk) compactify the otherwise noncompact phase space; the fixed-point discussion restricts to expanding universes. The open-case analysis is summarized from prior work.

Embedding-tensor constraints and flat directions of the gauged scalar potential generate solution families. Generalized Scherk–Schwarz twists and scale factors implement consistent uplifts; an explicit spinorial extension promotes SO(8,8) twists to E8(8) twists.

Deformations act on the internal generalized metric as Hdef=Γ Hround Γᵀ, with constant Γ∈SO(7,7) decomposed into GL(7) transformations, B-field shifts and TsT transformations. Worldsheet variations use E=g_s+B and products of currents that become chiral upon imposing equations of motion.

ExFT spectroscopy expands fluctuations in scalar harmonics of the round configurations and Fourier modes on circles. Mass operators preserve harmonic levels, reducing the spectrum to matrix diagonalization. Goldstone modes and decoupled vectors must be removed; scalar stability is tested against (mℓAdS)²≥-1.

Duan's mapping expresses the topological current using a Jacobian and δ²(φ), localizing charge at vector-field zeros. Winding numbers are assigned using positively oriented loops around isolated zeros, and total topological charge is their sum.
The imported Wei construction uses H(r,θ)=√(f(r)/h(r))/sinθ and φ=(√g ∂rH, ∂θH/√h). Its zeros locate photon spheres; the radial null-orbit condition is (f/h)′=0, obtained from Veff=0 and ∂rVeff=0.

The authors inspect metric roots, vector-field zeros, winding numbers, and potential plots on fixed parameter slices. They define RPLPS as the minimum or maximum possible unstable-photon-sphere radius while retaining their black-hole parameter classification.

The authors derive local rules inductively through successive decompactifications, translating tower and cutoff gradients between different Planck units. Gram matrices then determine the frame geometry up to rotation.

Global constructions glue frame simplices and use convex hulls and normalized polar duality. Polygon classification uses discrete tower labels and their fixed adjacent angles, reducing the search to finitely many tuples under dimensional bounds.

Finite genus is recovered by genus reduction. The Siegel Φ map contracts degenerating handles with vacuum states; an alternative takes partial traces. The authors argue that these two reductions give the same Abelian construction when the number of removed handles tends to infinity.

For level-k AB theory, topology classes are organized by Lagrangian subgroups of H1(Σ,Zk), called symplectic codes. Their maximal commuting Wilson-line subgroups define stabilizer states; genus reduction produces states proportional to these representatives, with coefficients requiring separate counting.

The central construction compares two representations of the projector onto modular-invariant states: a sum of projectors onto normalized code states and an average of mapping-class-group operators. Their simple equality is asserted only in the infinite-genus limit, where distinct code states become orthogonal.

Reviewed asymptotic-safety analyses use functional RG flows of the effective action. The Abelian example has βe = −fg e + β0 e³, with fg > 0 encoding gravitational fluctuations and β0 the one-loop coefficient.

Reviewed string arguments use worldsheet currents as gauge-boson vertex operators and modular invariance with long-range-force calculations. The holographic no-global-symmetries argument uses boundary splittability and bulk entanglement wedges.

Derive a charged Λ-dependent TOV equation, impose boundary matching, and study null motion through an effective potential. Obtain p(ρ) by inverting the density ansatz, then assess its logarithmic slope, sound speed, and energy conditions.

Integrate the radial field equation for the mass and electric contributions; combine pressure isotropy with U=e^Φ, x=r², and a logarithmic variable w to obtain Uww+KU=0. This supplies trigonometric, linear, or hyperbolic solution forms according to the sign of K.

Classify finite-order integer matrices using cyclotomic companion blocks. Construct invariant Gram matrices, generate lattice bases by symmetry orbits, and search integral Gram data computationally. Glue nonunimodular blocks through discriminant-form isometries to obtain even unimodular lattices.

Compute orbifold spectra using twisted sectors, shifts, level matching, invariant-state projections, and modular covariance of partition functions. Six-dimensional examples are tested with Green–Schwarz gravitational, gauge, and mixed anomaly conditions.

Lattice gluing matches discriminant groups D(Λ)=Λ*/Λ with compatible norms, reversing the quadratic form of the second component. The 4d construction uses determinant-five quasicrystalline lattices and an eight-dimensional determinant-five lattice L to obtain unimodular lattices.

The one-loop cosmological constant is calculated by integrating the worldsheet partition function over the torus modular fundamental domain. Appendix B supplies twisted-sector partition-function expansions and approximate integral values.

Twisted-sector spectra are obtained from orbifold projection, twist-dependent ground-state energies, fractional oscillator modes and shifted momenta in the dual of the fixed lattice. The review states level matching as E_R−E_L∈Z/N for a Z_N orbifold.

Neutral-background vector perturbations are diagonalized using A±=Ax±iAy. Ingoing solutions are expressed through Heun functions, with boundary Dirichlet conditions and the Kubo formula determining AC conductivity; poles are studied numerically as quasinormal modes.

Fefferman–Graham boundary expansions, regulated on-shell action, Gibbons–Hawking term and counterterms implement holographic renormalization. A finite boundary functional implements alternative quantization through mixed boundary conditions; thermodynamic derivatives yield magnetic response.

Dimensional reduction in the smeared approximation gives Einstein-frame scalar potentials. Scaling in selected dilaton/volume combinations yields on-shell relations between vacuum energy and diagonal Hessian entries; a negative diagonal entry implies a tachyon by Sylvester's criterion.

Independent ten-dimensional arguments combine Einstein and dilaton equations to cancel classical sources, then integrate over the compact space. Singular regions are excised and represented by boundary integrals, matched in a shrinking-hole limit to classical and higher-derivative probe-source contributions.

Toric intersection data, divisor topology analysis using cohomCalg, and Kähler/Mori-cone inequalities establish the geometric setup. D3/D7 tadpole accounting and Freed–Witten flux conditions constrain the brane construction.

A worldvolume flux on the D3 divisor, with fluxes on D1 and D2 set to zero, imposes τ1=qτ2 through vanishing FI parameter. Perturbative LVS fixes V; winding-loop and higher-derivative F4 contributions supply the remaining inflationary potential. The authors infer no KK-type loop correction for the stated intersecting-brane configuration.

Slow-roll analysis uses εV=V′²/(2V²), ηV=V″/V, horizon-exit observables and an e-fold integral. A staged numerical exploration turns on steepening parameters R1 and R2, fixes the overall normalization C0 from the scalar amplitude, and translates working parameters into string quantities.

Reviewed mass-reconstruction methods include Doppler rotation curves, virial estimates, X-ray gas profiles under spherical hydrostatic equilibrium, and weak gravitational lensing. These use different tracers and assumptions rather than a single universal mass estimator.

Analytical halo treatments combine collisionless equilibrium with Poisson’s equation, yielding the singular isothermal sphere in the idealized Standard Halo Model. N-body simulations provide complementary halo distributions fitted by NFW or Einasto profiles.

Detection calculations use nonrelativistic DM–nucleon operators, nuclear form factors and velocity integrals for recoils, and mediator-based simplified models for collider production. Comparing probes requires the coupling structure and the energy regime of each process.

Combine the Friedmann and interacting-fluid equations with quasi-stationary radiation production, then reconstruct temperature, dissipation and slow-roll parameters. In the high-dissipation approximation, truncate a Taylor expansion to obtain H(N) and express inflationary diagnostics in terms of e-folds.

Use warm-inflation scalar and tensor spectra with Bose–Einstein occupation and the growth fit G(Q)=1+0.0185Q^2.315+0.335Q^1.364. The high-Q treatment keeps G≈0.0185Q^2.315 and quotes ns=1+1.815ε1−ε2+3.815β and a thermally suppressed tensor-to-scalar ratio.

Use the rank-126 supersymmetric integral flux lattice, period-matrix quantization constraints and small-length basis vectors. Exhaustive searches and S7 identifications classify minimal-tadpole fluxes; broader mass-rank sampling uses restricted combinations of basis vectors.

Compute periods and arbitrary superpotential derivatives from minimal-model contour integrals, tensor products and orbifolding. In the Ω-basis, modular selection rules require L=1+Σkα≡l̄ mod 3 componentwise, substantially reducing higher-order calculations; mixed τ derivatives require complex conjugation of flux coefficients.

Eliminate Hessian-constrained field combinations recursively, then solve residual polynomial F-term equations order by order, retaining distinct branches. Gröbner bases are used where feasible. The spacetime Jacobi/Milnor ring is finite-dimensional exactly when the critical point is isolated.

Introduce form–polyvector double complexes, primitive decompositions relative to h or h^{-1}, and decomposed differentials such as ∂=∂₊+h^{-1}∂₋. Ellipticity is addressed by replacing derivatives with nonzero covectors and showing exactness of the resulting symbol sequences.

Complete the square and perform the Gaussian μ path integral. For the dilaton, compare quadratic elimination with elimination from the unexpanded e^χ-dependent action, tracking the variable-change Jacobian. The authors find agreement through quadratic order in the remaining fields, with higher-order nonlocal interactions from the latter procedure.

The GW calculation adopts a domain-wall scaling solution, simulation-based annihilation parameters, and a broken-power-law spectrum with low-frequency slope 3 and other shape parameters approximately 1. Detector reach is estimated by integrating the squared signal-to-noise-spectrum ratio, using SNR=10 contours.

Numerical coupled Boltzmann equations track the singlet scalar and χ, including scalar decays, inverse decays involving thermal right-handed neutrinos, and annihilation contributions. The majoron thermalization estimate compares the Nη→Nη interaction rate with H.

Sterile production is estimated by integrating a freeze-in Boltzmann equation, dn_k/dt+3Hn_k=(sin²2θ_k,eff/4)Γνnν. Plasma suppression is modeled by sin2θ_k,eff=sin2θ_k/[1+(T/T_Vk)^6], with Γν≈G_F²T^5 below the weak scale and entropy-dilution factors included.

Matter-density estimates sum the produced tower with lifetime-dependent survival factors, approximated by step functions. The radiation calculation instead integrates coupled energy-injection equations for light neutrinos and the electromagnetic plasma, accounting for their different shares of sterile-decay energy.

Compute the cubic five-dimensional prepotential from classical six-dimensional terms, including Green–Schwarz couplings, and one-loop contributions obtained by integrating out massive fields and KK modes.

Higgs using charged KK hypermultiplets to obtain simpler rank-1 prepotentials. Include intervening flop transitions: when a hypermultiplet mass q·t changes from positive to negative, F changes by −(q·t)³/6.

Identify candidate primitive particles using worldsheet current-algebra unitarity: SU(2) level k=Qb has h_j=j(j+2)/[4(k+2)]. Candidates have charges (Q·a/2+m,Q,−j), with integer m>0 and h_j≤m<j/q_max. The U(1) analogue uses h_ℓ=ℓ²/(2k).

Uses the Legendre–Weyl transformation and an inverse parametric Einstein-to-Jordan-frame map. The latter supports the author's argument that slow-roll scalar potentials correspond to leading F(R) proportional to R².

Summarizes a left Painlevé-series background solution, a slow-roll approximation, potential slow-roll parameters, and CMB scalar-amplitude normalization. These supply the background evolution, mass normalization, and leading spectral predictions; the cited calculations are not reproduced in this pass.

s-channel unitarity expresses loop discontinuities as products of trees. Taking the additional t discontinuity isolates the nearest light-particle threshold: ρ_st=Disc_t Disc_s M. The resulting quadruple-cut calculation reduces to field-theoretic boxes with tree-level factorization data.

Analytically continued t-channel partial-wave unitarity provides a second formulation. Cross terms between an EFT exchange and a Regge pole change the residue, while the product of two Regge-pole contributions produces trajectory corrections. Finite-energy sum rules also receive numerical tests using explicit state sums.

A finite-radius t-plane dispersive contour reconstructs the inverse-mass-enhanced part of Disc_s M from ρ_st. The arc is omitted only for power-enhanced terms; this avoids an infinite-t dispersion integral requiring many subtractions for string amplitudes.

For several moduli, negative logarithmic gradients of potential terms and masses define force vectors. Following earlier work, the authors express stationarity through origin containment in their joint convex hull; mass vectors acquire a factor two because masses enter squared.

The authors solve homogeneous scalar/Friedmann equations using initially frozen configurations, small-time series and estimates N ≈ H0 tdS. Numerical solutions illustrate the two scenarios and selected higher-tower populations; these remain author-reported results.

Weighted Hodge theory: closed representatives satisfying d(wΦ⋆Yω)=0 are constructed using a wΦ-weighted inner product and modified adjoint/Laplacian. An alternative auxiliary-metric argument applies only when n≠2p.

The cutoff estimate sums gluon KK contributions to the axion propagator, counts modes using Weyl’s law, and estimates perturbative breakdown at Π(Λ)∼1. Matching the higher-dimensional gauge kinetic term gives scaling Λ≲f/g, with a model-dependent prefactor.

Heuristic tension arguments combine cycle-volume scaling, Bogomolnyi completion of axion–saxion instanton/string actions, and electric–magnetic tension-scale comparisons. Calibrated Calabi–Yau cycles supply explicit examples; these arguments do not constitute a general proof.

For photons and gluons coupled through the Higgs, triangle loops are integrated into effective Higgs–gauge operators, which are then used in the amplitude comparison. The gluon estimate additionally includes running α_s.

The authors compare absolute scattering amplitudes and derive cutoff or coupling inequalities from selected angular and high-energy limits. Their calculations are restricted to tree-level amplitudes; forward scattering gives the strongest stated bounds in several mediator examples.

Uses an imported ten-component period vector for one nonzero twisted modulus, expands around χ=0, and applies hypergeometric asymptotics at large complex structure to construct the flux effective action.
Numerical root searches use Mathematica FindRoot and randomly generated integer fluxes in −10 ≤ NF_a, NH_a ≤ 10, for both isotropic and anisotropic configurations.

For the undeformed, flat-connection CS theory, the authors replace unavailable electric-flux observables with Wilson loops and line defects; AdS3/CFT2 and Sugawara reasoning motivate the operator construction.

Construct mass-squared and charge-squared operators from commuting principal SL(2,R) observables L0 and C2, then evaluate them on discrete-series states |Δ,N⟩. Casimir dependence supplies the proposed higher-spin charge.

Bayesian MCMC parameter estimation using Planck CMB distance priors, a BAO compilation, and Pantheon+ supernovae. Four analyses combine fixed/free present curvature with fixed/free initial scalar velocity.

Autonomous background dynamical system in dimensionless variables {x,y,z}, with N=ln a as time; polar coordinates expose curvature evolution. A numerical initial-condition grid over x²+y²−z≤1 tests matter domination and subsequent acceleration.

Evaluate Euclidean instanton and background actions, including membrane, gravitational and boundary terms. The imported semiclassical decay prescription is Γ=P exp(−B), with B=S_E[instanton]−S_E[background] and P accounting for quantum fluctuations.

Use the Hodge-dual description ∗₆F₂=F₄ and review Brown–Teitelboim membrane nucleation. A membrane charged under the three-form potential separates constant fluxes with Eᵢ=Eₒ−e; flux energy contributes to the cosmological constant, Λₒ=λ+4πGEₒ².

Impose T=0 to obtain explicit five-dimensional limiting entropies. For unspecified D, compare the general entropy-dependent expressions without explicitly solving the dimension-dependent extremality condition.

Solve the horizon equation Δ(rh)=0 for the mass parameter, express rh through entropy, solve for ε, differentiate with respect to entropy, and combine the inverse derivative with temperature to construct −T(∂S/∂ε). Compare this with the ε derivative of the physical mass.

Use the variable-tension Nambu–Goto equations, impose a circular-loop ansatz, and average rapidly oscillating subhorizon loops with ⟨a²Ṙ²⟩=1/2 to obtain the evolution of physical length and comoving amplitude.

Estimate survival using PGW=ΓGμ² with time-dependent tension, and estimate percolation by comparing growing loop sizes with initial inter-loop spacing. Include gravitational radiation as a source that can terminate kination.

Two independent analysis teams use optimized direct calculations and neural-network spectrum prediction. Preparation uses simulated data and model blinding through an unknown final-states variance change; unblinding follows fixation of procedures and inputs.

Joint maximum-likelihood inference uses Gaussian count likelihoods for nominal analyzing-plane data and Poisson likelihoods for shifted-plane data divided into 14 patches. The mass parameter is shared; endpoint, normalization, and background vary across campaigns and patches.

Convolve a Fermi-golden-rule differential beta spectrum, including an ab initio molecular final-states distribution, with transmission and inelastic-scattering response functions. Fit signal normalization, background, effective endpoint, and squared neutrino mass.

Compute flux periods through mirror symmetry and genus-zero Gopakumar–Vafa invariants, continue toward a conifold, and construct perturbatively flat vacua. Racetrack solutions provide initial guesses for numerical roots of the complex-structure and axiodilaton F-terms beyond the PFV approximation.

Use an AdS precursor as a numerical starting guess, include uplift and shifts in both moduli sectors, and search for positive-energy stationary points with positive-definite Hessian. The authors check derivative formulas using finite differences and automatic differentiation.

Search selected favorable trilayer toric geometries and quantized fluxes. Require a conifold disjoint from orientifold planes, sufficient contributing rigid divisors, Qflux=QO+2 and conifold flux M>12. The reported search finds 33,371 anti-D3-brane PFVs.
Use dM=ω(ω−qhat Φhat_h)rh²dt and dQhat=qhat(ω−qhat Φhat_h)rh²dt+(Qhat/2C)dC. Linearize the horizon equation in M, Qhat, rh, and C, then differentiate S=πrh²/G to obtain entropy changes.

Separate the charged Klein–Gordon equation into e^(−iωt), a radial function, and spherical harmonics; introduce a tortoise coordinate and study the near-horizon radial equation. Energy and charge transfer are obtained from stress-tensor and current fluxes.

Test horizon survival through the minimum of h: initially hmin=δ≤0, with vanishing first radial derivative and positive second derivative. Taylor-expand its change under the flux-induced parameter variations.
Apply canonical normalization Yijk=Wijk exp(K/2)(KiKjKk)^(-1/2) and imported intersection-angle/gonion asymptotics. A toroidal Z2×Z2 Pati–Salam toy model illustrates the scaling mechanism.

Estimate the species cutoff using ΛQG≈MP/N^(1/(D−2)) and two multiplicative light towers, N≈(ΛQG/mlight)^2. Identifying this cutoff with the string scale is an expectation supported by toroidal examples.
