Use Wilsonian universality classes, the CFT state–operator construction, finite-volume effects and high-energy scattering behavior to formulate a diagnostic separating QFT parameters from vacuum choices.

Use dimensional reduction and MSSV consistent truncations for group manifolds, Kähler potentials and superpotentials for supersymmetric flux models, and an explicit DGKT reduction retaining quadratic, quartic and sextic axionic terms.

Identify canonical coordinates and fixed transverse values with V=V1(transverse)+V2(longitudinal,transverse), where V1(0)>0, V2→0 and its longitudinal derivative→0. Orthogonal field rotations expose plateau directions and nearby trajectories with nonzero limiting slopes.

Intermediate KK reductions geometrize localized gauge flux as an internal fibration with prescribed monodromy. Generically, the exceptional fiber is X/U(1); fixed points determine boundaries or singularities, with KK 5-branes supplying selected boundary conditions.

Embedding-space AdS boosts move probe defects to ρ≥|β|: one boost in Euclidean signature and two boosts in the Lorentzian construction. Joining oppositely oriented defects introduces a defect–antidefect fusion product extending toward the boundary.

Dimensional reduction of higher-dimensional topological terms, including a T-dual/M-theory description, supplies defect symmetry data. The degeneration-induced map π_n:H_n(X)→H_n(X′) identifies collapsing wrapping classes whose associated operators can end on the defect.

On-shell reverse unitarity matches products of tree amplitudes onto scalar bubble and box integrals. Integration-by-parts identities, implemented with LiteRed, remove triangles. General-dimensional matching also determines rational terms; EFT-only, mixed, and pure-gravity contributions are separated.

Fixed-t and crossing-symmetric contour dispersion relations equate calculable IR arcs to UV partial-wave integrals. Smearing must make the IR integrals finite and the UV integrals positive. The crossing-symmetric slicing holds p²=2stu/(s²+t²+u²)>0 fixed.

Polynomial smearing functions are optimized with SDPB using finite-spin constraints, sampled energies, and large-spin fixed-impact-parameter information. Loop shifts are primarily evaluated on tree-level extremal functionals; the authors also compare direct optimization including gravitational loops.

Frobenius expansions characterize horizon and asymptotic solutions. A tidal Green function constructs the horizon-regular first-order perturbation; contour operations on an overlap involving ψ(0)D(1)ψ(0) extract constant response terms or logarithmic running.

Heavy neutral particles of spins 0, 1/2 and 1 are integrated out at one loop using the heat-kernel expansion through b6. The scalar and vector are real, the fermion is Dirac, and Majorana contributions are half the Dirac ones. The reduced result is reported to match prior work.

Operator reduction uses integration by parts, leading field equations, Gauss–Bonnet topology, Bianchi identities and dimension-dependent curvature identities. A non-reduced basis is retained to test dependence on field redefinitions.

For H regular in the fundamental domain, the review invokes a representation built from holomorphic Eisenstein series, eta factors and a polynomial in the j-invariant. Candidate ten-dimensional corrections are motivated separately through instantons, homotopy and previously identified non-perturbative terms.

The reviewed construction uses modular covariance to constrain K and W, computes the F-term potential, and parametrizes dilaton-sector supersymmetry breaking by A(S,S̄). Stabilization conditions are organized by modular-function parameters and the location of T within the fundamental domain.

The paper sketches the chain from probability distinguishability to the Fisher metric, then from its isometries and additional state-space postulates to the Born rule. It examines i.i.d. sampling, sufficient statistics, non-contextuality and Hilbert-space factorization as potentially vulnerable premises.

A perturbatively dressed scalar around Minkowski space illustrates nonlocal gauge-invariant observables and dependence on boundary data. The toy model then uses sequential conditional probabilities and the expected squared score to discuss Fisher information for an entire outcome string.

For inverse reconstruction, minimize the sum of squared differences between model and reconstructed scalar spectra using Levenberg–Marquardt. A manually adjusted slow-roll spectrum supplies the initial guess, followed by full numerical mode evolution.

Numerically evolve the background in e-fold time and solve the Mukhanov–Sasaki equation separately for real and imaginary mode components. Bunch–Davies initial conditions are imposed five e-folds before each mode's horizon crossing; spectra are evaluated at inflation's end.

Evaluate an imported cubic-interaction one-loop expression with original numerical code. Its nested time integrals weight periods of large η′, and its loop momentum integral is restricted to modes crossing during USR; instantaneous transitions are not assumed.

Uses fourth-order Runge–Kutta integration and rescaled variables. Fits asymptotic scalar coefficients α and β, subtracts scalar-dependent mass divergences, and estimates the critical superpotential parameter sc through both direct superpotential integration and large-|α| spherical-soliton asymptotics.

Treats the conserved mass as a functional of the radial scalar profile at fixed apparent-horizon radius r*. Varying this functional gives an integro-differential stationarity condition, converted into coupled ODEs using auxiliary functions H and Γ and integrated outward from a chosen horizon scalar value.

Probe pseudo-Dirac oscillations through their δm²L/Eν dependence: identify source distance through multimessenger observations and search for an energy-dependent active-neutrino deficit in the measured source spectrum.

Use the common pion-production origin of high-energy neutrinos and γ-rays to connect their energy budgets and constrain BSM emission components. Photon absorption, cascading and propagation losses must enter interpretation of observable fluxes.
Constrain merger-produced ALPs through photons from their subsequent decay, analyzing the predicted signal's spectral and temporal features to limit the ALP–photon coupling.

Use the imported higher-derivative attractor equations Y^A−Ȳ^A=ip^A and F_A−F̄_A=iq_A, with Υ=−64, and the entropy formula S_BH=π[|Z|²+4 Im(Υ∂_ΥF)]. Both the area and explicit Wald correction depend on the F-terms.

Evaluate the D0 tower through a Schwinger proper-time one-loop determinant. Fourier/Poisson resummation supplies nonlocal perturbative contributions; contour deformation and residues isolate additional nonperturbative terms where the contour prescription is admissible.

Analyze factorial asymptotics using Borel resummation and resurgence. For imaginary α, rotate the Schwinger contour and subtract the low-genus terms at the origin to obtain a convergent integral, instead of using the problematic closed-contour residue sum.
Solve BPS attractor equations and minimize entropy over charge hierarchies reaching a chosen boundary. With vanishing axions, STU regularity selects D0/D4, D2/D6 and constrained D0/D2/D4/D6 families.

Encode asymptotic black-hole scales through vectors −∇log ΛBH. Each vector applies only to the trajectory sector accessible with its corresponding charge fixed; sectorwise polar plots are assembled for comparison with species scales.

For the truncated 9d model, extremize Sen’s entropy function on AdS2×S7. The authors supplement near-horizon extrema with a positive effective-potential Hessian and an explicit constant-modulus, double-extreme solution.

Construct invariant forms through Maurer–Cartan equations and shifted orbifold actions, solve the geometric supersymmetry conditions in terms of fluxes, and obtain scalar spectra from the normalized Hessian of the real-superpotential potential. Appendix A reduces a solvmanifold Laplacian equation to a Mathieu equation.
Use bispinor/Killing-spinor supersymmetry conditions together with the sourced Bianchi identity. In the smeared approximation gs F3=(W1/6)Φ−⋆W27; μ²=LAdS^−2 and W1=(12/7)μe^−A.

Rotate the left- and right-moving supercurrent bases using external automorphisms, selecting an N=(2,2) subalgebra in which the connecting deformation is chiral plus antichiral. Apply the known A-type interface diastasis argument in that subalgebra.

Fold an interface into a boundary condition for a tensor product with a parity-conjugate theory. Spectral flow converts normalized NS–NS vacuum overlaps into R–R overlaps; tt* equations determine their Kähler-potential dependence using the coincident-theory boundary condition.

Combine tt* curvature relations with the external SO(4) action. Holomorphy and independence from the complementary moduli imply constant Yukawa couplings and covariantly constant curvature; completeness and simple connectedness of the covering space enter the symmetric-space argument.

Numerically evolve the three background fields in e-fold time and project fluctuations onto tangent, normal and binormal directions. Use turning, torsion, projected masses and an adiabaticity diagnostic to motivate approximate horizon-crossing observables.

Compute the F-term potential from the corrected Kähler potential and constant W0 using the N=1 supergravity formula, then expand at large volume. Leading terms leave flat directions; subleading mixed corrections and F⁴ terms are used to lift the remaining saxion directions.

Introduce an approximately canonical field basis from the leading Kähler metric, derive small-y and small-α approximations for extrema, and compare with numerical minima. Inflation uses the unexpanded form of the retained potential rather than the small-y approximate potential.

A modified healpy dipole fit jointly estimates monopole and dipole coefficients from peak angles using weighted least squares, with W=diag(1/σi²). The authors state that mask-induced fitting bias is negligible for their adopted mask.

Polarization is transformed into radial Stokes components around temperature and E-mode extrema. Ur profiles probe the map-space equivalents of TB and EB. Gaussian-field peak theory supplies Bessel-J2 profile templates, with bias parameters calculated separately for each peak height.

Each peak receives a linear least-squares angle estimate by fitting the observed Ur profile to 2β times a theoretical template. Peak estimates are combined with inverse-variance weights. Simulation uncertainties use the distribution of 300 simulation estimates; data uncertainties use the weighted-mean variance to accommodate component-separation noise differences.

Classical stability is analyzed through linearized Kaluza–Klein towers and the Lichnerowicz spectrum on transverse, tracefree internal symmetric tensors. Integration by parts gives a sufficient bound using the largest Riemann-tensor eigenvalue; failure of that sufficient bound alone does not establish instability.

Coset harmonic analysis rewrites the relevant squared operators using curvature, Casimirs and an H-covariant derivative. Explicit eigenmode construction turns the problem into algebraic matrix equations. For squashed S7, G2 projectors, octonionic tensors and Killing vectors enable construction of two-form modes, including a double-derivative operator.

Unbroken supersymmetry is counted by solving the internal supercovariant Killing-spinor equation. Weyl-tensor integrability and generalized holonomy organize the analysis; generalized SO(8) holonomy distinguishes orientations that have the same displayed integrability condition.

Analyze extrema and relative vacuum energies using tree-level estimates, a one-loop logarithmic quartic with approximately constant βλ, and an extension retaining C6h6/Λ². The auxiliary parameter c=C6μI²/(Λ²|βλ(μI)|) organizes the vacuum phases.

Phenomenology uses two-loop scalar/Yukawa RG evolution, three-loop gauge running, one-loop matching corrections to λ and yt, and nonlogarithmic contributions to λeff. RGBeta and Matchete generate the stated running and matching inputs.

Compute masses from the kinetic-normalized Hessian divided by |V|, then apply Δ=1+√(1+m²L²). Analytic flux families and large-G expansions determine stabilization and approach to the limiting spectrum.

Use the imported G2-compactification superpotential, evaluate it for chosen harmonic-form flux expansions, and solve Px=Py=Ps̃a=0. Tadpole conditions and the flux equation H3∧⋆7F4=0 constrain admissible choices.

Compute tree-level massive spin-2 elastic scattering from s-, t- and u-channel graviton exchange, retaining helicity dependence. Separately analyze compensating higher-dimensional gauge transformations required to preserve unitary gauge in the orbifold reduction.

Construct the R-multiplet by supersymmetry variations of the axial Noether current; decompose its stress tensor into a Hilbert tensor and single- and double-divergence improvements. Classify quadratic axial-current improvements satisfying parity, dimension and linear-superfield constraints, then cancel the inadmissible single-divergence terms.

Use fixed-negative-t contour dispersion relations to express EFT arc quantities Mn as UV partial-wave moments. Compare the leading 1/(−t) graviton singularity with derivatives of loop logarithms, rather than simply discarding the graviton pole.

The improved construction smears over t=−q² using normalized power-law weights, integrates Legendre polynomials into hypergeometric kernels, and applies Hölder with exponent two to a five-derivative quantity. A spin-dependent upper integration limit isolates singular contributions from finite tails.

The preliminary forward-limit construction takes eight t derivatives of tM2, subtracts finitely many low-spin contributions and applies Hölder's inequality with exponent five. The eighth derivative supplies the large-angular-momentum growth needed for convergence of the auxiliary sum and integral.

Uses the quantum information metric from the leading deviation of squared overlaps between neighboring ground states, together with imported S-matrix unitarity and causality arguments for weakly coupled gravitational UV completions.
Conceptual synthesis of topology sums, cobordism, gravitational solitons, and semiclassical black-hole entropy arguments, organized into kinematic and dynamical consistency constraints.

Construct extended first laws, Smarr relations, equations of state and Gibbs free energies for Schwarzschild-AdS, equal-charge dyonic and Kerr-AdS solutions. Determine phase boundaries and map pressure to stabilized internal size; the dyonic coexistence boundary is evaluated numerically.

Integrate the internal instanton and curvature contributions, transform by gμν=e^(−4f)g̃μν, and locate extrema of the size-modulus potential. CP2 and the equal-size/equal-flux S2×S2 specialization give the same reduced potential structure after parameter identification.

Twisted KK mode expansions and dimensional reduction of BF/Stückelberg couplings identify surviving charges and confinement. Orthogonal projection onto invariant charge subspaces, lattice duality, Dirac quantization, and Aharonov–Bohm phases relate electric sublattices to magnetic superlattices.

BPS brane tensions determine extremality bounds in string examples; string dualities extend the analysis beyond a single weak-coupling/large-radius frame. Euclidean bounce estimates assess flux-tube fragmentation by monopole pair creation.

Match the horizon-averaged delta-H/H correlator to the Carlip–Solodukhin ansatz. Obtain tensor angular momentum using Noether currents and Wick contractions, regulate its orbital contribution, and match to a small-angular-momentum Kerr entropy distribution.

Fit a power-series parametrization of epsilon at horizon crossing to samples generated from Planck 2018 summary results. Repeated Python curve fitting and distribution fitting characterize parameter estimates; this is not presented as a new likelihood analysis of raw CMB observations.

Borrow classical cosmological perturbation equations in comoving gauge, solve approximate mode equations using Bessel functions and de Sitter symmetry, and supply HST statistical initial conditions rather than quantized bulk-field fluctuations.

The microscopic calculation uses a Stratonovich transform, integrates out fermions, and expands the resulting functional determinant in gradients at large charge. ζ-function regularization is used for spectral quantities; the edge estimate employs a Mellin transform of a heat kernel.

Renormalize edge divergences using either a physical δ-layer cutoff with edge counterterms or dimensional regularization. Goldstone-EFT integrals are analytically continued Beta functions; Gamma-function poles isolate logarithmic divergences, while power divergences disappear in dimensional regularization.

Construct marginal EFT operators using dilaton dressing, then integrate out the gapped radial mode to obtain a Goldstone-only description. In the latter, U=χ̇−A_0−(∇χ)^2/2; bulk dressing uses U, whereas edge dressing uses [(∇U)^2]^(1/3) and the operator-valued distribution δ(U).

Gaussian disorder averaging introduces bilocal G and Sigma. Their large-N saddle equations are solved by iterative Fourier methods, supplemented by conformal ansätze and an analytic large-q expansion.

Expand the bilocal action to quadratic order; solve the conformal ladder-kernel eigenvalue-one condition for background-field dimensions. Analytically continue to a retarded kernel and study late-time OTOC double commutators for chaos.

Compute holonomy integrals either through polynomial fits and Gaussian/Hermite integration or through complex saddles on the imaginary-u axis. The latter implements the grand-canonical to canonical Legendre transform. Compare both approaches with disorder-averaged exact diagonalization.

Discrete theta angles are found from fractional fixed points C=S′(C+u), with integral axionic shifts u. Cyclotomic companion matrices encode island actions; redefining RR two-forms as C̃_i^(2)=C_i^(2)−C_i^(0)B^(2) exposes the shifted string coupling q+C_i^(0)p^i.

Sen–Vafa dual pairs are constructed using U-duality conjugation and the adiabatic argument for freely acting circle shifts. Spin(4,4) triality converts the RR charge action into the twist of the dual quasicrystalline construction.

The classification uses primitive lattice embeddings, discriminant forms and lattice uniqueness results attributed to Nikulin. After an additional T^4 compactification, invariant-lattice deformations lead to Γ8,8 ≃ E8 ⊕ E8(−1) and holomorphic worldsheet factorization.

Injection spectra follow from Lorentz boosting isotropic ALP-rest-frame distributions, including subsequent radiation or showers. Photon production inputs are borrowed from existing numerical code; the direct-photon examples include Gaussian energy smearing with σ(E)/E ≃ 0.1.

ALP-dependent scalar rephasings and anomalous fermion rotations connect derivative and non-derivative bases; authors calculate observables in both. Relic abundance uses numerical Boltzmann evolution with the full thermal average, rather than only the illustrative s-wave expansion.

Test homogeneous scalar reconstructions through Friedmann identities, then analyze phantom-scalar perturbations in spatially flat gauge with a slow-roll assumption. Compare scalar/tensor spectra and dark-energy equation-of-state parameters with the observational inputs quoted in the paper.

Use the dilaton/form-field bulk action and probe DBI–Chern-Simons action. Expand the rigid D3 Lagrangian to first subleading order, impose conserved worldvolume energy, and pull back the bulk metric to obtain the cosmological scale factor and Friedmann equation.

Estimate the thermodynamic black-hole transition by matching lower- and higher-dimensional black-hole entropies, including a Gauss-Bonnet correction. Differentiate the resulting scale with both constant and moduli-dependent coupling.

Evaluate regularized BPS mass sums and express the free energy through Dedekind η functions. Compute logarithmic gradients with the Kähler metric using Eisenstein E2, then extract subleading terms from q-expansions.

Griffiths bilinear relations and graded Frobenius algebras constrain couplings and Gauss–Manin connections. Picard–Fuchs ideals are obtained by GKZ reduction or residue-period integration; one-parameter operators admit a coupling-based special local normal form.

Mirror symmetry and the Γ̂-class fix asymptotic rational/integral period bases near maximal unipotent monodromy. Analytic continuation and monodromy calculations connect coordinate patches; Wronskian minors construct antisymmetric-product period systems.

Imports off-shell adiabatic subtraction: Lren_W(M)=LW(m)−LW^(0−4)(M), including finite subtraction terms. M has adiabatic order zero, while Δ²=m²−M² has order two; the subtraction retains orders 0, 2 and 4.

Uses WKB adiabatic modes and the DeWitt–Schwinger expansion of the one-loop vacuum effective action; obtains the vacuum EMT by metric variation. Dimensional regularization is auxiliary, and its scale μ cancels from the stated renormalized result.

When YM thermalization is fast enough, integrates out the gauge sector to obtain a damped homogeneous-inflaton equation and a kinetic equation for inflaton particles. Condensate friction and particle production sample different momentum regions of the same thermal spectral correlator.

Constructs parametric phase boundaries by comparing thermalization, production, decay, oscillation and Hubble rates. Uses Γth≈cN²α²T with c≈10, nonlinear saturation A_NL≈kinst/(2gN), and magnetic screening mM≈g²NT.

Average the dark-matter oscillations, introduce Hubble-normalized variables, and analyze the resulting autonomous system through fixed-point existence, acceleration conditions and Jacobian eigenvalues. Numerical background trajectories and phase portraits illustrate selected histories.
Split V(ϕ,χ)=W(ϕ)+g(ϕ)U(χ) and assign the χ-dependent potential energy to ρχ. Derive separate continuity equations and encode their opposite energy-momentum transfers in an interaction vector Qν.

For each source and QPO model, profile χ² over spin, mass and emission radius at each dilaton charge. Masses vary within the adopted observational ranges, while rms≤rem≤rms+20Rg. Report charge-dependent minima and one-parameter Δχ² intervals.

Use conserved test-particle energy and angular momentum, an effective potential and the marginal-stability conditions to determine circular orbits and the ISCO. Small radial and vertical perturbations provide orbital and epicyclic frequencies, which enter the QPO prescriptions.

The Bayesian exercise uses 64 chains with 10,000 samples per chain and a Gaussian frequency likelihood. Priors are flat over allowed ranges except Gaussian mass priors for GRO J1655−40 and XTE J1550−564. The authors explicitly choose likelihood maximization without nuisance-parameter marginalization.
The holographic argument uses an AdS5 Yang–Mills asymptotic expansion and boundary counterterm, then compares its renormalized on-shell variation with the boundary variation of BF theory.

Canonical quantization identifies wavefunctions on Aflat/𝒢 with background-dependent partition functions. For π1(Md)=Z, a character Fourier transform between conjugacy classes and irreducible-representation labels interprets gauging as changing polarization.

The operator calculation absorbs Uα into a delta-supported curvature insertion, shifts A locally, and evaluates a path-ordered Wilson line. Haar averaging and Schur's lemma produce an action proportional to the normalized character χR(g)/dim R.

Charged geodesics in static coordinates define radial acceleration for a probe initially at rest. Near an extremal horizon, the authors impose F′(rh)≥0; for multiple U(1)s, the resulting projection inequality becomes a convex-hull condition.

The charged-field effective action is evaluated through Euclidean worldline instantons. The Schwinger threshold is located by degeneration and disappearance of periodic trajectories; a near-horizon quadratic expansion gives an analytic threshold even though the full spatial analysis requires numerics.

A near-horizon scaling extracts AdS2 × S^(D−2). The charged scalar's gauge-shifted effective mass is compared with the AdS2 Breitenlohner–Freedman bound, retaining a finite-wavelength correction when needed.

From F(T,q), the authors compute S=−∂TF, Φ=∂qF, and M=F+TS. They also invoke the imported entropy–extremality identity (∂εMext)q=−lim(M→Mext) T(∂εS)M,q, and use homogeneity to obtain an extended Smarr relation.

An imported first-order thermodynamic method evaluates the higher-derivative Euclidean action on the unperturbed RN metric. The perturbed and unperturbed solutions must have identical boundary data, here temperature and charge; the method avoids solving the corrected nonlocal field equations.

The calculation uses the background-field one-loop effective action. Local coefficients are absorbed into corresponding logarithmic scales; equations of motion, Bianchi identities, and field redefinitions are used to express the relevant operators in a geometric basis.

Generalized Scherk–Schwarz reductions use an E_n(n)×R+ frame obeying a generalized Lie-derivative algebra with constant coefficients encoding Θ. Uplift constructions use a gauge-group coset G_g/H, section constraints on projected embedding-tensor data, and integration of background fluxes.

The embedding tensor defines generators X_M=Θ_M^α t_α. Supersymmetry imposes a linear representation constraint; consistency imposes quadratic closure [X_M,X_N]=−X_MN^P X_P. In D=4, the locality constraint Ω^MN Θ_M^α Θ_N^β=0 ensures an electric frame exists. Inequivalent gaugings are organized by G-orbits satisfying these constraints.

For homogeneous scalar manifolds, move a candidate critical point to the origin while transforming Θ. Stationarity becomes quadratic algebraic conditions on Θ; imposing preserved supersymmetry adds linear BPS constraints through the fermion shifts.

Select operators by a large-mass expansion near the extremal horizon. Reduce the basis using background-vanishing invariants, four-dimensional Gauss–Bonnet, electromagnetic and Riemann Bianchi identities, and integration by parts, followed by coefficient redefinitions.

Use metric perturbations ψ(r), m(r) and an electric-field correction F(r). Integrate coupled radial equations to obtain m(r) and the corrected metric factor; integration constants are absorbed into M̄ and Q̄.

Integrate out graviton fluctuations in the unique-effective-action approach, vary the resulting action, and solve the corrected gravitational and electromagnetic equations perturbatively around classical Reissner–Nordström.

The authors numerically solve the modified Klein–Gordon equation in Python, evaluating H through the Friedmann equation at each epoch, then compute wϕ and weff from the resulting field position and velocity.

For fixed M, ϕ0, α and β, the initial velocity is zero and the initial position is manually adjusted to match the present field value and observed dark-energy density. Both matching accuracies are stated as 0.01 without a clear absolute/relative normalization. Parameters are varied until curves lie within reconstructed DESI confidence bands.

Cobaya MCMC uses MFLike or foreground-marginalized ACT-lite likelihoods with CAMB, CLASS or CosmoPower theory predictions. Chains compute spectra to ℓmax=9000, generally reach R−1<0.01, and are analyzed with GetDist.

Baseline theory uses CosmoRec in CAMB or HyRec in CLASS, PRIMAT BBN predictions, and HMcode-2020 dark-matter-only nonlinear corrections without baryonic feedback. For models changing late-time growth, custom prescriptions or linear-scale restrictions replace unsupported nonlinear modeling.

Models are assessed through marginalized posteriors and maximum-a-posteriori comparisons with ΛCDM. Informative nuisance priors enter the MAP; uninformative-prior contributions are discarded from its effective χ². EDE optimization uses multiple minimizer runs, including PROSPECT, with full CLASS calculations.

IterativeFFT density-field reconstruction partially restores the acoustic peak. Galaxy/quasar clustering uses the post-reconstruction Landy–Szalay two-point estimator, Legendre monopole/quadrupole moments, and RascalC covariance estimation.

Template fits vary isotropic/anisotropic BAO shifts and marginalize amplitudes and spline broadband nuisance parameters. BGS uses the monopole alone; DR2 ELG1 and QSO support two-dimensional fits. Analysis choices were fixed before unblinding.

Cosmological posteriors use Cobaya Metropolis–Hastings MCMC with CAMB predictions. iminuit searches from chain MAP points determine best fits; model comparison uses Δχ²_MAP and the deviance information criterion.
Flexible reconstructions use Chebyshev expansions of w(z) or fDE(z), tanh-smoothed redshift bins without prior inter-bin correlations, and PCA obtained by diagonalizing the inverse bin covariance.

Metropolis–Hastings MCMC in Cobaya uses modified CAMB, with PPF perturbations permitting w = −1 transitions; quintessence uses modified CLASS. Supernova absolute magnitude is analytically marginalized, and iminuit finds best-fit points starting from chain MAP points.

GP reconstruction uses a squared-exponential kernel, mean w = −1, fixed amplitude σf = 1 and a generalized inverse Gaussian correlation-length prior. Tests varying the latent sampling redshift and marginalizing σf reportedly leave conclusions reasonably robust.

Bayesian inference uses Cobaya Metropolis–Hastings MCMC, CAMB or CLASS Boltzmann calculations and getdist posterior summaries. External information includes BBN and correlated Gaussian CMB parameter priors.

An imported effective-mass continuation permits negative neutrino energy contributions consistently at background and perturbation level, while matching the standard model exactly for positive effective masses. The massless-neutrino parameter is adjusted between Nur = 0.00441 and 6.08627 to preserve early-time Neff = 3.044.

Frequentist profiles fix the neutrino mass sum and maximize over other parameters using Minuit. Calculations sample the positive-mass region, retain prescribed nuisance penalties, fit a parabola and extrapolate it to obtain Feldman–Cousins confidence limits accounting for the zero-mass boundary.

Compare intrinsic and ambient balls: an isometric embedding puts the intrinsic radius-D ball inside the ambient radius-D ball while preserving its volume. Combining this inclusion with the tame-volume theorem gives the intrinsic growth bound.
For a sharply definable embedded image, bound its affine-plane intersection complexity using sharp o-minimality, then translate the component bound into a bound on the volume-growth coefficient.

Apply the imported tame-volume theorem: for an l-dimensional tame A⊂R^N, Vol_l(A∩B^N(r))≤c(N,l)b_0,N−l(A)r^l. The Gabrielov number uniformly bounds connected components of intersections with affine (N−l)-planes.

Expand currents on supervielbeins, impose differential closure, and integrate them over embedded cycles using distributional Poincaré duals. Exact changes of the dual describe embedding deformations; explicit examples reduce integral-form expressions to ordinary superspace Berezin integrals.

Couple currents minimally to external gauge superfields. Generator and defect insertions select backgrounds; removing the generator background by a gauge transformation leaves an anomalous phase that determines the charge. The allocation of anomalies depends on the chosen background couplings and transformations.

The authors combine the Wilson-loop heat-kernel master equation with their compact ansatz, integrate in local B-model propagators, and test elliptic P2 genus-zero expressions against compact Picard–Fuchs equations at low fiber order.

Geometric computations use stable one-dimensional sheaves, perverse-sheaf pushforwards and hypercohomology, relative/ordinary hard Lefschetz actions, curve gluing, and projective-bundle or Hilbert-scheme descriptions.
Wilson-loop calculations use instanton/ADHM localization and equivariant Chern-character insertions. E-string elliptic genera, evaluated by Jeffrey–Kirwan residues, supply additional inputs.

Integrate out a massive charged bulk scalar to estimate nonlocal symmetry breaking; perform KK reduction to identify the uneaten gauge-invariant axion. Bulk Chern-Simons terms communicate cancellation of boundary gauge anomalies.

Identify symmetry-breaking operators through Wilson lines and their NSNS/RR gauge completions. Estimate contributions using open string worldsheet areas and Euclidean D-brane actions, including fermion zero-mode saturation.

Cosmology combines imported string-network scaling and a semi-analytic abundance formula with estimates of white-noise isocurvature and domain-wall decay. A cylindrical field ansatz classifies additional string solutions in the four-dimensional limit.

The imported interacting-DMDE formalism uses a canonical scalar coupled to fermionic dark matter through m0 A(ϕ)ψ̄ψ. The background effective potential is Veff = V + ρDM(ϕ), and the supplied linear perturbation equations use synchronous gauge.

A modified CLASS implementation computes background cosmology and linear perturbations for two benchmarks. Parameter variations around Model 2 examine changes in expansion and growth histories; these are illustrative numerical solutions.

Finite-density quark-condensate corrections, the Gell-Mann–Oakes–Renner relation and the pion–nucleon sigma term are used to construct the density-dependent axion potential and axion-dependent baryon mass.

LG contour integrals compute classical periods and their all-order complex-structure expansion. Integral A-brane homology bases impose flux quantization, while RR ground-state bases make symmetry charges manifest.

The analysis tests ranks of symmetry-allowed superpotential Hessians, compares with classical scalar mass spectra, and enumerates dS flux configurations with up to three nonzero eigencomponents. These calculations are evidence within the stated approximations.

A BPS domain-wall argument motivates a superpotential at most linear in fluxes. Expansion in discrete-symmetry eigencomponents then yields charge selection rules for W; invariant-function selection rules allow arbitrary flux powers in K and V.

State–operator correspondence gives Δ(q)=EqR. Fixed-charge boundary wavefunctions define a Euclidean path integral whose stationary, spherically homogeneous saddles and quadratic fluctuations organize the semiclassical spectrum; periodic-orbit stability supplies a further interpretation.

The EFT construction imposes Weyl and diffeomorphism invariance using dressed metrics. Homogeneous solutions yield q=∂L/∂μ and Δ=μq−L; fluctuation power counting estimates derivative and perturbative-unitarity cutoffs.

A likelihood relative to a=0 is formed from 724 available residual-frequency data points, treated as independent Gaussians with common σy=1.4×10^−14. Since the predicted residual is linear in a, the resulting likelihood is Gaussian in the polarization-weighted coefficient.

Geometric optics gives gμνkμkν=8aRμναβkμkαϵνϵβ. The authors evaluate this in the weak solar metric, integrate the velocity correction along the round trip, and differentiate the travel time to obtain a fractional frequency shift.

Differentiate the potential, divide by V, restore Planck factors, and evaluate the resulting functions on a specified field interval. Compare the slope and curvature alternatives separately; take the asymptotic slope limit with model parameters held fixed.

Identify canonical maxima, match their heights and curvatures, and compute the first unmatched Taylor coefficient. This supplies a local comparison dictionary and a controlled small-field diagnostic, rather than a claim about fitted cosmological observables.

The source evaluates and compares potential curves at fitted or illustrative parameter choices. It supplies no residual metric, observational likelihood for the S-dual model, or quantitative criterion for indistinguishability.

BPS charge sums are reorganized using Schwinger-like integrals, geometric series, and derivatives with respect to moduli. Small-modulus expansions and endpoint saddle estimates give asymptotic behavior; inverse gauge-kinetic mixing is incorporated through a matrix generalization.

One-loop scalar and spinor QED vacuum polarization is Fourier transformed into a Uehling correction to the Coulomb potential. Modified Gauss-law flux then determines an effective charge and its radius derivative. Explicit computations cover four and five dimensions, followed by a general-dimensional formulation.

Use rough uniform smearing for analytical intuition, smooth Gaussian/Lorentzian smearing for numerical bounds, perturbative bounce expansions, and numerical solution of the Cuscuton differential-algebraic background equations. The uniform window is explicitly acknowledged to lack the required differentiability.

Translate the stress-tensor SNEC into a smeared Ricci-curvature inequality. Rewrite null-affine integrals using physical time or scale factor; apply component inequalities while retaining the total cosmological background in H(a) and the affine parameter.

Review product-mode separation of the Lichnerowicz operator and the connection between Euclidean negative modes and Lorentzian Gregory-Laflamme thresholds. A complementary argument compares a one-loop thermal tachyonic contribution with the BF stability bound.

Compare Euclidean saddle free energies and microcanonical entropies. Estimate the Jeans threshold by equating thermal radiation energy to the mass of an AdS-sized black hole; retain subdominant saddles because they contribute to tunnelling.

Convert published piecewise E^-2 flux normalizations and their uncertainties into approximate astrophysical event counts using sample livetimes and flavor-dependent, zenith-averaged effective areas. Integrate each candidate propagated spectrum against those areas to predict counts.

Integrate the flavor-transition probability over source redshift, weighted by the emitted spectrum evaluated at E(1+z), production flavor fractions, and ρ(z)/H(z). Compare SFRD and several alternative source-population histories.

Construct a per-bin Gaussian likelihood below 100 TeV and a calibrated Poisson likelihood above 100 TeV, matching the reported one-sigma variations. Minimize the summed −2 log likelihood over flux parameters; use 100 BPL-null pseudoexperiments to construct illustrative 95% bands.

Numerically integrate the stiff ODE system in Julia using autoTsit5(Rosenbrock23), switching between Tsitouras Runge–Kutta and Rosenbrock-W methods. Compare lifetime estimates with numerical runs; fit invertible auxiliary functions to the approximate-attractor lifetime integral.

Nondimensionalize the equations, separate Hawking- and Schwinger-associated functions, and derive approximate trajectories by suppressing one contribution at a time. Locate an approximate attractor by setting the Schwinger exponent to zero; integrate or fit lifetime expressions and rescale parameters to dark-sector cases.

Extend the Hiscock–Weems coupled mass/charge evolution equations: a T^4 Hawking term with a geometric-optics scattering cross-section, plus electrostatic energy loss accompanying Schwinger discharge. The factor α corrects the cross-section and is not the fine-structure constant.

Introduce a target-space boundary gauge field a to preserve b-field gauge invariance, derive boundary couplings by Noether's method, and track terms surviving half-space integration. Varying the resulting defect action reproduces the on-shell current matching imposed by c|γ=0.

Use a doubled gauged NLSM: auxiliary torus coordinates make locally defined WZ gauging data global and act as periodic Lagrange multipliers. Multiplying their coupling by p enforces flat gauge fields with holonomies in (2π/p)Z; completing the square integrates out the quadratic gauge fields.

For the complex superconformal saddle, positive real gθθ reduces KSW to a three-dimensional problem. The authors analyze the horizon and conformal boundary analytically, then report numerical q=0,1 tests at 10^6 random interior points satisfying 0<r⋆<1 and r⋆<r+<r<10^3.

Construct and interpret saddles by Wick rotating Lorentzian charged black-hole families, imposing Killing-spinor integrability and global spin structure, and sometimes additionally continuing rotation or electric charge. Charges and chemical potentials are defined by analytic continuation from Lorentzian conventions.

Imported KSW criterion: at every point the real part of the metric-induced quadratic form must be positive for every nonzero real q-form, for all 0≤q≤d. Equivalently, in a diagonalizing real tangent-space basis, Σi|Arg λi|<π, with principal Arg in (−π,π].

For several charges, the authors use charge-to-mass vectors, convex-hull kinematics, and the triangle inequality. The sufficient condition applies along every fixed charge direction; the necessary decreasing sequence may change direction between steps.

Magnetic Einstein equations give ft=fr=f and an integral expression for f in terms of LF. Horizon degeneracy is imposed through dM/drh=0. Renormalization-group and trace-anomaly reasoning relate the strong-field action to running gauge coupling.

Decay arguments use charge conservation, strict loss of total daughter rest mass, and extremality bounds. Monotonicity of Z̄ implies strict subadditivity of Q̄; iterative selection of a daughter with larger charge-to-mass ratio yields a necessary discrete condition.

The review organizes mass mechanisms using sterile-sector mass hierarchies and the dimension-five Weinberg operator LLHH/Λ. Type-II and type-III seesaws use triplet scalars and fermions; radiative models forbid the tree-level operator through particle content or symmetries and generate Majorana masses through loops.

An adapted constraint map covers sterile mass versus electron-flavor mixing: astrophysics/cosmology dominate below MeV, beam dumps and meson decays around MeV–GeV, colliders around GeV–TeV, and electroweak precision measurements above TeV. Muon and tau maps are referred elsewhere rather than supplied.

Reconstructed w(z) curves use best-fit coefficients and pointwise errors propagated from the MCMC parameter matrix after burn-in removal. Best-fit χ² and AIC are also compared across ΛCDM and the four parametrizations. These are reported calculations, not independently reproduced here.
Extend w(a)=w0+wa(1−a)+wb(1−a)²+wc(1−a)³. CPL− varies only w0; CPL varies w0 and wa; CPL+ also varies wb and marginalizes over it; CPL++ varies all four coefficients and marginalizes over wb and wc.

MCMC varies Ωm, h and the coefficients allowed by each parametrization. The authors report approximately 500,000 points and converged chains, then obtain marginalized one-dimensional distributions and 68.3%/95.5% two-dimensional contours. They state that their baseline pipeline reproduces the DESI DR1 ΛCDM and CPL constraints.

The authors implement the models in CLASS and sample with MontePython MCMC, requiring Gelman–Rubin R−1≤10⁻². Six standard ΛCDM parameters and one coupling amplitude are sampled. GetDist provides posterior summaries and marginalized contours.

Model comparison uses best-fit χ² and AIC=−2 ln Lmax+2N, with a parameter-count penalty. Individual BAO predictions are additionally compared through residuals normalized by observational uncertainties; correlations among the BAO distance observables are incorporated.

The author evaluates DBI and Wess–Zumino probe actions, including displayed order-α′² tangent- and normal-bundle curvature corrections and flux-related terms. Gauss–Codazzi relations express these curvatures through bulk curvature and the embedding's second fundamental form.

The four-dimensional Planck scale is obtained differently for the two spatial topologies: projected bulk gravity for k=0, and a spherical bubble separating nearby AdS vacua with Israel junction matching for k=1.

Time-translation invariance gives conserved momentum conjugate to bulk time T. Setting this energy to zero for the observer used to describe nucleation at rest, then changing to comoving proper time, yields the late-time Friedmann equation.

Dimensional reduction of Type IIB form fields on localized degeneration modes supplies worldsheet scalars. Their chirality determines central charges; field dependence of their kinetic terms distinguishes free currents from interacting modes and guides the heterotic interpretation.

Limiting mixed Hodge structures and the Hodge-norm growth theorem determine asymptotic couplings. Mayer–Vietoris and Clemens–Schmid identify Gr2 with H²(Z)/(im i*+im j*) and Gr3 with H³(X1)⊕H³(X2), connecting algebraic asymptotics to degeneration geometry.

Translate δK<<1 into volume/coupling bounds and logarithmic field-distance inequalities. The appendix sketches previously calculated one-loop moduli two-point functions; Poisson resummation and steepest descent are used for the axio-dilaton expansion.

Construct lattice-summed functions E_s from symplectic period pairings and |n_I Z^I+m^I F_I| denominators; isolate a lattice sector to identify proposed large-field growth. Compare with the axio-dilaton Eisenstein series.

Separate modulus and flux directions using an orthogonal field basis. Remove the modulus contribution from the external Weyl variation while retaining its contributions from Weyl rescalings to Einstein frame.

Promote solution parameters to infinitesimally spacetime-dependent off-shell configurations, reduce the action, and extract quadratic derivative coefficients after imposing algebraic relations defining the vacuum family.

Vary fluxes in an electric frame through gauge potentials depending on the AdS radial coordinate. Include the top-form boundary-term sign and an auxiliary radial metric variation σ1 chosen to cancel linear derivative terms.
Find an approximate valley from ∂VE/∂h=0, substitute it into the action, and neglect slow-roll-suppressed derivatives of VJ to obtain an effective single-field description.

Estimate the cutoff from field-space Ricci curvature near vanishing Higgs components. Estimate perturbative reheating using modulus and Higgs decay rates, oscillation-averaged energy densities, and an approximately sum-separable energy budget.

Use covariant multifield background equations numerically, including initially displaced trajectories, to assess the analytic valley. Compute slow-roll observables and impose CMB amplitude normalization.

Extend the field content recursively: reinterpret dual equations of motion as Bianchi identities, introduce dual potentials, and match general transformation ansätze after imposing duality relations. Young-symmetry restrictions and field redefinitions reduce the dual-gravity ansatz.

Use the circle-reduction field dictionary to uplift known β variations into GL(11)-covariant metric and four-form variations. Directly vary the equations of motion and Bianchi identity to establish the reported closed transformation multiplet.

Spherical reduction gives a one-dimensional effective action and Hamiltonian constraint. Constant-scalar AdS2×S2 configurations satisfy algebraic Bertotti–Robinson equations balancing gradients of the cosmological and charge-induced potentials.

The authors use perturbative extremal Reissner–Nordström flows for Model 1, algebraic and numerical near-horizon branch analysis, and linearized scalar/S2-volume equations. Stability is assessed through mass-matrix eigenvalues and the AdS2 Breitenlohner–Freedman bound.

The pivot crossing time is determined by following post-inflationary evolution until effective radiation domination, w≈1/3. This gives N*=58.27 for the WLIF Q*=0.27 benchmark and N*=55.86 for the WLIS Q*=100 benchmark, replacing earlier fixed N*=60 evaluations.

WI2easy evolves background dynamics and coupled curvature perturbations, numerically determining G(Q). All reported results include stochastic noise in the radiation perturbation equation required by total stress-energy conservation.

Flat differential characters retain discrete holonomy and torsion data. A Zk connection č gives the degree-four gauge background Č=č*č; on Lk⁷(m) its characteristic class is m²x². Quadratic refinements refine the torsion pairing (x²,x²)=−1/k.

Universal constraints follow from Q̃(jn)=nQ̃(j)−j²n(n−1)/(2k) modulo one and Q̃(0)=0. Chosen refinements are constructed using a bounding eight-manifold and an odd integral lift of the Wu class; Appendix B uses localized bordism and generalized homology.

Seven-dimensional invertible anomaly theories encode partition-function phases. Reduced Dirac η-invariants are evaluated using equivariant index theory on lens spaces, with product formulas for Lk³×K3 and separate treatment of Spin structures.

Gauge transformations and corrected field strengths are built successively by canceling noncovariant three-bracket terms. The mixed two-/three-bracket fundamental identity and trace cyclicity are used to establish the stated infinitesimal gauge invariances.

The construction explicitly computes associators, ordinary commutators and their Jacobiator, then implements a two-term L∞ algebra with V0=V1=VB⊕VC. ℓ1 identifies V1 with V0 and vanishes on V0; ℓ3 on three degree-zero inputs is minus their Jacobiator.

Replace the ordinary open-string trace by a quantum trace. The proposed worldsheet description dresses Chan–Paton endpoints with Chern–Simons ribbon graphs attached to worldsheet boundaries, whose summed interactions generate the deformation.

Implement cutting and gluing through large-N q-deformed two-dimensional Yang–Mills. Chern numbers add componentwise under gluing; worldvolume holonomies label boundary states, and brane–antibrane annihilation glues open-string amplitudes into closed-string amplitudes.

Use the Euclidean extended-Hilbert-space construction: impose an isometric cutting map and a shrinkable entanglement boundary condition so that cutting and regluing preserve the original correlations and produce a subregion trace.

Impose f(re)=0 together with f′(re)=0, equivalently zero Hawking temperature, to determine extremal configurations. Insert re into the mass relation and numerically examine the extremal charge-to-mass ratio; high-order equations motivate numerical treatment.

Construct a geometry-dependent photon-sphere potential and a two-component field φ with φr=√f ∂rH and φθ=(1/r)∂θH. Its zeros locate photon spheres; normalized-vector winding and total topological charge classify the configurations.

Compare metric profiles, extremal mass–charge diagrams, numerical tables, and vector-field plots across selected parameters. The photon-sphere analysis uses a delta-function topological-current representation and the conservation law stated in the paper.

The authors also compute AIC=χ²min+2n and BIC=χ²min+n ln N. Separately, they fit CPL and its quadratic/cubic extensions in (1−a) to the mean quintessence equation of state, holding w0=wϕ(0); these approximation exercises differ from fitting those parametrizations directly to observations.

MCMC scans cover flat ΛCDM, curved ΛCDM, flat exponential ϕCDM, curved ϕCDM and flat CPL. The authors report at least approximately 150,000 points per case and converged chains; MCEvidence supplies Bayesian evidence comparisons. Without shooting algorithms, some present-day parameters are derived by postprocessing.

Uses slow-roll reduction of the gravitational field equations, flatness and current-Hubble-scale inequalities, a tail-duration TCC inequality, and energy-density/e-fold matching to reheating temperature.

Studies separate autonomous systems in e-fold time N: an F(R)-only system with constant m=−Ḧ/H³, specializing to m=0, and a two-dimensional scalar–matter system. Fixed points, Jacobian eigenvalues and numerical trajectories supply the dynamical evidence.

Represent the coupling by constrained Schwinger integrals/Eisenstein series. Solve the heterotic half-BPS condition Σi ni mi=0 as a linear Diophantine equation, treating winding numbers as coefficients and introducing unconstrained momentum integers.

Apply Poisson resummation and modified-Bessel integral representations to organize contributions into worldsheet-instanton bound states. Their coefficients satisfy C12 C34+C14 C23+C13 C24=0, which restricts allowed configurations.

Regulate the ultraviolet-divergent integrals, minimally subtract regulator divergences, then apply ζ-function regularization to infinite sums. Arithmetic reorganizations of coprime sums and regularized factors such as ζ(0)=−1/2 expose cancellations between winding sectors.

Power counting, metric-background expansion and saturated-propagator spin decomposition organize the renormalizability and mode discussion. Quadratic gravity uses a fourth-order kinetic Gaussian with UV propagator behavior 1/p⁴; the GR EFT uses 1/p².

The paper surveys three ghost prescriptions: negative norms with Feynman poles; positive physical norms with anti-Feynman ghost poles and modified loop rules; and purely virtual fakeons using averaged prescriptions. It reports unitarity results under these alternatives while retaining interpretational questions.

An auxiliary scalar and conformal transformation to the Einstein frame expose the scalaron potential. Leading slow-roll expressions for the scalar spectral index and amplitude are then matched to quoted CMB data.

WZW-like interactions are defined by integrating closed invariant forms over a bulk extension; integer coefficients ensure bulk independence. Anomalous abelian defects are instead dressed by auxiliary defect gauge fields implementing fractional Chern–Simons terms.

Background gauge transformations and modified Ward identities diagnose 2-group structure. Quantization of its Postnikov class supplies symmetry matching along RG flows, analogous in use to anomaly matching.

Rewrite Noether conservation as closure of a differential-form current, integrate and exponentiate it to obtain topological operators, and define their action through linking with charged operators. Discrete symmetries are identified directly through defects and charged operators.

Use the Dirac index density, A-roof genus and Chern characters; decompose representation traces through sixth order into reference traces. Tensor-product identities, symmetric/exterior-power characters and branching rules provide representation indices and identify spectra inherited from E8.

Match the boundary anomaly polynomial to the special factorization supplied by M-theory, rather than an arbitrary Green-Schwarz factorization. Cancellation of the irreducible gravitational term requires sum_i n_i dim(r_i)=248. For a general simple algebra, eight equations remain; they are linear in multiplicities at fixed boundary coefficient a, with polynomial dependence on a.
Frequency ratios obey ΔR/R=(Kµ,1−Kµ,2)Δµ/µ. Adopted sensitivities are Kµ=0 for optical electronic transitions, −1/2 for molecular vibrational transitions and −1 for microwave hyperfine transitions.

Bayesian emcee MCMC and Fisher forecasts are applied to frequency-domain signals. Clock noise is modeled by a one-sided white-plus-flicker PSD, Sy(f)=h0+h−1/f; independent clock PSDs are summed. The authors compare Fisher and sampled posteriors.

The released forecast package accepts clock instability, accuracy, sensitivity coefficients, clock pairs and frequency-domain signal models, then generates simulated data, amplitude uncertainties and theory-parameter projections.

Theory predictions are projected into the CPL (w0,wa) plane by fitting predicted observables using their observational errors. A constant field shift is used to remove the linear term in the nonminimal coupling.

Theory predictions use hi_class. Official likelihoods are implemented through Cobaya; PolyChord nested sampling yields posteriors and Bayesian evidence. Best-fit χ² and Deviance Information Criterion provide additional comparisons with ΛCDM.

Integrate w(a) to obtain the density evolution h(a), then constrain CPL, BA, EXP, LOG and JBP parameterizations analytically and numerically. Appendix A tests maxima of a²Ωde h(a), conditional on possible TCC violation occurring during late dark-energy domination.

For selected f(T) models, insert F(T) into the modified Friedmann equation and apply the logarithmic TCC bound to the resulting expansion history; interpret their effective phantom/quintessence evolution.

Dimensionally reduce the Einstein-frame metric ds^2_(4+n)=exp(2A phi) ds4^2+exp(2B phi) dsn^2, with 2A+nB=0. Read KK masses from internal Laplacian eigenvalues after the Weyl rescaling, rather than directly from the higher-dimensional metric radius.

Translate entropy bounds into (LambdaUV/LambdaIR)^gamma <= (MP/LambdaUV)^(d-2), with gamma=1 for CEB and 2 for CKN. Substitute the KK-dominated species scale and the chosen cosmological IR scale. A separate thermodynamic argument relates CKN saturation to extremizing a radiation box's free energy with respect to its time-dependent size.

Apply known late-time attractors for V=V0 exp(-lambda phi). For k=0 and lambda^2>6, a(t) scales as t^(1/3); for k=-1 and lambda^2>2, a(t) scales as t. Track the canonical rolling direction and calculate the time exponent of LKK/LH.

Linearization around magnetic RN in unitary gauge decouples the charged W perturbation into a complex Proca equation. Angular separation gives a radial Schrödinger problem; negative eigenvalues diagnose instability and zero modes locate bifurcations. Multiple shooting constructs radial modes and nonlinear spherical solutions.

After gauge fixing, the axial problem comprises ten elliptic equations. The authors use FreeFem finite elements with Newton–Raphson iteration and assess accuracy through virial relations, gravitational constraints, and agreement between asymptotic and integral ADM masses.

Sensitivity uses a Poissonian χ² with normalization uncertainties implemented through nuisance pulls. Significances assume Wilks’ theorem, including √Δχ² for one degree of freedom; this statistical calibration is assumed rather than independently established here.

Potential bounds are translated into mediator-mass/effective-coupling contours using Yukawa potentials and summed Earth, Moon, Sun, Milky Way and cosmological contributions. The adopted source populations and spatial models are inputs to this translation.

The authors modify the GLoBES probability engine to include LRF potentials and numerically calculate probabilities, event spectra and sensitivities. They avoid relying on small-new-physics expansions when the LRF potential approaches the standard matter scale.

Scalar profiles are substituted into the five-dimensional action and integrated over the extra dimension. Radion stabilization is assessed from stationary points and positive second derivatives; some effective potentials are evaluated numerically rather than in closed form.

The imported CMS singular-perturbation construction combines an outer solution obtained by dropping Φ″ with a visible-brane boundary-layer solution obtained by dropping the potential term. Asymptotic matching supplies an approximate scalar profile.
For the backreacted example, the imported superpotential method reduces the coupled second-order system to first-order equations, with V=(W′)²/8−κ²W²/6 and specifically matched brane potentials.

The construction starts from the Schwarzschild maximal extension, introduces outgoing Vaidya mass loss, and attempts to integrate double-null Einstein equations using first integrals and a local spherical mass function before adding charge.

Horizon discussion uses radial null expansions and distinguishes local apparent horizons from globally defined event horizons. Mass and charge evolution are described through Bondi energy balance and Maxwell charge-flux balance rather than a solved microscopic emission model.

Analyze photon spheres through H=√(f/h)/sinθ and a vector field built from metric-weighted derivatives of H. Normalized vector fields and their topological charges classify photon-sphere behavior; the conventional reference conditions are Veff=∂rVeff=0.

Determine horizons from zeros of the metric function and extremality from simultaneous horizon and zero-temperature conditions. Compare extremal mass–charge curves with Q=M; numerical parameter exploration is used where higher-order equations are analytically impractical.

Potential slow-roll analysis computes ε and η from canonical-field derivatives, then ns≈1−6ε*+2η* and r≈16ε*. The scalar amplitude fixes the potential scale; the e-fold/reheating relation determines the pivot field value.

The authors compare classical inflaton trajectories and total expansion across initial field values and coupling choices, including rapid descent followed by Hubble-friction-induced slow roll. These trajectories supplement the pivot-scale observable calculations.

Use exceptional field theory and a consistent S3 truncation to three-dimensional N=4 gauged supergravity. The lowest-level mass matrices follow from the embedding tensor, dressed T-tensor and Yukawa couplings; scalar harmonics on the round S3 extend them to the infinite KK towers.

The spectral prescription decomposes the known N=(4,0) enhancement-point representations under the surviving bosonic symmetry and replaces n by −1+ΓB for bosons or −1+ΓF for fermions. Here ΓB²=1+cosh²α[n(n+2)+u²sinh²β], and ΓF²=ΓB²+coshβ sinhα(coshβ sinhα+2qu sinhβ coshα).

Analyze the assumptions attributed to Čencov's uniqueness theorem—permanent i.i.d. measurements and sufficient statistics—using recording-device backreaction and the transfer of statistics between observers. 'Local information objectivity' denotes agreement of their resulting inferences.

Introduce a state-dependent metric and a cubic probability deformation, motivate compatible nonlinear evolution through Kähler–Finsler geometry and nonlinear-optics analogies, and connect leading-order intrinsic triple interference to matter-wave Talbot patterns.

Numerically integrate the homogeneous scalar equations and Friedmann equation for three benchmarks. Covariant multifield quantities, including trajectory turn rate and isocurvature mass, assess whether inflation behaves approximately as a single-field model.

Numerically evolve linear Fourier modes with canonically normalized kinetic terms and prescribed Bunch–Davies initial conditions a few e-foldings before inflation ends. Late-time Bogolubov coefficients yield spectra and integrated comoving abundances; inflaton and modulus modes are coupled, while the axion mode evolves independently at linear order.

Combine asymptotic FRW attractor scalings with the tower/species gradient identity and EFT scale inequalities. Analyze potential-and-kinetic tracking, kination, and a proposed asymptotically negligible scalar-kinetic contribution separately.

Use regular mode choices in de Sitter and Milne examples, followed by power-law scalar-mode superpositions, to distinguish past trans-Planckian tracing from future cutoff crossing. A three-stage curvature-dilution model supplies the accelerated-expansion bound.

Control thermal tails with Markov's inequality, then use Cauchy–Schwarz, Hölder and trace-norm estimates to compare truncated states and swap expectations. Fannes' inequality supplies a separate existence argument for a single-copy distinguishing operator.

Double the bulk and boundary systems. A bulk swap exchanges ab with a′b′ while leaving i,i′ untouched. Its exact expectation is tr(ρσ), or tr(ρ²) for identical reduced states, giving a purity diagnostic supported entirely in the causal wedge.

Encode the bulk swap through V⊗V using S_∂(V⊗V)=(V⊗V)S. Causal-wedge isometry preserves its expectation values and allows a boundary calculation without specifying an encoding map for the baby universe.

Vacuum-energy discussion uses dimensional regularization, ε=4−D, and subtraction with finite reparametrization freedom. The displayed free-field result sums n_i m_i^4 ln[m_i²/(4πμ²)]/(64π²), with signed internal-degree weights.

Homogeneity and isotropy reduce Einstein’s equations to FLRW equations, closed with an equation of state. Expansion is inferred through redshift and luminosity distance: a small-z series is distinguished from fitting the full distance-redshift relation.

Newtonian toy construction uses Gauss’s law, conserved mechanical energy and mass conservation to obtain scale-factor equations resembling dust Friedmann equations, after setting aside the infinite-distribution boundary problem.

Power-law scaling with an unbounded quantum number N is imposed on fluxes, geometry and coupling, then constrained by ∂ρV=∂τV=0, Bianchi identities and flux equations. A canonically normalized two-field Hessian assesses the universal scalar sector.

Dimensional reduction and Weyl rescaling determine the volume/dilaton dependence of each potential term. Rewriting in terms of gs=e^ϕ and ρ isolates a common D-dependent factor, also appearing in mKK², so the relevant potential-to-KK ratios have D-independent scalings.
Invert S=f̃(rh) to obtain rh(S), substitute into the horizon mass and metric Hawking temperature, solve the mass expression for ε, and compare extremal mass and fixed-mass entropy derivatives.

Lambert W functions express the inverse radius for logarithmic and exponential entropy ansätze. The EGB entropy example invokes integration of dM/T; a power-law entropy S=πrh^a supplies an additional diagnostic.

A twice-subtracted complex-s dispersion relation is differentiated twice at s=2mϕ²−t/2. Low-energy absorptive contributions are subtracted, Regge states cancel the forward graviton singularity, and the optical theorem supplies positivity for the remaining high-energy integral.

Post-reheating production is computed with ṅϕ+3Hnϕ=R(T), including Higgs-portal, graviton-mediated and interference amplitudes. Thermal rates use Bessel/Meijer-G functions, followed by a high-reheating-temperature asymptotic integration.

The author calculates leading one-loop non-gravitational and portal-dependent gravitational amplitudes using FeynRules, FeynArts, FeynCalc and Package-X. A leading two-loop gravitational self-coupling contribution is imported and combined with these results.

Construct scalar charge-to-mass vectors ζ=-∇log(m/M_Pl), analogous vectors for sqrt(T), and convex hulls for towers, strings and species scales. The projection α=ζ·T̂ gives the exponential decay rate; hull generators identify towers leading in some asymptotic direction.

Use dimensional-reduction mass scalings and KK, oscillator and wrapped-brane interpretations. Divide multi-monomial volumes into ordered saxionic growth sectors, approximate each by a dominant monomial, and track sliding when joining sector descriptions.

Use a Gaussian compressed-CMB likelihood for θ_*, Ω_bh² and Ω_mh². Compute sound horizons assuming standard pre-recombination cosmology, and fit the supernova magnitude–Hubble combination as a nuisance parameter.

Sample uniformly in ε using δ_i=ε(m_A/H_0+1)^1.5 exp(−m_A/H_0), to cover very small initial displacements. For birefringence, compute β=0.42 deg ×(c_γ/2π)(A_0−A_LSS)/F_A from the same background solution, with c_γ an additional parameter.

Numerically integrate the axion background equation and Friedmann evolution; determine F_A iteratively by enforcing E(a=1)=1, with a reported convergence tolerance of 0.01%. Perform MCMC inference with emcee.
Uses a semiclassical Euclidean bounce, an exponential bounce ansatz, and one-loop counterterms. The stated corrected potential is Veff=V+(ℏλ/2)⟨ϕ²(t)⟩, evolved with ϕ̈+3Hϕ̇+dVeff/dϕ=0.

Reports separate and combined MCMC fits using Pantheon+SH0ES, BAO, and cosmic-chronometer data, with imposed priors and χ²-based likelihoods; KDE and posterior contours summarize parameter distributions.

Introduces a Breit–Wigner-inspired dark-energy density combining Λ(t), residual energy ER, and an α-weighted function of J(t)/I(t); converts time derivatives to field derivatives to impose a steepness condition. Explicit J and I forms are delegated to an external reference.

Renormalization-group improvement identifies k(r)=ξ/r, substitutes prescribed running couplings into the lapse, and expands to first order in εG and εe. Horizon and extremality corrections are then sought using f(r+)=0 and surface gravity κ=f′(r+)/2.

Appendix B invokes the Wetterich functional renormalization-group equation and an Einstein–Hilbert truncation with gauge fluctuations. It supplies approximate beta-function parameterizations, including βg=(2+ηN)g and photon anomalous dimension ηF≈−cg g, with cg>0 and scheme-dependent gravitational coefficients.

Apply fermionic localization and the Duistermaat–Heckman theorem on coadjoint orbits. Sum thermal fixed points, remove global bosonic and fermionic zero modes, and evaluate determinants from roots and fermion weights using regularization.

Use the imported classifications of global and local superconformal symmetries to enumerate candidate soft-mode theories. Generate supersymmetric Schwarzian actions through supergroup BF/JT gravity with mixed boundary conditions and asymptotically AdS2 constraints.

Extract charge-resolved spectra using character expansions, Fourier/Poisson resummation and inverse Laplace transforms. Infer minimal quadratic charge-algebra deformations by symmetry, Jacobi identities and comparison with the calculated spectra.

Impose finite Hawking temperature, finite Ricci scalar and exterior-signature inequalities; separately solve the source-free Maxwell equations and Bianchi identity on the deformed geometry. Analyze extremality through simultaneous double zeros of f and h.

Solve the invariant-distance or proper-time integral self-consistently by local Taylor expansion, coefficient matching and series inversion. Recursion determines the relation between areal radius and the chosen invariant from deformation coefficients treated as physical input.
The authors use Singular to solve the constrained extremization problem and report the complete set of extrema at the origin within their restricted RSTU search.

Scherk–Schwarz reduction and a flux-to-embedding-tensor dictionary encode the scalar potential and consistency constraints. The authors report matching embedding-tensor quadratic constraints to the required flux Bianchi identities and tadpoles.

Mirror prepotentials and GV-invariant instanton sums determine periods; analytic continuation treats the shrinking conifold curve. Special flux choices yield perturbatively flat loci, whose instanton racetracks provide initial guesses for numerical solutions of the full flux F-term equations.

KKLT points initialise Newton searches for Kähler F-flat AdS precursors. The uplifted search solves stationarity of the full potential and includes shifts of complex-structure moduli and the axio-dilaton; the uplift-to-AdS-energy ratio Xi is used to select well-aligned configurations.

Geometry selection uses favourable polar-dual Kreuzer–Skarke polytopes and fine, regular, star triangulations. Requirements include trilayer orientifolds, a mirror conifold curve with GV invariant two, and enough rigid prime toric divisors after excluding the throat-intersecting divisor.

Black-hole construction expands a radial ansatz perturbatively in α′. In the two-charge example, inverse-radius series reduce the equations to algebraic coefficient relations; generating functions are identified with Mathematica, then integration constants are fixed by charges, mass and horizon regularity.

Compactification analysis combines perturbative ten-dimensional EOM/Bianchi identities, DBI charge–tension comparisons for fluxed branes, and Laplacian eigenmode expansions of cycle delta-forms to compare ordinary and smeared linking numbers.

Extended Wald analysis uses gauge-covariant symmetry variations, Noether–Wald and generalized Komar forms, and integration between infinity and the bifurcation surface to obtain first-law and Smarr relations.

The gravity truncation is Euclidean Einstein–Hilbert theory with a linear background–fluctuation metric split, ghosts and gauge fixing. Computations employ a Litim-type regulator, Landau–DeWitt gravitational gauge and Landau gauge for SM gauge fields.
The authors use the Wetterich functional RG equation to obtain beta functions, locate simultaneous fixed points and linearize the flow to classify directions through the stability-matrix eigenvalues.

RG trajectories connect ultraviolet fixed-point behaviour to specified low-energy couplings. Regulator-motivated changes of gravitational fixed-point values and variations of the gravitational gauge parameter estimate truncation uncertainty; the Appendix's mass-bound estimate neglects trans-Planckian running.

One-loop amplitudes are split into EW and gravitational contributions. The EW part is evaluated through a dispersion integral or total cross section; massive-vector contributions dominate at large cutoff. The leading gravitational part comes from loop-corrected matter–matter–graviton vertices in t-channel exchange and is negative in the studied models.

A twice-subtracted contour sum rule defines B^(2)(Λ,t) around the s–u crossing point s*=(Σ external pole masses squared−t)/2. Subtracting the graviton t-pole makes the defined quantity regular as t→0; contour deformation relates it to an absorptive-part integral.

The condensate is calculated from quantized left/right tensor modes in weak quantum gravity, using a Bunch–Davies vacuum in both stiff and inflationary eras and an ultraviolet momentum cutoff. The review attributes the dominant contribution to oscillatory subhorizon modes.

For planar axionic walls the treatment uses a local Minkowski background, decoupled helicity equations and a field redefinition to a one-dimensional wave equation with helicity-dependent effective potentials. Periodically modulated inflation is analysed through potential slow-roll parameters.

Assuming an approximately constant condensate produces V(b)=C b with C<0. Homogeneous, isotropic Einstein–axion equations become a dynamical system; the Friedmann constraint x^2+y^2=1 reduces it to a two-dimensional phase portrait using x=cos(phi), y=sin(phi) and zeta=lambda/(lambda+1).

Temperature follows from surface gravity and entropy from the Wald formula. The authors test the first law by fitting M(S) at fixed Q and M(Q) at fixed S, then comparing their derivatives with T and electric potential Φ.

A massless test scalar is separated into spherical harmonics and evolved using a Schrödinger-type radial equation in tortoise coordinates. Light-cone finite differences and Prony extraction are compared with third-order WKB frequencies, principally at l=6 and overtone n=0.

Numerical shooting integrates the reduced radial field equations from a high-order near-horizon Taylor expansion toward infinity. Horizon data are tuned to obtain asymptotic flatness, and mass is extracted from the asymptotic metric.

Supplemental calculations include explicit SMEFT RG combinations, UV matching examples and finite-radius dispersive contour integrals within the EFT regime. The contour analysis explains why positivity of an amplitude-derived arc need not imply positivity of an individual dimension-eight coefficient.

For s and u cuts, equal operator dimensions isolate a nonnegative homogeneous contribution; even powers make the channels add with the same sign. Spinor-helicity counting and Lorentz invariance of single-scale bubble integrals establish the forward t-cut result.

Dimensional regularization and on-shell unitarity extract one-loop running from coefficients of ln(si/μ²). Scale independence of the full amplitude relates tree-level coupling running to discontinuities, evaluated as phase-space integrals of products of tree amplitudes across all s, t and u cuts.

Integrate fixed-point relations and analyze linearized eigenvalues/eigenvectors for existence and stability. A series near the curvature-dominated origin supplies a special closed phase-space heteroclinic expression, subsequently integrated into an implicit proper-time solution.

Rewrite cosmological evolution using Hubble-normalized scalar velocities and potential, N=ln a, and the effective slope γ=−∇ln V. Supplementing its evolution gives an autonomous double-exponential system, with γ constrained to a line in exponent space.

Analyze additional non-chiral open-string states through boundary-state overlaps and loop-channel orbifold projections before evaluating one-loop beta coefficients; intersection numbers alone do not determine the full light spectrum.
Impose the N=1 angle condition Σθi=0 mod 2π, its wrapping-number equation and the inequality A/xA+B/xB+C/xC+D/xD<0; impose twisted/untwisted RR cancellation and K-theory congruences modulo four.

Construct fractional cycles from one-quarter bulk and twisted-cycle contributions, with fixed-point charge signs; calculate chiral bifundamental, symmetric and antisymmetric multiplicities using intersections with branes, orientifold images and O6-planes.

WGCHull(II) searches for a hyperplane placing all supplied hull vertices on its designated interior side and minimizes its distance from the origin. The paper rewrites this as positive-definite quadratic maximization under linear constraints and asserts polynomial runtime; that optimization premise remains unresolved in this pass.

WGCHull(I) adapts Quickhull: initialize a simplex, repeatedly add exterior points, replace visible facets using the beneath-beyond construction and retain the supporting half-spaces and vertex list. The Quickhull algorithm and its complexity estimates are imported.

Minimal realizations are approached through exhaustive subset enumeration and through a restricted maximum-volume N-simplex search. The latter additionally assumes the chosen simplex vertices are vertices of the full hull.

Determine the pivot-to-end e-fold count through horizon matching and entropy conservation, including aend/areh for the transition to radiation domination. Although no separate reheating mechanism is required, the paper allows approximately 1–6 e-folds between inflation ending and radiation domination.
Evolve the coupled inflaton–radiation background: φ̈+(3H+Υ)φ̇+V,φ=0 and ρ̇r+4Hρr=Υφ̇², with the Friedmann equation and ρr=(π²g⋆/30)T⁴. The numerical study adopts Υ=CΥT and Υ=CΥT³/MPl².

Use WI2easy for background and coupled perturbation evolution. Numerically generated enhancement functions G(Q) are spline interpolated into the scalar spectrum; spectral tilt, running and tensor-to-scalar ratio are evaluated at Hubble exit. The four potentials give almost indistinguishable G(Q) for each adopted dissipation law.

For rotating branes, regard S, J and Q as a complete extensive set and define T, Ωi and U through mass derivatives. Apply the chain rule to the explicit η dependence and state-variable responses, using dM=T+dS+ΣiΩidJi+UdQ, then select different quantities to hold invariant.

Use f(r+,c)=0 to express the mass in terms of horizon position and the deformation η. Vary η under a fixed-mass constraint, allowing horizon position and entropy to change, and invoke the horizon first laws to obtain entropy-response identities.
