Match the gravity-sector density to PI/NFW or Gaussian/Lorentzian densities and integrate for the shape function with a throat condition. The nonlinear f(Q) branch instead uses embedding class I through the Karmakar condition; nonlinear noncommutative f(Q,T) equations are solved numerically.

The Volume Integral Quantifier is defined with the paper’s normalization IV=8π∫(ρ+pr)r²dr. A finite cutoff r1≥r0 replaces the infinite upper limit; the reported small-exotic-matter result is IV→0 as r1→r0.

TOV force balance is used to assess equilibrium and is interpreted by the author as stability. The supplied discussion describes oppositely directed balancing forces; it does not supply a perturbation-spectrum analysis.

The imported screening treatment uses a narrow axion transition near a dense source's surface. Its gradient changes the exterior dilaton charge; minimizing interior and exterior gradient energies determines the local field configuration.

Coarse-grain the action over rapid axion oscillations, introduce Madelung density and phase variables, and derive continuity/Euler equations. Bianchi identities determine energy-momentum exchange among the scalar and matter components.

A modified CLASS implementation evolves homogeneous backgrounds and linear perturbations. Numerical examples use fixed cosmological parameters and adiabatic Gaussian primordial initial conditions based on the Planck 2018 ΛCDM best fit.

Identify the 5d curvature with that of the classical type-IIA saxionic slice after separating the logarithmic volume coordinate. The resulting expression is R_M=−3(n−2)(n−1)/4−K^{ab}K^{cd}K^{ef}K_{ac[e}K_{b]df}, where K^{ab} inverts K_ab=K_abc M^c.

Analyze trajectories t^a=t_0^a+e_0^a ϕ+Σ_i e_i^a ϕ^{γ_i}, with nef directions and 1>γ_1>γ_2>…≥0, then map them to M-theory variables. Adapted divisor bases and asymptotic matrix expansions isolate divergent curvature contractions.

Use BPS-string charge-to-tension ratios and no-force relations to diagnose rigid sectors. For rank two, the leading rigid curvature is expressed through det M/(det K_μν)^2; the finite-distance sign analysis also uses the Hodge index theorem.

Numerically integrates background trajectories and reconstructs density fractions and equations of state. Present-epoch initial conditions are constructed analytically from Planck 2018 and DESI DR2+CMB+Pantheon+ CPL parameters, using slow-roll and non-slow-roll prescriptions.

Constructs a four-dimensional autonomous system using potential-specific closures Γϕ(λϕ), where Γϕ=V″V/(V′)². Uses Jacobian spectra, discussion of nonhyperbolic/center-manifold stability, and Poincaré compactification of reduced constant-slope branches.

Solve bulk Einstein equations, Israel boundary conditions, and scalar equations for spherical and spatially flat brane embeddings. Analyze signals traveling through the bulk as well as along the induced brane geometry.

Use autonomous systems, fixed points, and center-manifold asymptotics to resolve potentials marginal at leading order. An auxiliary reconstruction procedure obtains potentials from expansion profiles under expanding, monotonically rolling scalar assumptions.

Linear gravitational perturbations use a Schrödinger-like radial equation, outgoing waves at infinity, and mixed ingoing/outgoing waves at the object's surface. A viscous membrane can encode an effective interior boundary condition.

Model-specific boson-star inspiral templates jointly include spin-induced quadrupoles and tidal deformability tied to common structural parameters. The reviewed recovery studies find biases when one finite-size contribution is omitted.
EHT interpretation compares total-intensity, polarization, and multiwavelength constraints with GRMHD image libraries varying spin, magnetic flux, and ion-to-electron temperature ratio.

Double holography replaces the coupled geometry–quantum-correlator problem by classical bulk Einstein equations with an end-of-the-world brane obeying Israel junction conditions. Bulk black holes localized on the brane map to solutions of the induced semiclassical equations, incorporating all orders of quantum matter backreaction and, in principle, arbitrary matter states.

The essay uses horizon formation, reported overspinning tests, and an exact AdS3 quantum Penrose inequality as indirect diagnostics. Generalized entropy replaces horizon area and includes gravitational entropy plus quantum matter entropy on one side of a codimension-two Cauchy-splitting surface.

Define observed matter by its a^−3 scaling and absorb coupling-induced variation into effective dark energy. For matter coupling alone, ρDE=ρφ+(Am−1)ρ̄m and wDEρDE=wφρφ. These definitions preserve both Friedmann equations and the usual effective dark-energy continuity equation; an analogous construction includes radiation.

Numerically solve the scalar equation and second Friedmann equation in N=log a, using the stated constraint identity to preserve the first Friedmann equation. Fix present densities, tune wφ0 for past radiation domination, and compare the resulting wDE with CPL constraints, including a linear fit for the first example.

For a geometric frame generated by KK vectors v_i, the author obtains α_p = Σ_i[((D_i−d)P/(D−2))+p−P_i]v_i, with integer P_i, P=p+Σ_i(P_i−p), and D=d+Σ_i(D_i−d). Simultaneous projection constraints form a lattice; a radion-to-dilaton prescription supplies stringy-frame analogues.

Principality is tested using the Diophantine norm condition |α_p|²=1/n+1−p+p²/(d−2), where n is a positive integer or ∞, and the product bound α_p·α_q≤1−q+pq/(d−2) for every other present principal norm candidate with q≤p. A principal brane supplies winding modes whose deletion spoils the lower-dimensional conjectures.

Toroidal reduction tracks wrapped and unwrapped brane tensions along a canonically normalized radion. Circle reduction and T-duality reinterpret string winding modes as KK modes, allowing radion lattice conditions to yield dilaton lattice conditions.

Analytic condensate and heat-capacity expansions determine β and α. Scaling relations yield γ and δ; hyperscaling supplies ν and η conditionally. The zero-frequency scalar response is separately computed and fitted to test the susceptibility exponent.

The author constructs eight gauge-invariant perturbations matching eight on-shell degrees of freedom. QNMs use incoming horizon conditions and vanishing scalar sources at the boundary, solved numerically by shooting. The reported calculations focus on decoupled channels.

Holographic renormalization uses a finite boundary functional F=−(ϕ_(1)²+χ_(1)²)^(3/2)/2, interpreted as a triple-trace deformation. The leading scalar coefficients define the operators, while mixed source conditions impose Jϕ=Jχ=0.

Solve the ADM lapse and shift constraints to first order, obtain the cubic action in spatially flat gauge, and transform to comoving gauge through second order in fluctuations. The retained interactions comprise an equation-of-motion vertex and three leading vertices of second order in Hubble-flow parameters.

Compute equal-time two- and three-point functions using the doubled-field Schwinger–Keldysh path integral with Bunch–Davies contours and Wick contractions. In this formulation temporal total derivatives give zero for the stated tree-level three-point observable, while the equation-of-motion vertex contributes.

Use Hankel mode functions, rotate interaction-time contours to modified-Bessel triple-K integrals, and treat odd and even d separately in the late-time expansion. Restrict bulk correlators to the brane by analytic KK sums; the bispectrum sum enforces n1+n2+n3=0.

Propose generalized Dynkin diagrams using charge-vector inner products. Choose a1=ω_k/κ_k, append an affine root to an ADE component, and use a second Wilson line from the shift algorithm before deleting another node. Charged long-root nodes depend on the selected E tensor.

Construct asymmetric orbifolds by g(−1)^F, where F is spacetime fermion number. Obtain modularly required twisted sectors using Poisson summation and theta-function modular transformations; extract spectra through level-matched q,q-bar expansions of lattice partition functions.

Directly compactify the E8 string with metric, antisymmetric tensor and Wilson-line moduli. Solve p_R=0 with P_L²=1 or 2 for gauge vectors, and P_L²=1 for massless co-spinors. For T², select supersymmetric enhancement data with both Wilson lines of duplicated form (a_i,a_i).

Partial-wave unitarity is applied to axion-mediated, color-singlet gluon scattering. The most restrictive channel considered has total angular momentum J=0 and equal gluon helicities; the bound formally assumes a weakly coupled ’t Hooft limit.

CYTools supplies intersection, volume and Kähler-metric data. For each h1,1≤60 the authors sample up to 100 favorable polytopes and 500 triangulations per polytope, totaling about 1.7 million compactifications; mass eigenstates are approximated using hierarchical instanton scales.

Dimensional reduction relates axion kinetic terms, gauge-cycle volumes, total compactification volume and the string scale. Factorizable examples reproduce the model-independent axion decay constant; nonfactorizable examples permit additional geometric dependence.

Prime-local stable splittings reduce the eight-dimensional calculation to finite-group data. BSL(3,Z) splits into two BD₆ pieces at prime 3, and two BSL(3,F₂) pieces plus L(2) at prime 2; the latter maps are not all subgroup inclusions.

Cyclic-group multiplication supplies Pontrjagin algebra structures and module structures refining the Künneth map. Multiplicative spectral sequences and Leibniz rules organize differentials and generators; additional lens-space representatives supply classes missed by products.

First spin bordism is computed using the Atiyah–Hirzebruch spectral sequence and group Abelianization. Higher calculations use the Atiyah–Hirzebruch sequence at prime 3, Brown–Peterson homology to resolve extensions, and ko-homology Adams spectral sequences over A(1) at prime 2.

The autoencoder compresses 136 independent upper-triangle entries of matrices up to 16×16 through layers 512→256→64→16→2, with a mirrored decoder, ReLU hidden activations and MSLE loss. Different theories sharing G remain indistinguishable.

Numerical labels use spectral factorization, pseudoinverses and constrained SciPy optimization of the total current contribution. Maximization seeks restricted consistency; minimization seeks uniformly violating regions. Integer charge optimization is relaxed to real levels, and string tension is ignored.

Two dense classifiers use 136→64→32→16→8→4→2→1 architectures with sigmoid outputs. Majority-class undersampling produces balanced training and validation sets; reported balanced validation accuracies are 96.72% and 85.53%.

Approximate the joint CPL distribution P as Gaussian and restrict it to a model curve: p(w0)∝P(w0,wa(w0)). Truncate above w0,max and extend below −1. Define pnull as the normalized integral below −1 and Nσ=√2 Erf⁻¹(1−2pnull).

Fit a straight CPL line to numerical w(a) over a selected DESI-sensitive redshift interval, rather than relying on a local linearization. Compare the resulting model trajectories in the {w0,wa} plane with published contours.

Numerically evolve the homogeneous scalar equation φ̈+3Hφ̇+V′=0 together with the matter-plus-scalar Friedmann equation, then calculate the scalar density, pressure, and w(a). Scan exponential slope β and hilltop curvature k and initial displacement φi.

Translation to a free-bosonic torus description exposes Wilson-line backgrounds. A Z2 internal twist and a Z2 Wilson-line action construct an orbifold partition function in which discrete torsion selects massless spinorial or vectorial states.

The reviewed EFT investigations resolve orbifold singularities using massless states and employ gauged linear sigma models (GLSMs) to interpolate between singular orbifolds and smooth geometries, including tracking discrete torsion.

Free-fermionic classification fixes twelve boundary-condition basis vectors and varies 55 independent ±1 GGSO phases, analyzing spectra for the resulting vacua; exchanges of GGSO phases implement SVD.

Tree-level, one-graviton exchange: expand matter couplings to linear order in hμν, introduce gravitational and Yang–Mills gauge fixing, and contract vertices through the spin-projector propagator. Faddeev–Popov ghosts are omitted because loops are outside the calculation.

Construct the gluon s-channel amplitude from explicit momentum tensors, obtain other channels by crossing substitutions, and evaluate summed squared amplitudes in the center-of-momentum frame. The appendix attributes its tensor expressions to algebraic packages.

The argument combines holomorphy, mixed modular-gauge anomaly cancellation and the constancy of a nonsingular weight-zero modular form on the compactified fundamental domain. The valence formula identifies determinants whose only zero lies at the cusp.

An illustrative Yukawa texture uses Eisenstein series of weights 4 through 12. Positive, nonuniversal Kähler coefficients supply real rescalings after canonical normalization; χ² minimization fits fermion mass ratios, mixing angles and phases.

Gauge-unification estimates distinguish holomorphic from physical couplings. Anomalous canonical and super-Weyl rescalings are combined with one-loop holomorphic running and η-function string thresholds.

A universal dilaton/volume truncation uses the minimal three-dimensional supergravity potential V=2Gij∂iP∂jP−4P². Flux contributions to the real superpotential determine the classical vacua and the conifold-modulus extremum.

Conifold periods are used to estimate flux stabilization. Matching the local CGLP throat to the bulk determines warp-factor dependence; a probe DBI/Chern–Simons calculation supplies the anti-D2 uplift, followed by numerical potential extremization and tadpole/control tests.

For extremal black branes, the paper uses an imported attractor/fake-superpotential formalism, takes the minimum over locally defined branches, and computes inverse charge-to-tension ratios analytically or numerically. Monopole-energy, emergence and Bogomolnyi arguments are explicitly heuristic motivations.

The authors classify boundary scalings using linear homogeneous-coordinate paths, derivatives of the cubic prepotential, and gauge-kinetic eigenvalues. They test cone maps and alignment in explicit GMSV, KMV and GHMMR geometries.

The authors combine imported communication bounds with the first law, then examine a generalized Vaidya extension using Misner–Sharp mass and a corrected surface gravity. The de Sitter argument differentiates an imported IR-dependent entropy term and assigns energy to newly admitted EFT modes.

The physical-process first law is obtained by integrating the horizon expansion and using the linearized null Raychaudhuri equation with Einstein's equation. Quadratic expansion and shear terms are dropped.

Estimates the useful sterile-neutrino yield by integrating a thermal number spectrum over a narrow energy interval, multiplying by the assumed sterile fraction and conversion probability, and comparing the resulting PBH density with local dark matter. IceCube decaying-dark-matter limits are reinterpreted as a bound on ΓPBH fPBH.

Uses imported d-dimensional Hawking radius, temperature and entropy scaling, with lifetime estimated as τH ∼ S rs. These are order-of-magnitude relations used to contrast five-dimensional evaporation with the four-dimensional case.

Uses an effective two-state sterile–active oscillation model. A bulk shortcut changes the effective mixing angle, with resonance energy Eres = sqrt[δm² cos(2θ)/(2ε)]. Conversion is evaluated using Psa = sin²(2θ̃) sin²(δH D/2), followed by phase averaging.

Writes C(F,G) = FLF + GLG − L. The modified Smarr relation expresses M − 2ST − QmΦm as minus an exterior integral of C. The same integral controls derivatives of the extremal mass-to-charge ratio and normalized entropy.

Introduces the electromagnetic dual two-form H and rotates (F,H) into (P,W), constructing a corresponding dual Lagrangian. Choosing the rotation angle along the charge vector maps a dyonic solution to a magnetic solution of the dual theory.

Constructs the magnetic solution and expresses its mass as M(S,Qm). The first law and Euler-operator identities for L then yield temperature, magnetic potential and the previously known modified Smarr relation.

Use Gaussian-process acceleration reconstructions quoted from other work, particularly q0≈-0.3±0.1 and q(z=1)≈0.1±0.03, to estimate required intrinsic equations of state and density shifts. These are inputs reported by this paper, rather than a new data reconstruction performed here.

Rewrite the two continuity equations using effective component equations of state, then express the deceleration parameter in terms of bare dark-energy pressure and the evolved density fraction. Compare phantom uplift, conventional-dark-energy depression, and sign-changing tilt without choosing a general Q(a).

Replaces the previous sharp momentum cutoff by a Gaussian factor exp(−k²Rs²/4) in the Fourier–Bessel integral of the RN potential. The resulting potential is expressed with the error and Dawson functions; the paper emphasizes modifications to an imported construction rather than reproducing its full derivation.

Computes an effective anisotropic stress-energy tensor from the Einstein tensor, integrates its density to obtain the Misner–Sharp mass, and expands f near the origin to classify curvature behavior. Horizon locations are treated numerically, with a parametric double-root boundary obtained from f = f′ = 0.

Uses effective geodesic potentials and numerical equations/integrals for photon rings, critical impact parameters, light deflection and Shapiro delay. Scalar perturbations reduce to a Schrödinger-like radial equation and are evaluated by WKB with Padé approximants of order [6/7].

Microcanonical occupation-number counting uses an auxiliary generating partition function and saddle-point expansion. A complementary canonical calculation treats free species in a box; exponentially degenerate towers require the canonical treatment specified by the review, whose stated domain is T<T_H, below the Hagedorn temperature.

Holographic entropy and gravitational-collapse bounds motivate the frozen-momentum limit. Requiring energy matching after each change N→N+1 produces a recursion constraining the mass–degeneracy relation.
Weyl’s law parametrizes KK spectra; summing level degeneracies and solving the implicit species-cutoff condition relates the tower mass gap, species count and higher-dimensional Planck scale.
Supergravity constructions examine F- and D-term potentials, Kähler transformations and modular weights, then employ a nilpotent chiral multiplet X²=0 to realize nonlinear supersymmetry.

Modular completion uses the Dedekind η-function invariant I to interpolate between weak- and strong-coupling asymptotics. Species-scale ansätze and V=M_p^(4−α)Λ_sp^α connect the potential to KK and string towers.

The observational comparison fits an axion-like potential to the modular potential, compares its parameters with published BAO+CMB+SN constraints, and uses an analytic hilltop approximation to w(z) on a flat FLRW background.

One-instanton ’t Hooft-vertex estimates use explicit-breaking insertions, an instanton-size integral and one-loop gauge running. Cosmological estimates combine wall tension, horizon-scale wall density, collapse bounds and relic-abundance formulas.

Anomalous lepton and baryon field rephasings track the electroweak vacuum angle and determine whether Majoron dependence can be removed. The appendix repeats this analysis after adding fermions chiral under lepton number.

Fourier-expand automorphic coefficients in compact axions and retain constant terms. Power-law saxionic ansätze become exponentials in canonical fields, converting differential equations into algebraic constraints on species vectors.
Use circle reduction/uplift to construct exceptional operators: extract the IIA dilaton operator from the 9d equation, and uplift the axion-truncated 4d equation using F₅ = F₄/R₅.

Relate ambient and constrained-manifold Laplacians using normal Hessians and mean curvature. For the specified homogeneous metrics, the authors obtain vanishing mean curvature and Hessian contributions 2f/3 in 5d and f in 6d for ambient-linear f.

Use supersymmetric-domain-wall or fake-superpotential techniques to replace second-order equations by first-order flows generated by P. Dimensional reduction supplies the universal-modulus dependence of curvature, NS flux and RR flux terms.

Calibration examples recover the known Freund–Rubin cones, flat-space D3/M2/M5 pictures, and the ABJM orbifold after an eleven-dimensional uplift. These are reported checks against known brane descriptions.

Remove selected brane-sourced fluxes from the off-shell scalar potential, solve a horizonless radial running solution, and uplift it. The radial ansatz is ds_d²=dr²+e^(2A(r))ds_flat,d−1² with scalar profiles depending only on r.

Use a doubled-field-theory twist and Scherk–Schwarz reduction, organizing R-flux phase-space brackets through a Malcev algebra and Hom-Sabinin envelope. Reduce the heterotic action with torsionful connection ω(−)=ω−H/2.
Analyze stationary conditions for the two-field potential using a local single-exponential uplift, then report numerical scans and Hessian eigenvalues for a double-exponential condensate potential.

Separately explore a string-motivated potential built from N nonperturbative exponential contributions. For N=3, fix A3=-1.05 and a3=2π/70 and vary four remaining coefficients; investigate adding a fourth contribution to alter early curvature and the separation between AdS and positive-potential scales.

Modified MontePython-3.6 and CLASS implement MCMC sampling with Gelman–Rubin R-1<0.01. EDE sampling uses {ln(1+zc), fede} instead of potential parameters {V0,ϕi}; fede is the EDE energy fraction when the field starts rolling at zc.

Use previously computed SU(2) isolated-horizon state counting and one-loop Euclidean/replica entropy coefficients. The latter arise from differentiation with respect to a conical deficit angle and require ultraviolet renormalization of Newton's constant or Planck area.
Insert additive corrections Sbh=SBH+sbh into the generalized second law, expand sbh in logarithmic and inverse-area terms, and impose a stronger sign condition on the correction's merger change.
Uses reviewed Green–Schwarz–Sagnotti anomaly factorization and representation-theoretic anomaly constraints to select candidate spectra; at T=0, H_tot−V=273 and the anomaly coefficients are integral.

Combines affine/Potts character decompositions, integer conformal grading, modular constraints and the massless-spectrum coefficient to constrain the genus. Vector-valued modular forms are organized as a rank-four module over polynomials in j, with a basis constructed using Serre derivatives; affine expansions were computed in SAGE.
For cosmology, substitute Fμνσρ=λεμνσρΦ, transform to the Einstein frame with Ω²=1−μλ²Φ²/mP², canonically redefine the scalar in specified limits, and apply canonical single-field slow-roll formulae.

Evaluate corrections to first order in ci on the classical background, integrate backreaction to the zero-force boundary rb³=ℓ²κ²M/2, and calculate Wald entropy including both explicit operator and horizon-area corrections.

Use τs=(3V/(4λs))^(2/3)ϕ^(4/3) for canonical normalization, calculate potential slow-roll parameters and horizon-exit e-fold integrals, then scan parameters after fixing the scalar-perturbation amplitude.

Insert BBHL, logarithmic, moduli-redefinition and string-loop corrections into the F-term potential; expand through second order in loop corrections. Leading terms stabilize the large cycle, while subleading terms determine the blow-up potential.

Direct implicit differentiation compares horizon-radius responses at fixed mass with those at fixed entropy, keeping P and β fixed. Substitution into derivatives of M and S produces the entropy form of the proposed relation.

The full-differential method starts from M=M(S(η),P(η),B(η),η), separates explicit η dependence from state-variable response terms and inserts the first-law conjugates in the limiting constant-energy argument.
A composite-function method uses chain-rule derivatives through r+ to derive separate entropy and pressure response relations. Thermodynamic conjugates are identified using the extended first law.

An orthonormal coframe is used to compute exterior derivatives, connection one-forms, and curvature two-forms through Cartan structural equations; Riemann components are extracted and traced to obtain the Ricci tensor.

Einstein equations convert null stress-tensor contractions into Ricci sums. These are evaluated at the throat, where 1−b(r0)/r0=0, separately for radial, angular, and extra-dimensional null directions.

Numerics use Chebyshev spectral grids and relaxation for uncorrected modes, then linear equations for δω. Reported settings include n=300 with at least 100-digit precision, and n=250 with 300-digit precision for example ZDM calculations.

Regge–Wheeler gauge and gravito-electromagnetic master variables reduce perturbations to Moncrief equations. Factoring out ingoing-horizon and outgoing-infinity behavior and using y=1−r+/r yields equations with regular endpoint conditions.

The near-extremal analysis uses the AdS2×S² near-horizon limit, Gauss hypergeometric solutions and their transformations, followed by perturbative matching of large-distance exponents to extract EFT frequency shifts.

Expand untwisted and twisted partition functions, impose GSO and orbifold projections, include fractional oscillator excitations, and enforce left–right level matching to identify light multiplets and their momentum/winding towers.

Use the classical special-Kähler metric to normalize distances. Poisson resummation and cusp limits of the T2 partition function identify surviving sectors and match them to noncompact-boson partition functions.

Determine inherited dualities by taking the twist commutant and imposing preservation of the shift vector up to sign and lattice translations. Shifted Narain sums provide the corresponding partition-function test.

Robustness studies vary the residual gravitational gauge parameter and add R² and Weyl-curvature-squared operators. The next-order scalar analysis imports beta functions for powers of the kinetic term through Nmax=13, adapting real-scalar matter loops by a factor of two for a complex scalar.

Functional renormalization group flow of a scale-dependent effective action, with CPT-odd insertions in matter-graviton diagrams. Projection onto field monomials extracts coupling flows and matter anomalous dimensions. A linear metric split, flat background and Landau gauges are used; the main gravitational gauge parameter is βh=1.
Uses the N=1 F-term potential, racetrack terms Wᵢ=Aᵢe^(−aᵢTᵢ)−Bᵢe^(−bᵢTᵢ), RR tadpole constraints, and stationarity of reduced AdS-plus-uplift potentials to compare perturbative corrections.
Reviewed dimensional reduction tracks four-dimensional 4-forms using democratic RR fields. Equation-of-motion dualities G₆=−⋆₁₀G₄, G₈=⋆₁₀G₂ and G₁₀=−⋆₁₀G₀ avoid double counting.

Bound canonical moduli displacement using Hubble friction and maximal kination evolution; separately integrate a brane KK-emission source scaling as T⁸/M5D,pl³ and compare its recombination density with dark matter.
Compare horizon-mass and cosmic-string-loop mass bounds with the Gregory–Laflamme threshold MGL ∼ Mpl²/MKK. Apply the resulting mass bounds to the 5D evaporation lifetime.
Estimate the composite size by balancing flux-tube energy, Eflux∼Zv²L, against repulsive magnetic Coulomb energy, EMC∼Z²(2π/e)²/L. Numerical factors of order one are not controlled.

Quantize collective rotation as a rigid body using J² eigenvalues j(j+1), and approximate the collective size potential quadratically around equilibrium to obtain harmonic oscillations. Oscillatory energies denote differences from the ground state.

Superconformal compensator gauge fixing, Jordan-to-Einstein Weyl rescaling and integration of the kinetic metric supply the proposed canonical-field map. A quadratic Taylor truncation of 𝒦 around τ₀ organizes the effective correction parameter ε.

Numerical methods include Hamiltonian Wheeler–DeWitt/WKB vacuum tunneling with Runge–Kutta integration, and inflationary background plus Mukhanov–Sasaki evolution with subhorizon Bunch–Davies initial data. PBH abundances use Gaussian smoothing and Press–Schechter statistics, with collapse threshold δth=0.61 and radiation-era reentry.

The authors evaluate the supergravity F-term potential at bosonic S=0 and filter coupling functions using kinetic positivity, positive-energy minima, Minkowski limits and vanishing asymptotic F-terms. They report five viable dS cases and six allowed dS-to-Minkowski pairings; positivity inequalities alone should not be read as a demonstrated local minimum.

Decompose perturbations into scalar, transverse-vector and transverse-traceless tensor sectors. In five dimensions use Fourier momenta k in the isotropic subspace and q along the fifth direction, with gauge choice E=B=μ=Fi=0.

Introduce auxiliary scalar fields, solve their algebraic constraints and perform conformal metric rescalings. Integration by parts yields an Einstein-frame form for the pure theory and a Weyl-squared alternative frame for the conformal theory.

Eliminate constrained fields, introduce first-order variables for higher time derivatives and inspect kinetic-matrix rank. Background solutions are obtained analytically with one scale factor fixed, and numerically from reduced evolution equations plus the constraint.

Trace and integrate the external Einstein equations using τ=[(n−2)Tµµ−dTaa]/(D−2). Defining J(M)=∫M dVn e^{(d−2)ϕ} and K(M)=∫M dVn e^{dϕ}τ yields R̄J(Mtot)=K(Mout)+ΣiK(Mi), after cancellation of internal boundary terms.

Near-source stress conservation eliminates angular stresses and separates brane contributions into an effective external stress trace and corrections Δ1, Δ2. In the six-dimensional example, ring regularization, Israel junction conditions, the dilaton matching equation and the radial Einstein constraint connect localized tension and angular pressure to bulk profiles.

Empty-torus and empty-annulus blocks require different treatment because they are not normalizable in the Verlinde inner product. Vandermonde kernels define spectral matrix potentials; their functional inverses determine density two-point functions.

Cardy-weighted state sums become toroidal and annular surgeries, with half-surgeries turning connecting Wilson lines into asymptotic tubes or strips. The appendix supplies specific algebraic gluing and surgery consistency checks, rather than a completeness proof.

Construct tensor potentials by squaring bootstrap constraints with measures from the Verlinde inner product. Express crossing through fusion F, modular S and braiding kernels, then identify propagators and interaction vertices with three-dimensional gluing diagrams.

The cosmological equations become an autonomous system in normalized kinetic, potential and fluid variables, constrained by x²+y²+z²=1. Critical-point stability is examined after eliminating y, setting Z=z² and reparameterizing time.

The multi-field discussion uses the shortest vector from the origin to the convex hull of exponential slopes. Appendix B constructs critical points using an invertible square coupling matrix, with a stated reduction prescription for larger systems.

Quantum inequalities are tested by constrained numerical minimization and generated physical parameter samples. These searches supply evidence over scanned domains rather than an analytic proof for all charged rotating solutions.

Critical points and exponents are obtained numerically from free-energy coexistence and Maxwell equal-area constructions. Polynomial resultants and local expansions investigate removal of the original critical point; the charge analysis assumes its root varies smoothly with χ.

Israel junction conditions fix τ=1/(2πG4ℓ). Horizon geometry gives the temperature and generalized entropy Sgen=Area_bulk/(4G4); thermodynamic differentiation and homogeneous scaling produce conjugates and Smarr relations.

Constrained superspace, iterative auxiliary-field elimination and nonlinear field redefinitions distinguish actions exact at quadratic goldstino order from quartic-field truncations. Twice-subtracted forward 2→2 amplitudes give positivity bounds, compared with propagation on homogeneous scalar backgrounds.

Supercurrent superfields and their improvements classify leading couplings to off-shell supergravity; Kaluza–Klein reduction examines the alternative supersymmetry algebra. Klein-bottle amplitudes identify twisted orientifold-plane couplings.

Canonical normalization and Bogolyubov transformations compare Fock spaces diagonalizing the instantaneous Hamiltonian with those diagonalizing the energy derived from the covariant stress-energy tensor.

Use the real Gopakumar-Vafa Schwinger integral over half-BPS D2-D0 states and differentiate three times to obtain Yukawa couplings. Separate the constant, divergent zero-point sum from the instanton contribution; polynomially degenerate sums admit zeta regularization.

Near finite-distance degenerations, solve Picard-Fuchs equations, continue periods into the large-complex-structure integral symplectic basis, and transform B-side Yukawas with the inverse mirror-map Jacobian. Analyze divergent, constant and vanishing terms along specified paths.

For modular examples, introduce regulated Lambert/divisor sums, apply modular S-transformations and minimally subtract divergences. The heterotic STU example uses the Harvey-Moore identity, whose modular expression has biweight (-2,4).

Numerically solve covariant second-order background equations using e-fold time and the tree-level Kähler metric, progressing from one to three evolving fields. Extract canonical endpoint distances, slow-roll observables at horizon exit and vacuum mass-matrix eigenvalues.

Build the scalar potential from BBHL α′³ and logarithmic loop terms stabilizing the volume, winding-loop and higher-derivative F4 terms lifting fiber directions, plus Cup/V^p uplift. The geometric setup has no conventional KK-loop contribution in the stated construction.

Ruppeiner geometry is constructed from entropy fluctuations and the extended first law, giving dlR²=(dS dT+dP dV)/T in the paper's convention. Geodesic analysis uses conserved E,L and effective-potential extrema, supplemented by numerical trajectory examples.

Metric variation distinguishes the original nonminimal curvature term from replacing B² by its vacuum value before variation. A small cosmological-constant-scaled action deformation ε is then used to obtain perturbed masses, temperatures and entropy derivatives for the imported extremality identity.

Thermodynamic topology uses F=M−S/τ, ϕ=(∂rhF,−cotΘ cscΘ), normalized field winding, and W=Σζiηi. Photon-sphere topology instead uses H=√f/(r sinθ), with ϕr=√f ∂rH and ϕθ=(∂θH)/r; zeros identify photon spheres.

Three searches solve logarithmic supersymmetric F-term equations, solve full-potential extremum equations, or track solutions while increasing |W0| from KKLT starting points. Linear programming generates initial points inside the Kähler cone; scipy.optimize.root solves the resulting equations.

JAX automatic differentiation and just-in-time compilation generate the scalar potential, derivatives and F terms from K, W and holomorphic coordinates. The numerical implementation derives the potential directly rather than evaluating the analytic master expression.

Candidate solutions are checked for Kähler-cone membership and positive Hessian eigenvalues. LVS classification additionally examines approximate volume and small-cycle scaling. The Hessian criterion excludes AdS extrema with negative eigenvalues even when BF stability could allow them.

The argument follows the temperature-dependent angular minimum, invokes Hubble friction to retain an offset, and estimates suppression of coherent thermal fluctuations using thermal energy T in a region of radius R. No numerical cosmological evolution is supplied in this argument.

Expanding the radial potential around ϕr=fa gives the stated radial mass mr=2√(2λ)fa. A hidden-sector interaction proportional to χ^(2+2n)|ϕ|²[1−cos(θ+β)]/mpl^(2n) is used to motivate the temperature-dependent angular potential.

Separate an approximate fit using ΛCDM-like density powers and a modified dark-energy EOS, with Δ=0.1 and α=1 fixed, from an 'exact model' fit that solves the coupled density equations and varies Δ and α.

Use χ² likelihoods, Metropolis–Hastings MCMC and GetDist chain analysis. The H(z) sample combines 31 CC measurements over 0.070≤z≤1.965 with 26 BAO measurements over 0.24≤z≤2.36; supernova fits use distance moduli and a covariance matrix.

Derive coupled evolution equations for Ω_de, Ω_m and Ω_r using x=ln a and horizon differentiation, then solve numerically with SciPy RK4/5. Four interaction-density choices are analyzed: ρ_de, ρ_m, ρ_r and their total.

An arbitrary-dimensional Ewald extension splits lattice sums into rapidly convergent position and dual-lattice sums, with a tunable positive splitting parameter. The authors eliminate the volume modulus analytically and find extrema numerically in the remaining (x, β) variables.

Mellin transformation reduces the integrated Casimir energy to lattice sums over projected invariant subspaces. M-theory contributions are weighted by SO(9) little-group traces for the graviton 44, three-form 84 and gravitino 128.

Point-splitting regularization and image sums compute free-field propagators and Casimir energy. Summing physical polarizations introduces representation traces; supersymmetry of the covering space cancels the divergent identity-image contribution even when the quotient breaks supersymmetry.

Linearize the Type IIA equations around the flat background, fix internal diffeomorphism and gravitino gauges, and expand the fields in scalar, form, symmetric-tensor, spinor and vector-spinor harmonics.

Regularize the one-loop momentum integral and independent KK sums using zeta functions. Epstein zeta functions and their functional equation give lattice-resummed expressions; effectively one-dimensional short series use Hurwitz zeta functions.

Construct invariant harmonics by averaging covering-torus plane waves with the appropriate tensor or spin representation over the holonomy group. Fermions use spin-structure-dependent shifted dual lattices; transverse and traceless conditions select physical harmonic sectors.

Combine an entropy-motivated upper restriction on the species scale with ΛIR ≤ ΛUV, then substitute an exponentially falling species scale. The two inequalities define implicit potential-dependent endpoints of an allowed scalar interval.

Solve power-law endpoints using the principal Lambert W branch; analyze α-attractor endpoints and slow-roll parameters numerically. For observational constraints, use the scalar-amplitude relation, a Lyth excursion estimate and an imported lower bound on the species-scale decay rate.

Expansion-normalized variables and the Friedmann constraint reduce the scalar equations. Because λ(b)=−V,b/(κV) is noninvertible, the authors instead introduce an inverse-field variable and compactify the relevant half-line to obtain a two-dimensional autonomous system.
Fixed points are classified using Jacobian eigenvalues; center-manifold expansions address zero eigenvalues at |γ/δ|=1 and in the formal infinite-compactification-radius limit.

Numerical phase portraits, trajectories and equation-of-state histories explore initial-condition dependence. The authors report using Python/matplotlib and Radau integration, and reconstruct H, b and ḃ along trajectories to assess slow roll.

Invariant-form flux ansätze reduce field equations to algebraic systems. Numerical solution and maximization over auxiliary pure-spinor choices and world-volume fluxes give conservative stability bounds. The KE analysis also uses holomorphic calibrations and intersection-pairing signature constraints.

Compatible pure-spinor polyforms provide algebraic lower bounds on DBI energies. Modified differential equations isolate supersymmetry-breaking terms; closure of the relevant calibration makes integrated bounds depend on generalized homology.
Parameter inference uses Cobaya's Metropolis–Hastings MCMC, separately examining c≥0 and c≤0 with c′≥0. Additional fits test a hilltop potential, spatial curvature and two light scalar fields.
Background evolution follows coupled Friedmann and scalar equations with Veff=V₀e^(−cϕ)+m₀n₀a⁻³e^(−c′ϕ). The authors modify CLASS to evolve both the background and coupled linear perturbations.

A symmetrized-trace nonabelian DBI expansion through F⁴, without scalar fields, is varied to determine bulk-field discontinuities. The leading-source argument also uses Tr F=0 and the Chern–Simons couplings to R–R fields.

The authors diagonalize the electroweak contribution to the gravitational energy-density mass matrix around the Higgs vacuum in temporal gauge. Separately, equilibrium relativistic degrees of freedom estimate the gluon contribution to the preconfinement expansion rate.

Published lattice-QCD gravitational form factors, rather than new lattice simulations, supply Aq(0)=0.510±0.025 and Ag(0)=0.501±0.027. Their forward-limit momentum fractions are used to estimate proton gravitational mass after reversing the gluon contribution.

An alternative calculation sums tower-induced corrections to the modulus D-term correlator, then inserts auxiliary F-fields to obtain vacuum energy. Tower masses are rewritten using the species scale; topological-string species functions supply selected modular examples.

Cutoff one-loop supertrace expansion, separating light states from finitely many tower states. The quartic divergence cancels through StrM⁰=0; the authors retain StrM²Λ² as leading and argue that StrM⁴ logarithmic contributions are subleading.

The homogeneous axion equation θ̈+3Hθ̇+ma²(T)sinθ=0 is solved numerically across the three thermal phases, passing θ and θ̇ between phases. The kinetic and potential energy at TQCD is then redshifted to estimate the present relic density.

The gravitational-wave estimate uses sound-wave and MHD-turbulence templates, including finite sound-wave lifetime suppression. Transition strength and inverse duration are extracted from the effective potential and the temperature derivative of S3/T.

The electroweak effective potential keeps tree-level scalar interactions and leading high-temperature T² thermal masses. FindBounce computes the O(3)-symmetric three-dimensional Euclidean bounce action; nucleation is estimated using Γd≈H⁴, implemented as S3(Tn)/Tn≈140.

Bayesian HEPfit/BAT MCMC produces 68% and 95% highest posterior density intervals (HPDIs). Individual, simultaneous and dataset-omission fits are performed. Wilson coefficients have symmetric uniform perturbative priors; quark-mass/CKM priors are uniform, while specified precision inputs have Gaussian priors.

Predictions combine higher-order SM calculations with linear SMEFT interference at its lowest perturbative order, sometimes rescaled by SM correction factors. Collider parametrizations use MG5_aMC@NLO; B→Dℓν uses a BGL z-expansion through z² with lattice and unitarity constraints.

LO SMEFT running uses RGEsolver, followed by electroweak tree-level matching and LEFT running to each flavour scale. Quark Yukawas are evolved from the UV, mass matrices diagonalized, and operators rotated into the mass basis.

Sharpen local blowup counts using special-fiber discriminant multiplicities in the canonical bundle formula. Global constraints deg(Λ_{P¹})≤2 and f_i·B_i^h=2 limit high-multiplicity fibers and the number of vertical intersection points on each fiber.

Blow Z down to a Hirzebruch surface, then construct a maximal admissible blowup chain ending at Z_r mapping to Z. Preserve effectiveness and 1/6-lc singularities, split B_i into horizontal and vertical parts, and constrain subchains ordered by horizontal multiplicity.
Encode fibral degenerations by a pair (Z,B), with B=Λ+M and K_Z+B≡0. Singularities are measured through K_W+B_W=φ*(K_Z+B): ε-lc means every coefficient of B_W is at most 1−ε.

Represent exceptional curves by rooted trees. Single-type blowups occur on one fiber component and double-type blowups at two-component intersections. Bound clusters using horizontal multiplicities, special-fiber coefficient caps, and a correspondence between vertical intersection points and exceptional curves.
Reduce to a smooth surface, blow down to a Hirzebruch surface, and construct a maximal blowup sequence preserving effective 1/6-lc boundaries. The stated domination Z_r→Z gives ρ(Z)≤2+r.

Use the canonical bundle formula and reduction to elliptic surfaces, then apply Kodaira fiber classification to control discriminant coefficients. Replace the moduli part on a high resolution by a general effective divisor using its nef, free Cartier multiple, and push down to obtain a boundary.

Vary the action independently with respect to the axion, tetrad and spin connection; solve the torsion constraints on the cosmological background. Appendix A uses spin-connection antisymmetry and field equations to justify the reduced torsion ansatz.

Expand the tensor action to quadratic order and decompose into circular helicities. For the Nieh–Yan branch, solve the approximate mode equation using Coulomb-Hankel functions, Bunch–Davies initial conditions and canonical Wronskian normalization.

Use spatially flat gauge for scalar perturbations, eliminate lapse, shift and torsion constraints, and canonically normalize the remaining mode. Hankel-function solutions give approximate scalar spectra; numerical evolution and parameter scans supply the reported phenomenological examples.
For the bottom-up extension, combine string bordism, pairings of elliptic-genus kernels in TMF, normal-bundle homotopy groups, and SU(2)⊂SU(3) anomaly extensions for three-brane probes.

Match worldvolume anomaly polynomials to spacetime inflow and localized Green–Schwarz counterterms. The normal-bundle refinement constrains signed representation multiplicities through polynomial factorization.
Evaluate the anomaly theory X=η(N7)−∫H3∧W4 modulo one. For S7, extend SU(2) representations to Sp(2), use branching rules and extract the coefficient t giving A(1)=t/12.
Present action variations and modified FLRW equations, impose scalar and geometric slow-roll approximations, and estimate inflationary observables from slow-roll parameters.
Use benchmark potentials, leading-order e-fold relations and schematic parameter/observable diagrams. A phenomenological warm extension adds radiation and a dissipation coefficient Γ.

Electric-magnetic duality relates the BF coupling to a branched axion potential and represents its integer coefficient n as electric flux of a second three-form, with a Stückelberg-type gauge-invariant field strength.
Tunneling is estimated using an instantaneous thin-brane Coleman–De Luccia approximation, Γ∼mB^4 exp(−SE), with inflaton-dependent tension and vacuum-energy splitting.

Massive Hankel modes are matched to massless modes by continuity of δθ and its time derivative. The resulting spectrum is approximated by a broken power law and constrained using published bounds for that spectral shape.

Construct tree-level amplitudes from symmetry-allowed on-shell three-point vertices, factorization, and general contact terms using MassiveGraphs. Iteratively constrain leading energy growth with positivity; BCFW constructibility and SUSY are not assumed.

Contour-integral Arcs relate EFT coefficients to UV discontinuities. Nonforward and inelastic Arcs are bounded by positive forward elastic Arcs with minimal subtraction. The authors use these bounds to exclude dominant E^n terms with n>4 and require positive elastic E^4 coefficients.

Develop t–u symmetric dispersion relations at fixed p^2=tu/s, generating sum rules and null constraints; supplement them with fixed-t inelastic constraints. Use semidefinite programming with SDPB for numerical Goldstino coefficient regions.

Georgi describes effective field theory for separated mass scales: omit heavy particles in the low-energy calculation, match couplings across boundaries between effective theories, and run couplings between boundaries. Unified symmetry enters as a high-scale boundary condition.

Parisi recounts computing scaling violations through moments, running couplings and anomalous dimensions. Inverse Mellin transformation supplies an evolution kernel; the displayed non-singlet kernel is first order in α. The earlier calculation lacked the later branching interpretation.

Ting describes magnetic momentum measurement, independent Cherenkov identification and calorimetric E = P selection. J-peak checks included lowering magnet current by 10% and testing target-thickness dependence: linear yield for a one-step process versus quadratic yield for the proposed two-step background.

The tunneling calculation uses a thin-wall expression B=27π²S1^4/(2ϵ³), radius r=3S1/ϵ and prefactor approximately r^−4. A near-barrier approximation estimates S1; the percolation condition is expressed using Lambert W.

Variation of auxiliary three-form fields introduces integration constants M1, M2 and χ2. A conformal transformation ḡμν=χ1gμν produces Einstein-frame equations; an orthogonal scalar rotation separates a scale-invariant field ϕ1 from the shifting field ϕ2.

Parameter estimation uses a multivariate Gaussian likelihood with observational covariance and flat priors. The authors first fit acoustic-angle plus BAO data, then add the selected local H0 measurement; the CMB shift parameter is reserved as a compatibility check.

Einstein-frame dimensional reduction and canonical kinetic normalization precede the Hessian mass calculation. The dangerous shape-mode curvature is obtained by numerical quadrature and a centered finite difference with step 10^-5.

One-loop trace-log and Schwinger proper-time representations are related to heat kernels and propagators. Image sums, Jacobi theta functions, Epstein zeta functions and Poisson resummation organize the torus Casimir energy; individual contributions are regulated by subtracting the corresponding uncompactified geometry.

For traceless internal perturbations, the kinetic-operator correction is L1 = -∂i(hij∂j). Linearized kernel and propagator equations handle degenerate spectra without diagonalizing the perturbation. Fourier-mode estimates bound the response and support the claimed existence of its first functional derivative.

Use the extended first law dM = T dS + Ω dJ + U dQ + V dP0 + (∂M/∂η) dη. Thermodynamic potentials are obtained from partial derivatives of the mass function with the other independent variables fixed.

Treat mass density as a thermodynamic state function and apply the multivariable chain rule along η-dependent paths. Substitute first-law conjugates to obtain differential identities without explicitly solving for η as a function of each state variable.
Scherk–Schwarz reduction of the bulk action and nonabelian D5 DBI/WZ actions. The source expansion is retained through O(λ²), λ=2πα′, the order captured by the three-dimensional supergravity.

Embedding-tensor matching translates flux consistency into quadratic constraints. Singular solves the constrained extremisation problem; scalar masses test BF stability, while gravitini with m3/2 L=1 determine preserved supersymmetry.

For rotating and charged examples, alternative choices of independent state variables produce separate entropy, angular-momentum, charge and mixed response identities. These are applications of the first-law chain rule rather than independent microscopic entropy calculations.

Mass endpoints are located through ∂M/∂r=0. The response identities are evaluated in limits from the two-horizon coexistence region toward the maximum-mass and cold endpoints, keeping the selected thermodynamic variables fixed.

The authors differentiate mass and horizon entropy with respect to η, using the horizon equation to relate radius changes to thermodynamic changes. The first law then converts chain-rule terms into temperature, electrostatic-potential and angular-velocity work terms.
Differential K-theory and the homotopy fixed point spectral sequence for negation acting on KU; a heuristic hybrid RR action interchanging fluxes and Lagrange multipliers across the wall.
Arf-invariant stacking and Majorana-chain interfaces; half-worldsheet gauging of the GSO quantum symmetry; anomaly inflow and endability of topological symmetry lines.
Tachyon-kink descent, Berry/Aharonov–Bohm phases and proposed gauge-invariant WZ couplings support the fluxbrane interpretation; Type I Wilson-line constructions test the wall–vortex relation.

Tachikawa's appendix combines low-degree cohomology, the Künneth formula and an Atiyah–Hirzebruch spectral sequence. Degree-seven bordism reduces to E²6,1; dual d2 maps are expressed through Sq², with kernel/image cancellation.

Group-theory trace relations and representation indices determine the anomaly polynomial and its Green–Schwarz factorisation coefficients. Trace normalisations are fixed by unit charge for the smallest embedded SU(2) instanton.

Rank-two Gram determinants test lattice compatibility: vectors in a unimodular signature-(1,1) lattice must satisfy det M(x,y)=−p² for integer p. Characteristic-vector parity and explicit lattice descriptions are also used.
Use potential slow-roll expressions for r and the e-fold integral N=∫V dφ/(mpl² V,φ) to relate horizon-exit fields, end fields, excursions, and model parameters.
Plot model predictions in the (r, Δφ) plane, varying parameters and e-fold counts, and compare them with SDC and Lyth curves and the quoted observational upper bound.

Construct the vector-tensor terms through a d→4 dimensional regularization of differences of Gauss–Bonnet scalars built from Weyl connections. Insert static spherical metric and vector ansätze into the field equations and examine small-radius expansions and horizon degeneracy.

Use boundedness of the Kretschmann scalar to assess non-derivative curvature invariants in the static spherical family. The supplemental radial perturbation calculation expands to first order, Fourier transforms in time, and eliminates vector perturbations using their constraint equations.

The fermionic construction promotes constant worldvolume factors of skeleton Killing spinors to local supersymmetry parameters while retaining transverse Killing spinors. Gamma-matrix decompositions and intertwiners then separate host supersymmetry transformations into worldvolume and transverse factors.

A generalized harmonic-function rule retains the usual metric and dilaton products but modifies fluxes. With more than two flux types, the highest-rank RR contribution receives the opposite harmonic function; D3 flux corrections must also respect five-form self-duality. These rules were found empirically across the considered cases.

Embedding ansätze are inferred by matching intersecting-brane geometries to lower-dimensional black objects, restoring R-symmetry covariance, and identifying singlet fields through additional intersections. Remaining coefficients are fixed by reducing host equations or matching further charged solutions.

Impose FL(r0)=FR(r0) and FL′(r0)=FR′(r0), equivalently F(r0)=F′(r0)=0. The displayed equations are a²+(1−b)r0²−2Mr0+Q²=γr0^{1−3ω} and 2(1−b)r0−2M=γ(1−3ω)r0^{−3ω}. Subsequent algebra and parameter substitutions are used to advertise compatibility ranges.

Split the horizon equation into FL=a²+(1−b)r²−2Mr+Q² and FR=γr^{1−3ω}. Plot intersections for Q²/M²≤1 and Q²/M²>1; identify candidate extremal configurations by tangency rather than two distinct intersections.

Use a null-geodesic effective potential to obtain the photon-sphere condition (f/r²)′=0, equivalently 2rf−r²f′=0. Assess stability through the stated second-derivative test, and introduce H=√(−gtt/gφφ) and a normalized vector field to assign topological charges.

Analyze timelike circular orbits with β=f−r²Ω² and the displayed energy/angular-momentum relations. Negative β excludes real values of those quantities. Plot allowed orbit regions and Ω(r), seeking a reversal from decreasing to increasing angular velocity.

Locate horizons from metric roots and examine extremality using the horizon and temperature relations. The authors tabulate extremal radii, masses, and charge ratios for selected signs of the massive-gravity couplings.
The exclusion statistic is Δχ²=−2 log(LBSM/LSM), with LSM the best three-flavor likelihood. Separate normal- and inverted-ordering analyses produce contours labeled 90% and 99% confidence.

A joint frequentist profile-likelihood analysis combines binned MINOS/MINOS+, KamLAND and Daya Bay likelihoods. Oscillation parameters and experimental systematics are profiled while scanning R, the lightest neutrino mass and selected bulk-sector parameters.

KK decomposition solves the bulk Dirac equation with stated Dirichlet boundary conditions. Before Standard Model interactions, excited-mode masses obey mᵢₙ²=n²/R²+cᵢ²; physical oscillation masses require diagonalizing the coupled mass-squared matrix and incorporating the PMNS flavor rotation.

The axion–gravity effective action contains Einstein gravity, a massive pseudoscalar and a coupling −AbRCS. Expansion to quadratic order in weak tensor perturbations, followed by graviton quantization, is used to discuss nonseparable left/right polarization states.

The reviewed D-foam model represents kaon mass eigenstates as a two-level system. A stochastic interaction HI=−(r₁σ₁+r₂σ₂)k produces spin flips; ordinary perturbation theory constructs gravitationally dressed single-particle states and their entangled pair.

A locally conserved corrected current ∗j−v∧W defines a topological but potentially gauge-variant defect. Stacking an oppositely transforming TQFT restores gauge invariance; this dressing can make the resulting symmetry non-invertible.

The example computes a Yukawa-induced one-loop electron self-energy using Feynman parametrization and dimensional regularization, expands at low momentum, and Fourier transforms a propagator correction using modified Bessel functions to infer δq(r).

The effective charge is extracted from the infinitesimal-α logarithm of a normalized correlator containing a spherical symmetry defect and charged insertions with unit linking number. Breaking is diagnosed when the charge becomes approximately zero at a short-distance scale.

The construction imports IFS production, stress-tensor, lifetime, and effective-fluid results, motivated by the dilaton-gradient modification of the worldsheet Virasoro constraints. These ingredients enter coupled Friedmann, dilaton, and sourced radiation-continuity equations.

Analytical approximations include ESP stopping dynamics, an IFS slow-roll attractor, scale-factor-dependent competition between positive χ energy and negative decay radiation, an energy-momentum trace relation for dark energy, and a kinetic-to-potential ratio analysis for the final dilaton reversal. Numerical background solutions illustrate the approximations and complete cycles.

Thermodynamic calculations impose f(r+)=0 to express M in terms of the horizon radius, then use TH=f′(r+)/4π, G=M−THS, V=∂M/∂P, U=M−PV, and C=TH(∂S/∂TH). Parameter dependence is illustrated through tables and plots.

Geodesic Lagrangian reduction gives radial equations ṙ²+Veff=E² for photons and ṙ²+Ueff=E² for massive neutral particles, with Veff=L²f/r² and Ueff=(1+L²/r²)f. An inverse-radius substitution u=1/r produces the photon orbit equation.

Circular photon orbits are determined from E²=Veff and Veff′=0; the paper uses βc=rph/√f(rph) and a Lyapunov-exponent diagnostic involving −Veff″/(2ṫ²). Massive circular-orbit energy, angular momentum, and candidate stability radii are obtained from derivatives of Ueff.

Scalar-vector-tensor and Helmholtz decompositions separate metric perturbations and the electric/magnetic components of δB. Coordinate gauge transformations are derived, a gauge is fixed, and the action is expanded to quadratic order to obtain linear perturbation equations.

The decoupled scalar is treated using conformal-time redefinitions, Bunch-Davies matching, and Bessel/Hankel solutions. Coupled scalar equations are simplified analytically deep inside the horizon; six coupled vector equations are evolved numerically as twelve first-order equations.

Ghosts are diagnosed through eigenvalues of the quadratic kinetic matrix. Gradient behavior is examined using an oscillatory high-momentum ansatz and the resulting sound-speed eigenvalue problem. The minimal model and one non-minimal Ricci-scalar coupling example are considered.

Eleven-dimensional field redefinitions remove Ricci and scalar-curvature terms, and Riemann cyclic identities reduce the input to six curvature contractions. The standard metric KK ansatz then generates the ten-dimensional couplings.

The appendix uses xAct to generate 18,462 covariant candidates, then quotients by total derivatives, leading-action field redefinitions, and Bianchi identities. A local inertial frame and F=dC implement the identities, leaving algebraic relations among coupling variations.

Four-field comparisons linearize curvature and RR fields, transform to momentum space, and impose on-shell transversality and momentum conservation. For six-dimensional S-duality, both actions are extended to general schemes using a 19-term basis and field-redefinition parameters.

The authors report CUDA integration using memory reduction, warps, shared memory and thread synchronization; dynamical parallelism and stream techniques are used to obtain scalar-field versus horizon-radius relations.
They analyze the quartic horizon discriminant, solve g(rh)=0 for the mass, calculate Hawking temperature, and impose ∂P/∂v=∂²P/∂v²=0 to obtain thermodynamic critical curves.

The authors expand the supergravity scalar potential around small displacements of heavy symmetry-breaking fields and calculate slow-roll observables. For SO(10), they also numerically solve gauge-invariant scalar and tensor fluctuation equations to obtain primordial power spectra, including reheating-dependent pivot e-folds.

SU(5) phenomenology combines renormalization-group evolution and GUT threshold matching with soft-breaking boundary conditions, relic-density adjustments, Higgs-mass calculations, and dimension-five or dimension-six proton-decay predictions. The analysis compares CMSSM-like and pure gravity mediation (PGM) examples.

Worldsheet variational analysis replaces the usual measure with a density built from two scalar fields and introduces an auxiliary Abelian gauge field. A bulk-scalar-induced conserved current changes the tension. Special conformal transformations generate the paired flat metrics used in the braneworld examples.

The argument combines imported injectivity-radius, arithmeticity and superrigidity results with dressed charges v = ρ(gϕ⁻¹)q. Weight decompositions determine exponential scaling; invariant-polynomial mass expansions and convex separation connect this scaling to physical towers and hull extrema.

Cartan and Langlands decompositions, restricted roots, horospherical coordinates and reduction by Siegel sets organize geodesics and cusps. Rational weight-space bases provide infinitely many lattice points in fastest-decaying subspaces.

Imported tetrad and spin-connection formalism describes spin transport through successive local Lorentz transformations and Wigner rotations. A time-ordered exponential integrates the spin evolution; the circular setup reduces it to a rotation generated by σ_y.

Use V_eff=V+ρF to determine density-dependent minima and masses, expand F and V about the ambient minimum, and insert the coefficients into imported screened PPN expressions for G(ε), γ(ε) and β(ε). Compute CHSH expectations and scan screening-to-GR rotation ratios against adopted constraints.
Use a pure-tension brane action, induced-metric pullbacks and a Wess–Zumino charge coupling; expand in brane displacement and dimensionally reduce the bulk flux and brane terms.

Parent actions impose form-field exactness with Lagrange multipliers. Integrating different fields gives scalar/two-form duality or eliminates the four-form field strength to obtain a quadratic scalar potential; the massless Gaussian duality is local and boundary-sensitive.

Gauge-fix the PST M5-brane formulation, perform double-dimensional reduction on a two-torus, and dualize the surviving two-form. Kaluza–Klein identifications and bulk supergravity terms supply the D3 interpretation and three-form kinetic term.

Expand the Kähler metric, connection and curvature around the stabilized slice, project quartic coefficients along the goldstino direction, derive the dominant imaginary-field mass matrix, and solve quadratic stationary equations to estimate field deviations.

Factor W into an exponential phase and a holomorphic function, or move that phase into a linear term in K by a super-Weyl–Kähler transformation. Substitute representative superpotentials and evaluate their potentials in the ideal imaginary-field stabilization limit.
Add V_AMSB = m(φi∂iW − 3W) + c.c., minimize the moduli potential, and expand scalar kinetic terms to normalize the axion. Discrete anomalies and charges classify the allowed PQ-violating operators.

Follow a D-flat Higgs direction to pure Sp(4) super-Yang–Mills; match gauge couplings and use gaugino condensation to obtain W = [Λ10^23/(Pf A · Pf(AF̄F̄))]^(1/3). An overall coefficient is absorbed into Λ10.

Background-field Feynman-graph power counting tracks derivative order, loops, external legs, and scales M, Mp, f, v. Dimensional regularization and graph identities organize the estimates; explicit higher-dimensional solutions and flux quantization illustrate back-reaction.

Integrate out heavy fields in the path integral, expand the Wilson action locally to finite order in inverse heavy masses, and use Weyl and field redefinitions to organize the scalar–gravity theory in Einstein frame.

Compute leading slow-roll scalar and tensor spectra and derive ns, nt, and r using the modified H(ρ), including d(3H²)/dρ. The adopted tensor spectrum is Δt²=2H²/π², with nonminimal effects entering through H at this order.

Numerically evolve {ϕ,ϕ̇,H,R} using the modified Friedmann and continuity equations, with dN=Hdt. Initial slow-roll field data determine the initial density, Hubble rate, and curvature. Inflation ends when ε=−Ḣ/H² reaches unity or potential domination fails.

Analyze homogeneous de Sitter stability by rewriting the higher-order equation as a first-order system in {H,Ḣ,Ḧ} and examining Jacobian eigenvalues. The authors also relate the sign requirement to a Dolgov–Kawasaki-type stability condition.

Use a Jordan-to-Einstein metric transformation followed by scalar-field redefinition to obtain canonical variables. The review emphasizes that completing the theory with matter requires tracking the induced matter–inflaton interactions.
Illustrate potential flattening by allowing a sufficiently heavy scalar χ to track its instantaneous minimum in V(ϕ,χ)=ϕ²χ²+m²(χ−χ0)². The reviewed effective trajectory has V=m²χ0²ϕ²/(ϕ²+m²).

Canonicalize kinetic poles and expand the resulting potential near its plateau. For T-models, ϕ=√(6α)tanh[φ/√(6α)]; the leading exponential coefficient can be absorbed into a field shift, explaining the asymptotic independence from many potential details.

Solve autonomous fixed-point equations, impose reality/Friedmann and underlying field-function consistency conditions, and classify stability using Jacobian eigenvalues. Non-hyperbolic cases require nonlinear centre-manifold analysis when nonzero eigenvalues do not already imply instability.

Introduce separate normalized axion velocity x1 and kinetic-energy variable xf, together with yf=y1/f. This separates coupling behavior from axion motion and removes problematic ratios near xf=0 while preserving the linear structure needed for stability analysis.

The review organizes conjectural evidence into surveys of understood string vacua, low-energy quantum-gravity arguments involving black holes and holography, and microscopic arguments. Agreement among these approaches is an aspiration, not a general proof.

Explicit mathematical tools discussed include moduli-space distances obtained from metric variations of the higher-dimensional Einstein–Hilbert action, domain-wall tension as a quasi-distance, covariant scalar equations and Friedmann evolution.

The paper reviews imported finite-temperature free-energy and form-factor-bootstrap motivations for vacuum energy, integrates an assumed one-loop beta function, and solves modified cosmological equations: explicitly for pure vacuum energy and implicitly through erfi in a matter-dominated approximation.

A heuristic gravitational Casimir construction differentiates vacuum energy with respect to a spherical boundary, introduces an inertial mass, imposes time-independent vacuum density, and matches the resulting expansion equations to Friedmann equations in arbitrary spatial dimension.

Compute degree-one twisted bordism through commutator bounding arguments, James/twisted Atiyah–Hirzebruch spectral sequences, and relative Adams spectral sequences. The Adams calculation uses 2-completion, supplemented by odd-primary information from oriented bordism and H1.

Construct continuous covers using maximal compact subgroups and their fundamental groups, then pull back to arithmetic U-duality groups. Include reflections through semidirect products; use Lyndon–Hochschild–Serre spectral sequences to determine relevant Abelianizations.

Uses subgroup-counting bounds up to conjugacy to test permutation-orbifold rarity. Direct and wreath products construct transitive oligomorphic families; ordered-factorization asymptotics estimate how many constructions are available.

Constructs the ensemble using equal isolated-theory weights and the Zamolodchikov metric with stated conformal-manifold volume factors. Minimal-model accumulation sequences and their tensor products provide recursive upper bounds on central-charge spacing.

Evolve separate power-law Genesis, non-power-law Genesis, transition and inflation regimes. During the transition, solve the algebraic lapse constraint using its largest positive real root and numerically evolve H. Switch to cosmic-time scalar evolution when the ADM lapse becomes small.

Assess quadratic perturbations through GS, FS, GT and FT. Compute observables using imported slow-variation formulas ns=1−2ϵH−δF−ηs−s and r=16uSϵs. Expand late-time corrections, canonically normalize the scalar and express the approximate result as a potential or f(R) theory.

Construct the interpolation in unitary-gauge ADM variables, with A3=0 and A4=−B4. Auxiliary functions satisfy f→−ct and U→0 in the past, and f→1 and U→1 in the future; they interpolate the effective gravitational coupling and suppress Genesis terms.

Impose the measured zero-mode mass-squared differences to determine two couplings from the remaining parameters. Coupling positivity and the requirement that the prescribed mass be the smallest root impose additional consistency conditions.

Compute the differential spectrum by summing phase-space factors weighted by |Uei Li0n|². In the large-bulk-mass regime, replace the KK sum by an integral in n/|c̄| and use mixing unitarity to normalize the zero-mode contribution.
